I stopped asking people to use my tools and started watching them instead. The feedback got ten times better and it stopped being about taste.

Asking produces opinions. People are polite and they give you reasonable suggestions that you then spend a weekend implementing because it sounds plausible.

I have one rule for buying tools and it has saved me more than any discount ever did.

If I can't start using it in fifteen minutes on a real task, I close the tab. Not because a learning curve is bad, and not because I'm impatient, but because I have a drawer full of things I intended to learn later. Later doesn't come. There's always a different afternoon.

The tools that survived on my machine all had the same quality. That's the test. I did something useful in the first quarter of an hour, however small. That tiny win is what makes you come back tomorrow.

Anything that asks for a day of setup before the first win is asking me to trust it on faith. I have no faith left to allocate. I have given it away too many times.

This applies to free things too. Free isn't the same as cheap if it costs a weekend. The cost of a tool isn't the price. It's the price plus the days before it does anything.

The first hour of building is the hour I used to waste and now it's the most valuable.

I used to open the editor and start typing. Ninety minutes later I would have a shape I didn't want and a decision I had made accidentally by typing it out.

Now I sit with a notebook for the first hour. What is the input. What is the output. Where does it live. What breaks first.

It feels like nothing is happening. That's the whole problem with it. Procrastination and design look identical from the outside and only one of them is useful. The test I use to tell them apart. If I'm writing down decisions, it's design. If I'm reading about unrelated things, it's procrastination.

I get that hour back because decisions made on paper cost nothing to change. Decisions encoded in forty files cost a weekend. I still get it wrong. But the ratio has flipped and most of my rework disappeared, which is a strange thing to be able to say about rework.

The most useful thing I learned from physics wasn't a fact. It was a habit of asking what would change my mind.

Good experimental design has that built in. You state the result in advance and you state what would make it false. Otherwise the data gets interpreted to fit whatever you already believed.

I started doing the same thing with my own opinions about technology. What evidence would make me stop believing this. The answer is uncomfortable because I have to admit that nothing I have seen could do it.

That's the tell. If no possible observation would change your position, you aren't holding a belief, you're holding an identity. I have found this in my own work constantly. I was certain one tool was better until I wrote down what would prove me wrong, and then I noticed I had never tested the thing I was certain about.

Stating the test in advance is cheap. Skipping it costs years.

I write every post about my work as if my future employer is reading it, which changed what I write.

That sounds like a constraint and it turned out to be a good filter. It removes the performance. No dunking on tools I didn't like. No absolute claims about industries I have never worked in. No pretending to know what I don't know. That's the filter.

I deleted a cron job this week and nobody noticed for five days. That's the part that bothers me more than the outage did.

I've read more code than I've written this year. That surprised me.

The models generate the first draft. I read it, and most of my time goes into that read, not into typing. I check whether the error path is real. Whether the naming lies about what the function does. Whether a retry can fire a side effect twice.

My inference bill dropped from three hundred and forty dollars to eleven dollars and I lost no speed. The trick wasn't a cheaper model. It was deciding which calls deserve the good one.

I send a model a lot of boring work. Reformatting, extraction, short classification, tidying a config. A small local model handles that fine. A few calls a day need real reasoning, and those still go to the expensive one.

I put the routing in about sixty lines of Python. It looks at the task name, not the text. If the task is one of the nine on the cheap list, it goes local. Otherwise it goes out.

I got one part wrong first. I routed on prompt length. Long doesn't mean hard. A long extraction is easy. A two line question about a subtle tradeoff is not.

Classify your own calls before you optimise them. I was paying frontier prices for filler work for most of a year.

I stopped typing prompts and started talking to them. My commits got better.

I get terse when I type. I write the shortest possible instruction and then I'm annoyed when the model fills the gaps with something I didn't want. Talking takes ninety seconds. It produces a paragraph with the constraints inside it.

I tested a restore for the first time in two years and the backup was broken. The backup job had been reporting success the whole time.

It copied the database file while the writer was still writing. Most nights that produced a file that opened fine. The damaged cases ran about one in twelve, and I never noticed because I never opened one.

I fixed it in a way that feels too simple to mention. Stop the writer. Copy the file. Start the writer. Thirty seconds of downtime at four in the morning.

I learned something bigger than the bug. A success message from a backup job means nothing. A file of the right size in the right place proves nothing either. The one piece of evidence is a restore you did yourself.

So I restore into a scratch directory once a week. Four minutes. Once a week. It's the least enjoyable four minutes in my week and I'm keeping it.

The best review I got this year came on a forty line change. My worst came on a nine hundred line one.

That forty line change got four comments, all specific, all about the thing I was unsure of. The nine hundred line one got approved in eleven minutes with a thumbs up. Nobody read it. I know because it shipped a bug that a careful reader would have caught in five minutes.

Size is the review. If a change is small enough, a person can hold the whole thing in their head and tell you what's wrong with it. Past that, they can tell you it looks fine.

So I split. Every commit is one idea. Sometimes that's four commits for what I used to call one change. I've stopped caring about looking efficient.

Small changes get read. Big ones get signed. I'd rather write four commits that get read than one that gets approved.

I renamed eleven functions this week and changed no behaviour at all. The code is better for it and I can say why.

My old names described how the thing worked. processRows, handleEvent, doSync. The new names say what they're for. dropRowsOutsideWindow, queueEventForRetry, pushLocalChangesToRemote.

That difference matters at three in the morning when you're reading a stack trace. A name that says what a function is for tells you whether it should have been called here at all. A name that says what it does tells you nothing about that.

The halfway version is worse than either. A name like processAndValidateRows is two jobs wearing one coat. If you can't name it in a few words, it's doing more than one thing.

I treat naming as design. It's the cheapest design tool I have. Fix the name and the function tends to get smaller too, because the extra job the bad name was hiding has nowhere left to sit.

I tracked my own estimates for a quarter. I was wrong by about half on almost everything, and always in the same direction.

The pattern is consistent. I estimate the writing. I forget the four other things, which are finding the code, reading it, running it, and waiting for something to build. Writing is maybe a third of the actual work.

The other thing I get wrong is interruption rate. Roughly one job in three turns out to depend on something I don't control, and that dependency adds a day I never planned for.

What fixed it wasn't being smarter. I now double my gut number and add a day. It sounds like a joke. It's been right eleven times out of twelve.

An estimate isn't a prediction. It's a number you say out loud so someone else can plan. I'd rather give a big honest number than a small one I'll miss.

I spent an afternoon writing down how a system works and it saved me two days the following week.

I built that system myself. Six weeks later I couldn't remember why the retry limit is seven, or which of the two config files wins. Those answers lived in my head, and my head had moved on.

What I wrote is one page. What it does, the two entry points, the three things that will bite you. No diagrams. No architecture section. Nothing that was true six months ago and isn't now.

The test I used was simple. Could someone else start work tomorrow with just this page. If not, it's missing something I know and haven't written down.

People skip it because writing feels like not building. Then they spend two days rediscovering what they already knew, and those two days feel like work, so nobody counts them against the page that was never written.

I did my best work this year between eleven at night and two in the morning and I'm not sure that's a good thing.

My output is real. Fewer interruptions, better focus, and I'll finish a hard problem in that window that I'd have abandoned by four in the afternoon. What I write at that hour tends to be the code I keep.

My cost is real too. My next morning is gone. Not slow, gone. Twice this year I made a call at two in the morning that I reversed the next day, which is a day spent twice.

I leave a note for the morning now. Anything I'm unsure about gets written down instead of acted on. My morning self reads it with fresh eyes and disagrees about half the time.

Nights are where I do the work. Mornings are where I decide whether to keep it, and the mornings have been right about twice as often as the nights.

A listing near me has been on the market for nine months and dropped its price three times. The third drop is the interesting one.

The first two were small. Two percent, then two percent again, which is what you do when you're hoping rather than selling. The third was fifteen percent and it landed four days after a similar unit closed two streets over.

I think that's the whole story in housing. Prices don't move on average data. They move when a neighbour's identical unit sells and the number becomes public.

Sellers don't price against the market. They price against the last comparable sale they can see. One transaction can reset a street.

I'd rather watch individual sales than any index. Charts average away the thing that decides a price. I've watched three streets here for two years, and each time the number moved, it moved because of one closing, not because of a trend.

A result I read this week tightened the uncertainty on how fast the universe is expanding and made the disagreement worse. That's an odd thing for a telescope to do. Odd and useful.

I'd expected the measurement to settle a fight between two ways of getting the same number. One method uses the early universe. The other uses nearby stars. They disagree by more than the errors allow, and the new data didn't close the gap.

When better instruments make a discrepancy sharper instead of softer, that's not a mistake. It's a hint that something in the model is missing. Nobody knows what yet.

I like results like this. Most weeks the answer is that the earlier number was noisy. Some weeks the answer is that we don't understand the universe as well as we thought, and this was one of those weeks.

Being wrong in a precise way is progress. Being vague is not.

I wore a cheap step tracker for a month and the one number that changed my behaviour was the one I wasn't tracking. Sleep, not steps.

I treat the step number as a vanity metric. It hits ten thousand on any normal day, and going from six to nine thousand changed nothing I could feel. The sleep number did. Anything under six hours and the next day is worse, in what I ship and in how long everything takes.

The tracker wasn't the useful part. I'd been told the same thing for years. Seeing the pattern twice in my own week is what made it land.

Data changes behaviour when it's your data. Someone else's averages are just advice.

I protect the first two hours of the day now. Two hours. Not for morality. Because the tracker made the cost visible, and a cost you can see is a cost you stop paying.

A studio I follow spent four years on a game and shipped it into a market that had moved twice while they built. Nobody there did anything wrong.

The genre got crowded in year two. A platform shift landed in year three. The thing they designed around was old by launch, and the reviews said so, and the reviews were fair. Nothing broke. The market moved.

I'd call that the trap in anything with a long lead time. You commit to a design when you know the least, and you're judged on it when you know the most.

Short cycles aren't just cheaper. They let you make the decision later, with more information in hand.

I've started breaking my own work into four week pieces for the same reason. Not because I ship more. Because I decide later, and the later decision gets made by someone holding a month more information than the person who started.

I replaced a meeting with a document last month and the decision got made in nine minutes instead of fifty. Nobody has asked for the meeting back.

What the document does that the meeting didn't is let people disagree in writing, with time to think. In the meeting, the first person to speak set the frame and everyone else reacted to it. In the document, three people replied with the same objection, and that's what made it clear the objection was real.

I kept twenty minutes for the genuine disagreement that a document can't resolve. I cut the other thirty.

Not every meeting is waste. Status meetings are. Most of what I used to call alignment was people reading something for the first time together, in a room, at speed.

Read it before you meet. Then meet about the part that's still open, which has been about twenty minutes of every meeting I've run since.

I keep a note of the things that made me faster this year and not one of them is a new model. That surprised me when I wrote it down.

My list has four items. Writing the acceptance criteria before starting. Running the tests before I believe a change. Keeping changes small enough to read. And having a backup I've restored from by hand.

Those four are boring. None of them is clever. Each one has saved me days. The model upgrades have saved me hours, and the hours are in typing.

I'm not saying the tools don't matter. I use them all day. What changed my output was process, and process is the part nobody wants to discuss because it doesn't demo well.

If you're hunting for the next multiplier, check whether you've done the boring four first. Most people haven't. I hadn't until March, and the fourth one is the one that saved the data.

I have a test that has passed on every run for two years and it has never once been able to fail. I caught it while reading it for another reason.

It asserts that a list is not empty after a call that always returns a fixed list of four items. The four items come from a constant defined two files up. Nothing in the test path can change them.

So it's decoration. It reports green, it makes the suite look better, and it would keep passing if the function it tests were deleted and replaced with a stub.

I deleted it and wrote two tests that can fail. One feeds a bad input and expects a typed error. The other checks that the output ordering is stable. Both of those would have caught a real bug I shipped in August.

The lesson wasn't about that test. It was that I'd never asked any of my tests a simple question. What would have to break for this to go red. I found four more like it that afternoon. Four. All green, all doing nothing.

A job of mine ran an hour late for six weeks and I blamed the scheduler. It was me. I wrote the time in the wrong time zone.

I had the hour hardcoded as nine. My server keeps its own clock, and that clock isn't mine. Its nine is five in the morning where I live, so the report was always sitting there by the time I looked.

What broke was the email. A reader in a different country started getting it overnight instead of at breakfast, and asked me why. That question is the only reason I found it.

The fix took four lines. Store the zone with the time. Set the schedule in one place. Never write a bare hour again, because a bare hour is a promise you can't keep.

Six weeks of a job running at the wrong time and the system never complained. Cron does what you tell it. It just doesn't know what you meant. I keep the zone in the config now, written once.

I ran everything in a container for a month and the thing I gained wasn't reproducibility. It was the freedom to break my machine.

Cache invalidation has cost me more time this year than any other class of bug and I've stopped being smug about it.

The failures all look the same from the outside. A page shows yesterday's number. Someone tells me the data is wrong. I check the database, the data is right, and I spend twenty minutes discovering that a value from this morning is sitting in a layer I forgot existed.

What fixed it wasn't a clever scheme. I made the cached things short lived. Fifteen seconds instead of an hour. Nobody has noticed the extra load and the wrong number complaints stopped.

The next thing was naming. Every cached key now says what it holds and when it expires. When I read a stack trace at two in the morning I can tell whether I'm looking at a cache read or a database read.

Fast is nice. Correct and fast is the job.

I integrated a third party API in an afternoon and spent the next three weeks paying for how I did it.

I called it inline. Every request to my service that needed a quote made a live call to theirs. It worked, it was simple, and it was the wrong shape from the first line.

Their rate limit hit on the eighth day. My retry logic made it worse, because it retried the failures that were caused by retrying. Then their outage became my outage, and I had a page full of errors I couldn't fix.

What I should have done takes an extra hour. Store the last good answer, serve from that when the call fails, and put the call behind a queue with a budget.

The lesson generalises. Anything you don't control will fail, and the question is whether it takes you with it. Design the failure on day one, not in week three. I write the timeout first now. Then the fallback. Then the happy path.

I fixed a bug this week with a print statement after an hour of reading code, and I want to defend the print statement.

I'd been staring at a function and building a theory about which branch ran. The theory was wrong, and every minute I spent on it was spent making it more detailed rather than checking it.

Then I added one line that printed the value at the top and the branch it took. The output was on screen in nine seconds and the bug was obvious. The branch I was sure about never ran.

What I'd done wrong was reasoning instead of measuring. A theory about runtime behaviour is cheap to hold and expensive to be wrong about, and the check is one line.

I do this earlier now. Guess, then print, then read. If the print disagrees with the guess, the print is right. One line. Nine seconds. Tools don't have to be clever to be useful.

I write commit messages for myself six months from now, and that framing fixed a habit I'd had for years.

My old messages were useless. Fixed bug. Update config. They record that something happened and nothing about why, so the log reads like a list of events with the reasons deleted.

A database migration of mine locked a table for eleven minutes during peak traffic and I had the plan that caused it on a sticky note.

The change added one column. On my laptop it took a fraction of a second. On production, with a few million rows and a running workload, the same statement held a lock the whole time.

What saved me was a colleague asking one question before I ran it. Have you tried it on a copy with production sizes. I hadn't. That question was worth more than the review of the SQL, which looked fine.

I ran it again on a copy, saw the eleven minutes, and split it into three steps that each hold a lock for under a second. Same end state, no outage.

Test the migration on data that looks like the real thing. A fast laptop isn't evidence. A green test suite isn't evidence either. I copy production into a scratch database now, every time.

I read a book about engineering failures and it changed what I look for when I review my own work.

The pattern in most of the case studies isn't a bad engineer. It's a normal person in a place where one small omission was invisible until something else went wrong. Nobody there was careless in an interesting way.

That shifted my attention from the code to the joints. Where does this assume something else will be true. What happens if that assumption is false at three in the morning on a Sunday.

So I look for the boundaries. The default case, the empty case, the case where the network is up but slow. Those are the places where the small omission lives.

I don't review for style much any more. I ask what would have to be true for this to be safe, then check whether that thing is written down somewhere. Empty input. Slow network. Two users at once. Those three catch most of it.

A visual bug sat in my product for two months and nobody reported it because every person who saw it assumed they'd broken it themselves.

The button was misaligned on one screen size. Not hidden, not broken. Just off by about eight pixels at one width, and it looked like something you'd done with your zoom level.

I found it when I resized a window while showing the product to someone. I fixed it in a minute. What interested me is that about forty people had seen it and not one typed a message.

The reason is that a small cosmetic flaw looks like your own mistake. A broken flow looks like theirs. People report the second kind and absorb the first kind.

Since then I take my own screenshots at four widths before shipping. Four widths. Two minutes. The bugs nobody reports are the ones that live longest. It's the cheapest test I run.

A heat pump question from a friend sent me into the grid data for a weekend and the answer wasn't about the heat pump.

People worry that electrifying heating overloads the network. On the annual numbers it doesn't. Extra winter demand is smaller than the summer peak the wires were built for. I found that part reassuring and it isn't the hard part.

Timing is the hard part. Every heat pump pulls hard in the same cold hours, and local distribution equipment is sized for a street, not a country. Averaged over a year it's fine. Between five and eight in the evening it isn't.

So the useful fixes are dull. Better insulation. A thermostat that shifts load by an hour. A meter that pays you to charge the car later.

I spent about two days reading transformer and feeder reports to get this far. I still think the average number and the street reality disagreeing is the interesting part, and the street is where people live.

The fastest I've ever learned a tool was the week I had to use it to ship something for someone else, and it wasn't close.

A city near me removed a few hundred parking spaces and the shops on that street report more revenue, which is the least intuitive result in urban planning.

The mechanism is simpler than it sounds. A parking space moves about two people an hour past a shop front. A bus stop, a bike rack and a wider pavement move far more, and people on foot stop more often than people driving past looking for a space.

The fight about it was never about the numbers. It was about who the street is for, and that question is uncomfortable enough that people argue about parking instead.

What I take from it is that the loudest objection tends not to be the real objection. Parking is measurable. Changing who a place belongs to isn't. Both are real.

I see the same shape in software all the time. I've watched a team argue for a month about a feature. What they disagreed about was who the product is for.

A study on remote work landed on my desk and the finding that mattered was about who gets promoted, not who gets work done.

Output was fine. Measured by almost any definition, the remote group produced as much and often more. What differed was the informal record, the conversations that happen in the gaps and shape who gets handed the interesting job in eighteen months.

I stood at my desk for a month and the useful change had nothing to do with posture. It was the two minutes of standing still that came with it.

A podcast about a company shutting down spent an hour on the last two weeks and about four minutes on the eight years before it, which is the standard ratio and the wrong way round.

I stopped incrementing my version numbers for a while and the mess it made has changed how I name releases.

I'd been bumping the patch digit for anything, so every version looked equally important. Six releases all ending in a different third digit, and no way to tell from the name whether one of them fixed a data loss bug or a typo.

Now the number answers one question. Does the data need a migration. If it does, the first digit goes up. If it doesn't and there are behaviour changes, the second goes up. Otherwise the third moves.

Nobody outside my own projects reads these numbers, which is the point. They're for me at two in the morning when something broke and I need to know whether rolling back is safe.

A version is a promise about compatibility. If it promises nothing, it's decoration with a dot in it.

A regex took me an hour and a half this week and about forty minutes of that was spent convinced I understood it, which is a specific way to waste time.

I was matching a pattern I'd written two years ago. I read it, formed a theory about what it does, and then tested against my theory instead of against the string. Each failure made my theory more elaborate.

What broke the loop was printing the string with its whitespace made visible. There was a trailing space. The regex was right. My assumption about the input was wrong and had been for forty minutes.

I've started doing that first now. Show me the input before I touch the pattern. Most regex bugs I've had this year were never regex bugs.

The general version of the lesson is the one that keeps costing me. Verify the input, not the logic, and do it before you have a theory worth defending.

I wrote a page of notes for a system I'm going to forget, and the test of whether it works is whether I can restore the thing from a cold start without reading any code.

Write the restart page. Not the architecture page. The one you need when something is down.

I gave myself one task a day for a week and finished more than I do in a normal fortnight, which says something unpleasant about a normal fortnight.

The rule was simple. Pick the one thing that would make the week better, write it down at nine, and don't start anything else until it's done or the day is over.

Two of the five days produced nothing on the main task, because something else was on fire. That's the honest part. On the other three I finished early and had the afternoon for whatever the fire was.

What I've noticed in a normal week is that I start about nine things, finish four, and spend the difference in a low hum of guilt about the other five. That hum is what the rule removes.

I write one task down before anything else. It's the least clever productivity system I've used. It's also the first one I've kept. Six weeks now.

I spent two hours deleting code today. That was my whole afternoon.

Most teams don't have a performance problem. They've got a measurement problem. I've watched this happen four separate times now. Someone says the app feels slow. Everyone nods. Then a week of optimization starts with no baseline, no trace, nothing but a feeling in the room.

The fix is boring. Time one real user action from click to paint. Write the number down. Do it again after every change. That single number settles more arguments than any architecture debate I've sat through.

What surprised me was how often the number came back fine. The complaint was real, the slowness wasn't. Users were describing confusion as slowness, and no profiler was ever going to find that.

So the first question is always the same. Where's the number. Not what do you think is slow. I ask it in the meeting now, not a week later. That question has ended four arguments this quarter. I ask it before anyone opens a profiler.

The hardest part of shipping AI features isn't the model. It's the failure mode. A model that's wrong eight percent of the time isn't a model with an eight percent bug. It's a product where the user has to check every answer, and that changes the whole interface.

I built a summarizer that was accurate most of the time. Fast, cheap, good on clean input. Then a customer pasted a scanned invoice with a coffee stain on it. The output was fluent nonsense. Nothing crashed. Nothing warned. It just sounded confident and was wrong.

That's the trap. Silent wrongness is worse than an error message, because an error gets handled and silent wrongness gets trusted. I've watched a team ship both and the quiet one caused every support call.

Now the output carries its evidence. The answer comes with the sentence it came from, so a reader can check in two seconds. Accuracy barely moved. Trust moved a lot, and that's the thing I needed. I test for that before I ship anything.

A code review that takes forty minutes isn't a thorough review. It's usually a review that started too late. I noticed this on my own pull requests before I noticed it in anyone else's.

A small diff gets read line by line. A large diff gets skimmed, approved, and trusted. That's backwards, and everyone who's shipped for a few years knows it. The large change is exactly the one that needed attention.

The real cost isn't the review though. It's that nobody can tell you what a two thousand line change did three months later. Not the author either, and I've been that author twice.

So I split things now. Same work, landed in pieces, each piece readable in ten minutes. It takes longer to merge and much less time to understand. I haven't regretted a single split yet. Ten minutes is my limit for a real read. Past that I'm scrolling. Ten minutes. That's my cap. A diff I can't finish reading in ten minutes goes back with a request to split it, and I've never once regretted sending it back. I ask for the split every time.

Estimates aren't for the person asking. They're for you. When a founder asks how long something takes, they want to know if it can land this month. The number is a proxy. I spent years treating the proxy as the real question and getting it wrong.

The honest answer is a range with a wide tail, because the tail is where the surprises live. Integration turns out to need a new webhook. The API paging is broken. Someone's field name has a space in it.

So I answer with three things now. What I know, what I don't know, and what I'll know by Friday. That third one has ended more uncomfortable conversations than any estimate I've ever given.

Nobody's pushed back on it. They wanted to stop guessing, and that's all. I could've saved myself two years of false confidence by saying it sooner. I'd rather hand over a range than a promise.

Logs that nobody reads are the same as no logs. I learned this during an incident where everything got recorded and nothing could be found. Four services, one timestamp format, no request id anywhere.

We spent the first twenty minutes of that outage grepping. Not fixing. Grepping, while a customer waited on the other end of a support thread.

The change was small. One identifier that follows a request through every service, logged on every line. It costs almost nothing to add and it turns an outage from an archaeology project into a lookup.

I still think the discipline matters more than the tool. A log line should answer who, what, and which request. If it answers none of those, it's noise you're paying to store. That advice came from a person who'd been on call for a decade, and it's been right every time since. That's the whole fix. One field.

Every onboarding flow I've built has been one step too long. I know this from a number I used to ignore. The drop between step two and step three, always the biggest cliff on the chart.

The most underrated engineering skill is reading code you didn't write. Interviews test whether you can produce, and almost nothing tests whether you can understand. Yet that's where the hours go.

I joined a codebase once with a payment retry loop written by someone who'd left. No comments, no tests, two variables named data. I spent three days before I could change one conditional without fear.

Naming things badly is a decision you make once and pay for every week. I renamed a function last month and twelve call sites got clearer. It took an hour, and I'd put it off for a year because it felt cosmetic.

It wasn't cosmetic. The old name described what the function used to do two designs ago. Every time someone read it they held a slightly wrong model of the system. Twelve people, dozens of reads, one wrong idea repeated.

The cost is invisible because no single moment feels expensive. Churn shows up as things taking longer than they should, and nobody can point at the cause.

Names are cheap to fix. Misreads aren't. So I treat a misleading name as a bug now. I renamed it in an hour. The old name described a version of the function that stopped existing two designs ago, and every reader paid for that gap out of their own time. It goes in the same list, with the same priority, and it gets fixed while the file is open. Clean names and fast code are the same problem wearing different clothes.

Adding an index fixed a query that had been slow for six months. Six months of a page that took three seconds, and everyone had accepted it. Nobody filed the bug because nobody remembered the page being faster.

That's how performance debt works. It has no owner because it has no incident. The page is slow, people work around it, and the workaround becomes the normal way of using the product.

The fix took eleven minutes. I read the query plan, saw a sequential scan, added one index, and the page went to ninety milliseconds. Eleven minutes. I should have looked a year ago. The page had been loading in three seconds for six months and everyone had built a habit around it without ever filing a ticket.

So I keep a list of every place the product feels heavy. No budget, no ticket, just a list I read once a month. One item turns out to be cheap. That list has done more for retention than any feature I shipped this year.

There's a specific kind of tired that comes from holding a problem in your head for too long. It isn't the same as being busy. I hit it around hour six of debugging and I used to push through it, which is how I produced my worst work.

The tell is when you start trying variations instead of forming a hypothesis. Change a line, run it, change it back. That loop feels productive and it's gambling with a keyboard.

What works is leaving. Not a break of ten minutes. Stop for real, go outside, do something else for two hours. Twice this year the answer arrived before I sat back down, and once it arrived while I was washing dishes.

A flaky test is worse than no test. No test tells you the truth: this part is unprotected. A flaky test tells you the code is broken, then tells you it's fine, then fails your release on a Friday afternoon.

I had one that failed about one run in nine. It passed locally every time. My instinct was to rerun and merge, and for two months that's what we did.

Then I read the failure instead of rerunning it. A test that assumed a list had a stable order, against a query with no order clause. The test was right to be flaky. The code had a real bug that only showed up under load, and it had been in production the whole time.

Retrying is how you turn a signal into noise. Quarantine the test, read the failure, fix the assumption. Mine took an afternoon and removed a class of bug we'd been chasing for months. Flakiness is almost never the test being dramatic. Two months of reruns. Gone. I quarantine flaky tests now. I don't rerun them.

Meetings are how a small team becomes a slow one by accident. Nobody decides to add four hours of standing calls. It happens one invitation at a time, each one justified, until the calendar has no room left to think in.

Context switching was the number that surprised me. A thirty minute meeting in the middle of a morning doesn't cost thirty minutes. It costs the hour before it, where you avoid starting something big because you'll be interrupted.

The best pricing decision I made was raising the price. I spent four months at the low number because it felt safer, and every month the support load reminded me who I was attracting.

Low prices don't filter out hard customers. They invite them. At nine dollars a month, a person emails you seven times about a rounding error and expects a call. At ninety, they use the tool and ask for features.

I lost about a third of the accounts and made more money the following month. The work per account fell instead of rising, which is the part I didn't expect.

What I got wrong for years was treating price as a discount to overcome. It's a promise about who you serve. Deploys on Friday are fine. What isn't fine is a deploy nobody can roll back. The fear people have about a Friday release is really a fear about the last ten minutes of the process, which is the least rehearsed part.

I worked on a team where a release took forty minutes of manual steps and nobody had done a rollback in a year. We were afraid of the calendar, not the software.

The change was rehearsing the rollback once a quarter on a Tuesday. Nothing else. Once you've watched yourself go backwards safely, going forwards stops being scary.

We shipped on Friday after that when something was ready. Not because we were bold. Because we'd already practiced the failure. If a release scares you, the problem isn't the day. It's that you've never seen the undo. I practice the undo once a quarter. The day stops mattering after that.

The feature nobody asked for is the founder's favourite. I've built at least five of them. Each one began with me being annoyed by a user's workflow, which felt like research and was really me solving my own mild frustration.

The tell is easy to miss. I could describe the feature in detail and the customer's problem in one sentence. Depth on the solution, nothing on the problem. That's a warning sign I've learned to respect.

What broke the habit was asking people to show me their last attempt instead of describing their need. Watching someone screen share for five minutes tells you more than twenty interviews, and it costs a lot less time.

Half the features on my list died when I did this. The other half got smaller and shipped faster. Your instinct isn't data. It's a hypothesis that's been sitting in your head long enough to feel like evidence. That's the test.

Caching is the tool I reach for last and should reach for second. I've made the same mistake three times. Reach for a cache because a page is slow, feel clever, and create a class of bug that appears only when the data changes.

The stale read is quiet. Two users see different totals for a minute. Support gets a screenshot nobody can reproduce, because by the time anyone looked the numbers matched again.

What fixed it for me was writing down the invalidation rule before writing the cache. One sentence. When does this value become wrong. If I can't write that sentence, I don't add the cache. I make the query faster instead.

Often the query was the problem the whole time. One missing index, one extra round trip, one loop issuing two hundred small reads. Caching is a shortcut past a problem you haven't looked at yet. One sentence first.

The shortest path to a good product is talking to someone who stopped using it. Not a survey. Not a cancellation reason field. A ten minute call, and the first question is when did you stop opening it.

People are kind and will tell you the tool is great while describing why they left. You have to listen for the tense change. It used to be perfect for this becomes useful information, and it's usually the only real signal in the call.

I called eight churned users last quarter. Six gave me the same answer: it worked, they changed jobs, they never brought it with them. That isn't a product problem and no feature would've saved them.

Two gave me something real. A missing export, a workflow that broke at the second step. Both fixed in a week. Both accounts came back. I ask that question first, before anything else. I ask it on every call now, and it takes thirty seconds. Most exits aren't about your software. The two that are will tell you everything.

Vector databases get recommended for problems a keyword search would solve. I've seen this four times in review now. A search box over eight hundred documents, and the proposal involves embeddings, a new service, and a bill every month.

Eight hundred documents is nothing. Load them into memory at boot, scan them, return the top ten. That runs in single digit milliseconds and adds no dependency.

Embeddings earn their place when the vocabulary mismatch is real. Someone types cheap place to stay and the document says budget accommodation. That gap is worth paying for. A search for annual report over documents titled annual report isn't.

The cost isn't the money either. It's the second system to keep in sync, back up, and reason about during an incident. I measure first now. A keyword scan over eight hundred rows takes minutes to write and costs nothing to run. Boring search first, then measure whether it failed before adding a service you'll maintain for years. Nothing else. The system you add has to be backed up, monitored, upgraded, and explained to whoever is on call at two in the morning. I've watched that bill arrive twice now.

I write the commit message before the code now. Thirty seconds of thinking about what the change does, and the file list shrinks. If I can't describe the change in one line, I've got two changes.

That habit caught a mistake last week. It's paid for itself twice. I started writing, needed the word and, and realised I was fixing a bug inside a feature. Two commits, and one of them reverted a day later without touching the other.

Commit messages are the documentation that survives. The wiki goes stale and the design doc gets archived. The git log stays attached to the exact line that changed and the reason behind it.

One line for what changed. A paragraph for why. One line. Then the why. I write the why for a stranger. The person reading this in six months has none of the context I have right now, and the message is the only thing that travels with the line that changed. That reason is what saves a future afternoon. Six months from now I won't remember the context. The message will, and I'll be glad I wrote it.

Startups die from trying to serve two customers. I watched it happen to a company I worked with. Great tool for solo developers. Then one enterprise pilot arrived and every decision started being made for the pilot.

Pricing got complicated. Onboarding grew a settings page. The roadmap filled with permissions and single sign on. Six months later the solo developers had left because the product they loved had gotten heavier, and the enterprise deal hadn't signed.

Nobody chose that. Each step was rational on its own. The pattern was invisible because it happened one request at a time, and each request came from a person I liked.

The fix isn't saying no to everything. It's writing down who the product is for, in one sentence, and reading that sentence before any significant decision. If the sentence changes, that's allowed. I write that sentence on a sticky note now. It should be a decision, not a drift.

Reading source code taught me more than any course. Not reading documentation. Reading the actual implementation of a library I depended on, at the exact point where my assumptions lived.

I once spent a day convinced a library was buggy. It wasn't. It lazily initialised, and my first call was racing a second one. One function definition explained a whole day of confusion, and I found it in about four minutes once I stopped guessing.

The trick is to read with a question. Open the file, find the function you call, follow the branch that matches your input. You don't need to understand the library. You need to understand the one path your code takes through it.

Do that a few times and you stop being afraid of dependencies. Most of them are smaller than you expect, and the parts that frighten you are usually ten lines. Documentation describes intent. Source describes behavior. When they disagree, believe the source. I read the source first now. I read it with one question in mind, and I stop when I've answered it.

I've stopped adopting new tools the week I hear about them. My laptop holds four abandoned editors, three note apps, and a task manager I paid for twice. Each arrived with a promise of throughput and left with my migration time.

The cost isn't the license. It's that every new tool resets my muscle memory and my system. Two weeks of clumsiness for a small gain, and the tool rarely survives the next shiny thing I see.

So the rule is a ninety day delay. If I still want it after three months, and I can name the specific task it does better, I try it on one project. About one in five passes.

The rest were entertainment. That's fine. I just want to call it what it is instead of calling it productivity. The stack that survives is the boring one you've already learned. I know because I've paid for it twice.

The most useful thing I do each quarter is read my old code without fixing it. Just read, and write down what confused me. No editor open, no urge to tidy up.

Last pass produced eleven notes. Five were about a module whose purpose I couldn't reconstruct. Three were about parameter names that lied. Two were missing reasons for a decision that looks arbitrary now.

Not one of them was a bug. All of them were tax. Every future change to those files starts with a minute of archaeology, and that minute compounds across a team of six.

I fixed four in an afternoon. The module got a header comment saying what it owns. Parameter names got fixed. The arbitrary decision got three lines explaining the constraint that made it. I do this every quarter now. It's the cheapest quality work I know. I keep the notes in the repo where the next person will find them. Reading to understand, not to change, finds things testing never will.

Sleep is the one performance tool that has never failed me. I've tried the timers, the ambient sound, the two monitor setup. None of them moved my output as much as going to bed at the same time for a month.

The difference shows up in the afternoon. Tired, I write more code and understand less of it. I produce volume that has to be reread the next morning, which is negative work with a positive word count.

I measured this badly for years, comparing days by how busy they felt. Busy and productive diverge once you're short on sleep. The busy day is often the one you undo.

So the trade is unglamorous. Less evening output for a better morning. Nobody posts about that. Nearly every bad technical decision I've made came from a depleted brain, and that's a strong enough signal to schedule around. I go to bed first now. Everything else fits around it.

Small teams beat large teams on hard problems and lose on boring ones. That isn't a moral statement, it's arithmetic. Coordination costs grow faster than head count, and the tenth person adds less than the second did.

Where this bites is maintenance. A small team ships a beautiful thing and then has no capacity for the treadmill. Deprecations, certificate renewals, dependency upgrades, the migration that has to happen because a vendor changed a header.

I underestimated that treadmill for years. Every project has one and it takes a steady share of the week regardless of how clever the build is.

So I budget for it now. A line on the plan that says maintenance, separate from features, defended the same way. I've spent three weeks on upgrades this quarter. It never shows up on a feature list. A feature gets applause. The treadmill keeps the lights on, and both of them are the work.

The best code I wrote this year was a deletion. Not a refactor, not a rewrite. I removed a whole subsystem and replaced it with a configuration value.

It existed because two years ago a decision needed to be dynamic. Then the company changed direction and one value was ever used. Four hundred lines, three tests, and a background job nobody monitored, all maintaining a constant.

Deleting it removed a class of incident. That job had failed twice without anyone noticing, because it never mattered.

We talk about building like it's the activity that counts. Noticing that something is no longer needed is rarer and worth more. It takes understanding the whole system well enough to say a piece can go.

It comes from knowing what the system does at the boundaries, and that takes longer to build than the feature itself ever did. Writing the new code was always the easy part. I keep a file called mistakes. Every entry is a decision I got wrong, one paragraph, no moralising. When I started it I worried it would be discouraging. It's been the opposite.

The pattern is what makes it useful. Five entries about the same mistake in different clothes. Underestimating migrations. Believing a demo is a prototype. Trusting an estimate I made while optimistic.

Numbers don't appear in that file. What appears is the state I was in when I decided. Rushed, tired, hoping a customer would like me. Those are the conditions that produce my bad calls, and they repeat far more reliably than any technical circumstance.

So I have two rules for the conditions I recognise fastest. No architecture decisions after four in the afternoon. No promises in the same meeting where someone is upset. I read the file every quarter now, and I add to it after every project. I check it before I start anything new. That's it. Two rules, and the effect has been enormous.

I moved a table with four hundred million rows without taking the site down. It took nine days. The migration itself was fast. The part that took time was proving I could stop and go backwards at any point.

Here's what I'd tell anyone about to try it. Write the new path first and leave it dark. Backfill in small batches. Compare the two outputs for a week. Then flip reads over, and keep the old path alive for another week after that.

The temptation is to do it all in one deploy window. I've done that too, twice, and both times I spent the night fixing something the staging data never showed me.

Nine days sounds slow. It was the fastest migration I've run, because nothing woke me up at three in the morning. I'd do it the same way again. I've written the sequence down for whoever tries this next.

Version your API on day one. Not because you'll need it soon. Because the day you need it, you'll be in a hurry.

I shipped an endpoint that returned a customer object with eleven fields. Four months later, two of those fields had to change meaning. Renaming them would break every integration someone had built against the old shape.

So I added a version prefix and kept both shapes alive. It cost me an afternoon and a small routing table. The old shape still serves three clients today and nobody had to touch their code.

That's the whole argument. Versions aren't decoration. They're the difference between a change and a coordinated migration across every customer you have.

If you're just starting, the cheap move is a prefix in the path. Done. It buys you years. I've never regretted the prefix. I've regretted skipping it twice, on two different services and in two different years.

Feature flags rot. I've watched a codebase grow four hundred flags, and by the end nobody could tell which ones were still on. Every flag is a fork in the logic that has to be held in a reader's head.

The fix isn't fewer flags. It's a removal date. When I add one, I write the date it dies in the description. Every Friday I list the flags past their date and delete the dead branch.

I removed nineteen branches last quarter that way. Nineteen fewer paths through the code, and no behavior changed for anyone.

Flags are still the right tool for shipping dark. They're just not free. Treat each one as a temporary loan, and pay it off on a schedule instead of hoping someone remembers.

That's it. A date and a list. I keep a table of every dead flag in the repo. Three rows this month, all gone.

A design doc I'll read is two pages. Longer than that and I'm skimming for the decision, which means the writing failed.

What I put in mine is short. The problem in three sentences. The two options I considered. What I picked and the one thing that would make me change my mind. No diagrams unless a diagram is faster than a paragraph, which is rare.

The section people skip is the tradeoff. Everyone lists benefits. I want the cost. If there's no cost written down, the author hasn't decided anything yet, they've just described a wish.

I write these for myself first. Six months later I've forgotten the constraints, and a two page doc from a past version of me is worth more than an hour of guessing at old code. I read mine a year later and the tradeoff section was the one part that helped. That's the whole habit.

Postmortems die when they turn into blame. I've watched a good team stop writing them, and the reason was always the same. Two people defending themselves, everyone else quiet, nothing learned.

The version that works has no names in it. Not to hide anything, but because a person's name isn't a cause. The cause is a deploy with no rollback, a config nobody reviewed, an alert that fired into an empty channel.

I run them with three questions. What did we believe was true. What was true. What will we change. That third one needs an owner and a date or it's a wish.

We've changed four things this year from those sessions. Two were tiny. One prevented a repeat outage in the same week it was written. I run these on a Friday with no managers in the room, and the quiet people talk first because I ask them first.

Dates and time zones have caused me more production bugs than any other category. I'll take that fight. Four separate incidents, all from the same root cause.

A user picks a date. The server stores it. Someone in another country sees a different day. A report runs at midnight in a time zone nobody thought about, and the morning number counts the wrong window.

The rules I use now are simple. Store every instant against one reference zone. Store a user's time zone on the user, not the request. Never do date math on a string. And test with at least one zone that's half an hour off, because that's where the naive code breaks.

Half hour offsets feel exotic until you have one customer there.

I write a test for every one of these now. Four bugs was enough to teach me. I run the suite with one zone that's half an hour off.

Automation that fails without telling you is a liability. I built a job that synced two systems every night, and it worked for seven months. Then an API changed a field type and the sync wrote nothing for three weeks.

The lesson isn't test your automation. It's make it loud. A job that does nothing should say so. I now have every sync emit a count, and a check that compares today's count to the median of the last fourteen days. A drop to zero pages me.

That check took an hour to write. The silent three weeks cost me a customer who assumed their data was moving.

Boring plumbing deserves monitoring more than the exciting parts do, because the exciting parts are watched by everyone while the plumbing runs in the dark. I check that chart every Monday morning. It takes one minute and it has caught two dead jobs since.

Rate limits are a feature, not a punishment. I learned this after an integration partner hammered my endpoint with two hundred requests a second and took the whole service down for everyone else.

I hadn't set a limit because I was afraid of upsetting customers. What I did was let one customer upset every other customer, which is a worse trade and I made it by default.

Now every public endpoint has a limit and a clear response. The response matters as much as the limit. It says what happened, when to come back, and which header to read. Nobody writes an angry email about a limit they can see coming.

The partner in question still integrates. They added a small sleep between calls and their throughput didn't drop.

I set a limit on the partner endpoint the same week. Two hundred a second, with a clear header. Their throughput didn't change. Read the header. Then try again. Limits are how you keep one caller from becoming everyone's outage.

Retry storms are how a small failure becomes a large one. One service gets slow. Callers retry. Retries triple the load. Now the slow service is down and so is everything that depends on it.

I've watched it twice. The second time I was on call and I could see the request count climbing while the success rate fell, which is the signature you want to recognise.

Two fixes, both small. Retry with a cap and a growing delay between attempts. And add a small random amount of jitter, because a thousand callers all retrying at the one second mark is the same as not backing off at all.

Neither is clever. Both keep the system breathing while something upstream recovers.

I use two caps and one sleep now. Nobody notices it at all. If your retries are immediate and unlimited, you've built a small amplifier pointed at your own weak point.
#AI #BuildInPublic #VibeCoding #tech #Reliability #Distributed #Engineering #Backend #Software #SRE #SystemDesign #DevOps #Coding #Developer #Infrastructure #Startup #Learning #Architecture

Most technical decisions are two way doors. You can walk back through them. I spent a week on one of those, weighing a queue choice for a project with nine users.

That time was stolen from a decision I couldn't reverse. Which is the asymmetry people miss. One way doors deserve a week. Two way doors deserve an hour and a note about who to ask if it hurts.

Now I label them out loud in the meeting. This one we can undo in a day, so I'm going to pick and move. This other one changes the database shape, so let's talk for twenty more minutes.

The tool is crude. It's also the fastest way I know to stop a team from spending its best hours on the wrong decisions.

I say the label out loud in the meeting. One hour on a two way door, one week on the other. Two labels. That's all it takes.

Read the whole stack trace before you touch anything. I've wasted more time than I want to admit by jumping to the first frame that mentioned my code.

The bottom of the trace is where the real cause sits. The first frame is often a symptom three layers up. I've seen a null pointer in my handler turn out to be a schema change two services away.

So I read it from the bottom. Find the last frame that isn't library code, then work upwards asking what each caller assumed. Nine times in ten, the assumption is the bug.

The other habit is copying the whole trace into a note before I start. Something about reading it off my own screen instead of a scrolling console makes the shape of it obvious.

Bottom up. Every single time. One line at a time. It's slower for a minute and faster for an hour.

Deploy frequency is the health metric I trust most. Faster deploys mean smaller changes, smaller changes mean easier reviews, easier reviews mean fewer surprises in production.

I worked on a team that shipped once a month. Every release was an event with a bridge call and a rollback plan. It also had the most bugs, because a month of changes arrived at once and nobody could isolate the cause of anything.

We moved to deploying whenever main was green. Same people, same code quality, no process overhaul. Thirty days later our mean time to fix had dropped by more than half, and that was because we could see what changed.

The fear is that faster means riskier. What I've seen is the opposite. Small and often is how you keep every failure small.

I ship small, every day. That's the whole trick. Once a day is a good place to start.

Logs tell you what happened. Metrics tell you how much. Traces tell you where the time went. I had the first two for years and kept guessing at the third.

That gap shows up on slow requests. The log says the request completed. The metric says the average is fine, because averages hide the tail. What I need is the twelve slowest requests and the time spent in each step.

Once I had traces, one thing was obvious within an hour. A cache lookup was calling a network service it never should have touched, and it accounted for most of the latency on the slow path.

The average never showed it because most requests hit the warm cache. Those were the customers who mattered.

Three signals, not one. I use the small version of each and that's been enough. I found the culprit within an hour of seeing the traces.

Idempotency keys are the difference between a retry and a double charge. I learned this the expensive way, on a payment flow, at the end of a month.

A customer's card was charged twice because their bank timed out our request and our client retried. Both requests succeeded. The customer noticed before we did, which is never the sequence you want.

My fix is small. Your client generates a key per attempt. The server stores the key with the result. A second request with the same key gets the first result back instead of doing the work again.

It cost me a day to add. It covers every retry, every network blip, every impatient double click, and every webhook that gets delivered twice.

I added it in a day, and it now covers every retry, every blip, and every webhook that arrives twice. Cheap insurance. If money or messages move in your system, you want this before you want anything else.

Every abstraction has a rent. I've shipped three that I later removed, and each one started as a good idea about reuse.

The pattern is the same. Two places need similar logic. I extract a layer. Then a third place needs something different, so the layer grows a flag. Then the flag has a flag, and reading the layer takes longer than reading either caller would have.

What I ask now is whether the third caller exists yet. If it doesn't, I copy the code twice and wait. Two copies of thirty lines are cheaper than one abstraction that has to cover a case I haven't met.

I broke this rule last year and paid six weeks of confusion. The two copies I left alone are still fine.

Two copies. No layer. Reuse is a reward for a pattern you've seen three times, not a guess about a second time.

A comment should explain why, because the code already explains what. I keep relearning this when I read old files of mine.

The good comments I've written are short and about constraints. This runs before the cache warms, so it can't assume a value. We retry here because the vendor closes connections at thirty seconds. Both of those save the next reader an hour.

The bad comments restate the line below. Increment the counter. That comment costs the reader a second and teaches nothing, and a file full of them trains people to skip comments altogether.

So I write a comment when I know something the code can't show. A vendor quirk, a date, a ticket number, a reason we didn't take the obvious path.

I keep my comments to two lines. Anything longer means the code is doing too much. Every time. If I can't name the surprise, I don't write the comment.

A deadline that can't move needs a scope that can. Those are the two levers, and something has to bend when reality arrives.

I've been on both sides of this. The project where the date was fixed and the scope kept growing ended with a half finished product and a tired team. The one where we fixed the date and cut scope shipped something people used, then got the rest in the following month.

The conversation that makes this work happens at the start. Here's what we can do by that date. Here's what falls off the list if we keep everything. Pick.

That's uncomfortable for ten minutes and it saves the last three weeks, which is when everyone is already exhausted and least able to make good calls.

I write the cut list in the same meeting as the estimate. Agree on it while nobody's under pressure. That's it.

Build for a slow connection first. I did a month of testing on hotel wifi and it changed four decisions I'd already made.

The dashboard took nine seconds to look ready. It was fetching four endpoints in a chain. Two of them didn't need to block the first paint. Moving them made it two seconds, and the fast connection never showed me that.

The point isn't performance. It's that a slow network exposes the order of your assumptions. Everything I found would help a user on a train, in a basement office, or on a phone with two bars.

I test on a throttled connection now. I keep a throttled profile open in a second tab. Every feature, before I call it done.

Keep a decision log. One line per decision, the date, and the reason in one sentence. Ten seconds of work that answers the question everyone asks six months later.

Mine lives next to the code and looks like this. Chose Postgres over the managed alternative, March, because we need the extension that runs there. That's the whole entry. When someone asks why we're not on the managed service, the answer is already written.

One line. One date. One reason. It's the cheapest documentation I've ever kept, and the one I read most.

I read the log before every architecture meeting. It settles the argument about why we didn't pick the simpler option three years ago. Four hundred entries in three years. Not one has been wrong. I add the line before I leave the meeting.

Test with real data before you trust a demo. I've shipped two features that worked on my fixtures and fell apart on the first real upload.

Some metrics make people behave worse. I shipped a leaderboard for response time and watched quality fall within a month.

The team got faster. Tickets closed sooner. They also closed without a real answer, because a ticket that looks closed counts, and a ticket waiting on a customer doesn't get you a better number.

I killed it and replaced it with two things. A sample of five closed tickets each week, read by a person. And a customer effort question on the resolution. Slower to read, much harder to game.

Any number attached to a person's performance becomes a target, and targets get optimised whether or not the underlying thing improves.

Measuring is fine. Measuring a person is a different act, and it changes what they do next. I read those five with the person who wrote them. Ten minutes, no scores, no names. Two measures, both read by a person.

Deprecating something is harder than shipping it. I removed an endpoint last month and it took six weeks of finding callers before I could turn anything off.

Hiring your first engineer is a bet on someone's judgement, not their framework knowledge. I got this wrong once and right once, and the difference wasn't skill.

The second version of a product is where founders often ruin the first one. I've been close to doing it. The instinct after a good launch is to rebuild, because now you know how it should've been done.

A rebuild takes four months. It ships with the same bugs in new locations, plus a fresh set nobody's seen. Existing users spend a week relearning things that worked. Some don't come back.

What I do instead is a list. Every change I'd make, ranked by how many people it hurts. Then I ship the top three and stop. That's a third of the value of a rebuild for one week of work.

Batch or stream, the question isn't which is faster. It's which failure you can live with. I got this wrong on a data pipeline and spent a weekend on it.

Streaming gives you numbers that are current and approximate. Batching gives you numbers that are exact and late. Neither is better. They fail in different ways.

My mistake was building a stream for a report that runs every morning. It made the system harder to reason about, and the thing anyone wanted was a correct number at eight in the morning.

I replaced it with a job that runs once a night and takes eleven minutes. Nobody has noticed anything except that the numbers stopped disagreeing with each other.

That's enough. Start with the batch. It's simpler, it's easier to debug, and it's almost always enough. Move to a stream when someone can name a decision that has to happen within seconds.

A queue backlog is invisible until it's an outage. I had one grow for nine days because the consumer was slower than the producer and nobody had a number for either.

The fix took an afternoon. I added a check that compares the queue depth to the number of items processed a minute ago, and alerts when the first number is growing for two hours straight. That's the earliest signal there is.

The other thing I added was a ceiling. Past ten thousand items, the producer slows down and tells the caller to come back. Losing a request is better than losing nine days of data because the queue filled a disk.

Depth, rate, and a limit. Three numbers on one chart.

I check that chart when I'm bored now. Depth against rate, on one chart. That's how you find these before a customer does. I look at it for ten seconds a day.

A backup you've never restored isn't a backup. It's a file you hope works. I believed mine worked for two years before I tried one.

So there's a job now that runs once a month and restores the latest backup into a scratch environment, then runs three checks against it. Row counts, a sample query, and a foreign key.

A disk filled up and took three services down with it. Not a database. Not a network. A log file that nobody rotated because the service was small and the volume was quiet.

The fix was one line in a config. The cost was four hours of an evening I had planned around something else.

Here's what I do now. Every service writes logs with a size cap and a count. Seven files, fifty megabytes each. When the eighth arrives, the first one goes. That's the whole rule, and it takes ten seconds to write.

The other half of the lesson is about alerts. I had a disk check on the database and nothing else. Now there's one alert on any volume over eighty percent, and it has fired twice since.

Small services deserve the same care as big ones. They fail the same way, and they fail at worse times. I treat every one of mine that way now. I check that alert before I go to bed, and I've caught two full volumes before a customer noticed anything at all. Two calls.

Your staging environment is lying to you and it's not the code's fault. Mine had a different database version, no email sending, a feature flag I'd flipped months ago, and twice the memory.

Email is the least reliable thing I depend on. It looks instant and it's a queue of servers you don't control, run by people who don't know you exist.

I learned this when a password reset flow stopped for nine hours without a sound. Our logs said sent. The provider said delivered. The customer's inbox said nothing, because a shared IP had been flagged that morning.

What I added was a fallback and a check. Every outgoing message gets logged with an id and a status, and I query the provider once a day for bounces. If the bounce rate crosses two percent, I get a page.

The fallback matters more. If a reset email doesn't arrive in two minutes, the page offers a different path to prove identity.

Any flow that depends on a message arriving needs a second way through. I built mine after the nine hour outage. Two minutes is the limit now.

Offline support is not a checkbox. I added it to a note tool and spent three weeks on conflicts between two devices that had both edited the same paragraph.

A cron job scheduled at 2:30 in the morning runs twice a year or not at all, depending on the clock change. I found out from a duplicate invoice, which is the kind of bug nobody forgives.

Nothing in my code was wrong. The scheduler saw 2:30 twice on one night because the clocks went back, and it did what I told it to do both times.

Fixing it is about making the work safe to repeat, not about the schedule. My jobs now write a record when they start, keyed by the date they're meant to process. A second run sees that record and exits.

That one change protects me from clock changes, retries, a manual kick, and two schedulers running at once. All four have happened since.

If your job moves money or sends messages, make it safe to run twice. Times are less predictable than code. I add that record to every job I write now. Every one.

Feature requests are a signal about a problem and a guess about a solution. Treating them as instructions is how a product turns into a pile of unrelated buttons.

Webhooks beat polling when you can trust delivery, and you often can't. I've built both and each time the webhook needed a safety net underneath it.

The net looks like this. A webhook arrives, you store it with its id, and you answer fast. A separate job checks for events you expected and never received, using a cursor from the provider.

That cursor job was the whole fix. It caught eleven missed webhooks in the first month, including two that mattered, and it runs every ten minutes for a few milliseconds of work.

Polling alone would have been simpler for this volume. Two events an hour doesn't need a webhook at all, and I said so before building one.

Start with the schedule that pulls. Add the push when volume or latency makes it worth the second path. Both, in the end. Always both. I keep the pull job even when the push works.

Version numbers should tell a user whether to care. I stopped using semantic versioning on my own product and switched to two lines in a changelog that say what changed for them.

The library case is different and semantic versioning earns its place there. When a machine or a package manager reads the number, the number has to be precise.

For an application, nobody reads the version. They read the changelog, and if the changelog is good then the version is decoration.

What I keep is a date and a short label. October, faster imports. That's the release note and it tells a person more than a number going from two point four to two point five ever will.

The version still exists in the build for support. I just stopped pretending it's communication. Date and label. That's the release. I write it for the person using the app, not for the person building it.

Put new engineers on call in their first month. Not alone. Alongside someone, watching, with no expectation of fixing anything. The purpose is to see what an outage feels like from the inside.

I did this with two hires and both said the same thing afterwards. They had no idea how much of support and debugging is reading a dashboard and waiting, and they'd been designing features as if failures were rare events.

One of them went back and changed how a background job told the user it had failed, because he'd watched a customer hit that path and be told nothing.

If you keep new people away from incidents for six months, they build for a system where things work. Shadowing is the cheapest reality check there is. First month. Reading, no fixing.

It changes what they write. I put every new hire on that rotation in week two.

Timebox research to one hour and write the decision down at the end. I used to read about a problem for three days and then decide the same thing I'd have decided in the first hour.

What eats the time is comparison shopping. Two options is a decision. Seven options is a hobby.

The hour has a shape. Twenty minutes on the two candidates, twenty on how each one fails, twenty writing the choice and the reason. If the hour ends without a decision, I pick the boring one and move.

I've done this for four choices this year. Two were wrong and reversing them took a day each, because I'd written down what I expected and could see where the expectation broke.

The writing is the part that makes it fast. Decide, write, move. One hour. Every time. I set a timer and I stop when it rings, even mid sentence.

Read a competitor's documentation before their product. The docs tell you what they think the hard part is, and that's the most useful thing you can learn about a rival.

One competitor's docs spend four pages on permissions. That's where they've put their effort and where their users get stuck. If I ever add roles, I know what I'm signing up for.

Another's docs open with a two line quick start and nothing else. Their bet is that the product explains itself, which tells me they're chasing self serve buyers.

You can also see what they removed. Deprecated pages that still rank in search show you what people asked for and what got taken away.

I spend an hour in their docs each quarter. It's free, it's public, and it beats guessing at a feature list I can't see behind a login. One hour. That's it. I take notes with a pen, and three things from last quarter are in my product now.

Name variables so they can be found with a search. One letter names and common words make a codebase harder to work in than any missing comment.

I renamed two variables this year because I couldn't search for them. One was called data, which appears eleven hundred times in the repo. The other was a loop index used across forty lines.

The rule I use is that a name should be unique enough to find and short enough to read. Item total, invoice rows, retry count. Those search well and read fine in a line.

This matters more now that assistants read our code. A well named symbol can be followed through a file in seconds. A name like that gives a model nothing to hold on to and gives a person the same problem.

Ten seconds of naming saves an hour of finding, and I've paid that bill both ways this year. I rename the moment I notice. Ten seconds. Done.

A monorepo for one person is the right call. I split mine into three repos for a year and spent that year on version bumps and cross repo commits.

The split made sense when I imagined a team. Each repo had its own pipeline and its own version, and nothing shared. What I got was a dependency I had to publish to myself six times a week.

Moving back took an afternoon and removed two hundred lines of config. One repo, one pipeline, one version. Deploys went from three steps to one.

The case for splitting is real when ownership splits. Different teams, different release cadences, different access. For a solo builder none of that exists, so the cost is pure overhead.

I'd split again at four people. Not before. I moved back in an afternoon and deleted two hundred lines of config. One repo with one pipeline, and no version bumps. One repo. The cost of the split was a version bump six times a week, and that overhead landed on me because there was nobody else to hand it to.
