The first five minutes of a demo decide the rest of it. I used to open with the architecture. Now I open with the pain.

One sentence about what the person is doing today that hurts, then their own data on the screen. Nothing else until they ask a question. Questions mean engagement and silence means politeness.

I bring a real account with real mess in it. Imported files with duplicate rows, a half finished draft, a report from last week. Clean demo data makes a product look like a mockup and hides the parts that sell.

The five minute rule keeps me honest. If I can't show value in that window with their data, the feature isn't ready to be shown to anyone.

Ask them to bring a file before the call. Then start with the file. I ask for it the day before, so I can look at the mess first. I open with the piece of their data that looks wrong and let them tell me what they expected to see on that screen.

Always give users a way to take their data out. Not because they'll leave. Because knowing they can is part of why they stay.

I built an export in a week and it became my best support tool. Half the questions that used to arrive about reports turned into people pulling the data themselves and doing the analysis their way.

The other effect was commercial. Two customers told me the export was why they signed, because it meant the decision to stay was theirs to make.

The format matters. Comma separated values, one flat file where that's honest, and column names a person can read. A file someone has to email you about isn't an export.

An hour of work made the tool feel less like a trap. I built mine in a week and it's still the feature I mention first. Export everything, then let people walk. That's it.

A bad deploy at five in the afternoon gets one decision. Roll back or push forward. I've done both and rolling back has never been the wrong first move.

The instinct to fix forward comes from not wanting to admit the deploy was bad. That's ego and it costs the evening and sometimes the night. Rolling back takes two minutes and returns the product to a known state.

Then you investigate with the pressure off. Twice this year the bug turned out to be something that would have been obvious in the morning, and twice the second deploy was clean.

The one thing I do before rolling back is write a single line in the incident log with the time and the guess. Three words is enough. That line is what makes the postmortem possible an hour later.

Undo first. Think second. Fix third. I roll back first now, and I investigate with the pressure off.

Write tests for the boring paths and skip the clever ones. I've seen a team with eighty percent coverage and no test on the refund flow, because refunds were simple and moving invoices were interesting.

The boring paths are where money and messages move. Login, reset, upload, export, retry, cancel. None of them are fun to test and all of them are the parts a customer notices when they break.

My rule for a new project is five tests before anything else. Sign up, sign in, upload, export, delete. It takes an afternoon and it covers the flows I'd be paged about.

Coverage as a number pushes effort toward whatever is easiest to test, which is not what matters.

I write those five tests before I write a single feature, and it takes one afternoon. They cover the pages I'd be paged about at night. Five tests. One afternoon. Then I build the interesting thing.

Refactor one small thing every week and you'll never need a refactor project. I've run two big ones and both began with a year of nobody touching anything.

That version takes an hour. Rename a misleading variable. Pull one function out of a long file. Delete a branch that can't be reached. Small enough to read in a diff, big enough to matter over a year.

What it prevents is the moment where the change someone needs is buried under six layers of accumulated shortcuts. That moment is where teams decide to rewrite.

I keep a list of ten small things and pick one each Friday. Three of this year's fixes removed a class of bug rather than an instance.

An hour a week. Fifty a year. I'd rather have those than one heroic cleanup. I keep the ten item list in a file and I pick one each Friday.

A code review comment should describe a problem, not a preference. Comments I've learned from were about something breaking. The comments I've argued with were about taste dressed up as a rule.

My rule now is to say which it is. This will break when the list is empty, or this is a preference and I'll defer to you. That second sentence has ended more review threads than any technical argument I've made.

I separate the two now. My other habit is asking a question instead of writing an instruction. What breaks if the list comes back empty. Half the time the author answers it and the comment was unnecessary. The other half they find the bug.

Reviews are a conversation about a change. Comments that read like verdicts get defended instead of considered, and I've been on both sides of that.

I lead with the kind. That's it. I say which kind of comment it is, and it took two years of arguing about taste before I understood why the two kinds needed different words at all.

Give a spike two weeks and a written outcome or kill it. I've run four and two of them should have ended in week one.

A spike is research with a deadline. The output is a decision, not a branch. What we learned, what we'd need to build, and how long that build would take. Two pages, same as a design doc.

The failure mode is a spike that becomes a half built feature. It happens when nobody writes down the ending, so the work drifts from answering a question to producing a thing.

I write the question at the top of the notes before I start. Can we hold this much data in memory without a service. Yes or no. If the answer arrives on Tuesday, the spike ends on Tuesday.

Two weeks. One question. One answer. I write the question at the top before I open the editor, and I delete the branch when the answer arrives.

If you publish a library, plan the day you stop. I maintain one small package and the hardest part has been the exit, not the code.

What helped was writing the deprecation policy on the first day. What counts as a breaking change, how long a version gets support, and what happens if I disappear. Two paragraphs in the readme.

I've since deprecated two functions. Because the policy was public, nobody was surprised, and the migration notes were read.

The alternative is a package that stops working on a newer runtime while people still depend on it, and nobody finds out until something breaks on a Friday.

Own the ending. A maintainer who says when they'll stop is more trustworthy than one who promises forever, and I've stopped believing anyone who promises forever. I wrote mine in two paragraphs on the first day. Two years on, it's still the most useful file in the repo. Two paragraphs.

Build for yourself when you're the user, and for a market when you're not. Mixing those up is the most expensive mistake I've made twice.

The tool I built for my own workflow was good, because I could feel every awkward step. It reached about a hundred people and then stopped, and that was fine because I was one of them.

The second product was for a group I'd never been part of. I built features I thought they wanted and got polite interest and no money. I'd been guessing at a workflow I couldn't feel.

If you're not the user, you need ten real conversations before you write code. If you are the user, you need one honest look at whether anyone else has your problem.

Different products, different first steps. I confused them for a year. I ask one question now. Am I the user. If the answer is no, ten calls come first. The month I spent guessing at a workflow I'd never done taught me more about research than any book on the subject. One question. The difference between those two products wasn't the code. It was that in the first one, I could feel every awkward step because I was the person taking them.

The fix wasn't the product. I stopped paying for the directory and put that time into asking happy customers for one introduction each. Total signups fell and revenue rose.

Averages are comfortable because they're one number. The useful view is two columns, source and retention, and it takes an hour to build from data I already had.

Four percent overall. Eleven from one place. I build that table every month now. Two columns. It takes an hour and it has changed where I spend money twice. I'd rather see the split than the total, every single month.

Learn one new thing a quarter and let it be small. Mine this year were a query planner, a background job runner, and a text editor macro. None of them changed my stack.

The value isn't the tool. It's that learning something small teaches me how much I don't know, which keeps me skeptical of confident answers in areas I've never touched.

I timebox it to ten hours across the quarter. If it doesn't click in that window, I stop and write down what I learned, and that note has been more useful than the tool twice.

The alternative is reading about everything and building nothing, which I did for a year and don't recommend.

One thing a quarter. Small, finished, written down. I pick mine in January and I finish it before April every year. Ten hours, then I stop. That's the whole system. Four a year. Forty in a decade.

Saying no to yourself is the hard version. I have eleven side projects and two of them get time, and the other nine are a tax on my attention every time I open the folder.

What I changed was writing a status on each one. Active, paused, or dead. Nine are dead, and I stopped feeling like I owed them anything.

Eleven projects. Two alive. I wrote a status on every project and closed nine of them. The folder is still there and the guilt is gone. Say no to yourself first.

Read your own error messages out loud. I did this for twenty minutes and rewrote nine of them, and it was the cheapest product work I've done all year.

Mine said things like operation failed and invalid input, which told a person nothing about what to do next. Read aloud, that language sounds like a machine talking to itself.

The rewrite took no code. Your file is larger than the limit, try a smaller one. That address looks incomplete, check for the at sign. Both of those came from support threads where I'd explained the same thing by hand.

Nobody enjoys writing these. It's the kind of task that never reaches a roadmap because it never blocks anything, and yet it's the voice most of your users hear more often than they hear any marketing page.

Nine messages. Twenty minutes. I'd put that against most features I've shipped this year.

Find your slowest endpoint before you optimize anything. Mine was a small one I'd forgotten about, a lookup that ran on every page load and took four hundred milliseconds.

A small log line gave it away. I timed each request and printed the slowest one every few minutes. Two days of that and the picture was obvious, which a profiler had failed to show me because the cost was spread across requests that each looked fine.

The fix was a join I'd written wrong eighteen months earlier. One line. The median page went from nine hundred milliseconds to two hundred and forty.

What I'd been about to do instead was add a cache, which would have hidden a bad query behind a layer that could go stale. Two days of measurement saved me that.

I time the slowest request every month now. Time the slowest request. Then look at the query.

Charge each month and lose the people who wanted to commit. I moved to annual pricing and the churn number fell by more than half, which I expected, and support load fell too, which I didn't.

A customer who pays each month reconsiders your product twelve times a year. An annual one reconsiders once, and if you do your job they renew without thinking about it.

The surprise was the conversations. The accounts paying each month asked for small changes because they were paying attention. Annual accounts asked for less and stuck around longer, and the questions they did ask were about outcomes instead of features.

I offer both now, with two months off on the annual. About six in ten pick annual, and those accounts are the ones that refer people.

I moved everyone in January. Six in ten chose the year up front, and most of them are still here. Twelve decisions a year against one. I know which I'd rather earn.

A refund request is a message about the first ten minutes, not the last. Every time I've asked why, the answer turned out to be something that happened on day one and nobody mentioned.

Log what your system costs, not just what it breaks. I added a line for spend per request and found that four percent of traffic produced most of my bill.

It was a retry loop in a client library that ran for six hours after a network hiccup. Nothing failed. Nothing alerted. The invoice arrived at the end of the month and that was the first signal.

So now every expensive call writes its cost to the same log as everything else. Once a day I sum the last twenty four hours and compare it to the week before. A jump of forty percent sends me a message.

The alert has fired three times. Twice it was a real loop and once it was a customer who'd doubled their usage, which is the kind of problem I want.

Errors get alerts because they're loud. Costs are quiet until the end of the month. I check that number myself once a day.

A post went somewhere and I wasn't ready for it. Four hours of traffic arrived, the site stayed up, and I spent the evening in a support inbox instead of working on the thing that had just been validated.

What broke was the parts I never thought about. My signup confirmation email had no sending limit configured and got throttled. The free tier had no ceiling and two people used a month of capacity in a day.

Both were fixed in an hour, after the fact, by hand.

Now I keep a small list called if this blows up. Send limits, a hard cap on the free tier, a worst case cost number, and one line about what I'd turn off first. It lives next to the deploy script and I read it once a month.

I read mine on the first of the month. Two minutes. Then I close it. I add to it every time something goes wrong. Four lines. They cost nothing until the day they cost you everything. That's it.

A public roadmap turns customers into project managers. I tried it for two months and the requests became a queue I had to defend.

Every planned item became a commitment in someone's head, with a date they'd invented themselves. When something slipped, I got polite messages asking about it, which felt worse than an argument because nobody was being unreasonable.

What worked instead was a changelog with what already shipped, and one line saying what I'm working on now. No dates on the future. No voting. The past is public and the present is one sentence.

Requests still arrive. They just arrive as problems, which is what I want, instead of as votes on a list I published.

Two months of a roadmap taught me that. I'd rather show what I built than promise what I'll build. The changelog is one page and I rewrite it every Friday afternoon. No dates. Nobody has asked me for one since.

I stopped promising dates and started promising the next thing you'll see. That single change removed most of the stress from my customer conversations.

Dates were always wrong, and being wrong about a date costs more trust than being slow. A customer can forgive a delay. They can't forgive a broken promise, because that's about you and not the work.

What I say now is what I'll show them next. A working import, then a preview, then the schedule. They can see progress without a calendar, and I can cut the list when things take longer than expected.

Two customers told me they preferred it, which surprised me. It turns out people would rather know the order than the date.

Order you can keep. Dates you can guess at. I promise the sequence and I ship in that order. It has made every hard conversation shorter than a date ever did. Two things. That's all.

Write support replies for the person who is already angry, not for the person who is curious. I rewrote mine that way and the threads got shorter.

An upset message has two parts. The problem, and the fear that nobody is going to help. My old replies answered the problem and skipped the second part, which is why the next message was longer.

The opening line I use now acknowledges the frustration without being theatrical. That's annoying and I can see why you're annoyed. Then the answer. Then what happens next, with a time.

Four sentences. Two of my last three replies ended the thread there, which almost never happened before.

Empathy without a fix reads as empty. A fix without empathy reads as cold. Both together end the conversation, and the order matters more than I expected. I write the first line before I look up the answer now.

Two hundred lines is a feature. Anything past that needs a reason written down, and most of my reasons don't survive the writing.

I measured this after a review where a change came in at nine hundred lines and I couldn't hold it in my head. Not because it was clever. Because it did four things, and the fourth was unrelated to the first.

Splitting it into four diffs took an hour. Each one was reviewable in ten minutes and each one could have been rolled back on its own, which turned out to matter the next week when one of them was wrong.

The line count isn't the point. The point is whether I can explain the change in one sentence, and past a couple hundred lines the answer is no.

Small diffs aren't a style preference. They're how you keep the ability to undo. I split mine before I ask for a review.

Renaming a product costs more than naming it, and I found that out after two years of the first name. I moved from a long descriptive name to one short word and lost more than I expected.

Search rankings took four months to recover. The domain cost what it cost. Two customers thought we'd been acquired and asked whether their data moved.

None of that was fatal and I'd still do it again. The old name explained what the tool did and nothing about why anyone should care. The new one makes people ask, which starts a better conversation.

What I'd change is the timing. I renamed during a busy month, so support and the rename landed in the same week. That was my mistake, not the name's.

Pick the short name first. If you can't, rename in a quiet month and tell everyone twice. I learned that in the wrong month, which was the busy one. Two years of search traffic. Gone in a week.

Support macros save time and cost trust when they don't answer the question. I've received a few as a customer and the pattern is always the same. Long, polite, and about a different problem.

Mine were worse than silence, because a macro that misses tells the person you didn't read their message. And they know it, because the answer doesn't match.

What I use now is a set of openings instead of whole replies. One line that acknowledges the specific problem, plus my own words. It's slower per message and much faster per thread, since nobody comes back confused.

I keep about twelve of those openings and I rewrite them every few months. If one of them is used more than five times a week, that's a signal about the product rather than support.

Macros should be a starting point. If they're the whole answer, write the feature instead. Twelve openings. No canned answers.

Typography is product work and I ignored it for two years. I changed one thing, the line length, and my support questions about reports dropped.

My tables had lines running the width of a laptop screen. People lost their place reading across and asked me which row a number belonged to, which I'd assumed was a data problem.

Constraining the text column and aligning numbers to the right fixed most of it. Not one person mentioned it. The questions just stopped.

The other change was size. Two of my fonts looked the same, and one was a size I'd picked to fill space rather than to separate two levels of information.

I keep it dull now. One font, three sizes, and a limit on how wide anything gets. Dull here means readable, and readable is the feature. I check the line length on every new screen before I call it done.

Some months the right engineering decision is to ship nothing and pay down what you owe. I took one of those months last spring and the following quarter was my best for delivery.

Nothing went out for four weeks. I fixed three flaky tests, deleted two features nobody used, replaced a dependency that was two years behind, and wrote down how the billing flow works.

None of it was visible. All of it made the next three months faster, because every feature I built after that landed on ground that didn't move under it.

The fear is that a quiet month looks like nothing is happening. It does, from outside, and I've learned to accept that. An update that says I spent the month on maintenance is honest and unexciting, and it's better than shipping something to have something to say.

One month down. Three months faster. I'll take it every year.

Read your own numbers once a month, even if you're not a finance person. I put off looking at my costs for a year and found six hundred dollars a month of things I'd stopped using.

Two cloud instances for a project I'd shelved. A monitoring plan on a tier I'd outgrown. A domain I was holding for an idea I never started. None of them were big and together they were a mortgage payment.

The other reason to look is that it teaches you what your product is. Revenue from one customer group, costs from two, and the shape becomes obvious in a way no dashboard shows you.

I do it on the first of the month with a coffee. Thirty minutes, one spreadsheet, no judgement about the past.

Six hundred a month found. I do it on the first of the month. Thirty minutes. No judgement. The review is free and I'd been avoiding it for no reason at all. Every month.

Send yourself every email your product sends, and do it from a fresh account. I found three broken links and a signature with the wrong name that way.

I'd been testing with my own address, which meant I skipped the welcome, already had an account, and never saw the reset path at all. A new account walked through the whole thing and fell over twice.

What surprised me was how the broken parts weren't obvious. The links worked. The buttons landed on a page that needed a login the recipient didn't have yet.

Ten minutes, one throwaway inbox, and a checklist of the seven messages we send. I run it before any change to signup or billing.

If you haven't seen your own emails as a stranger, you don't know what your product says. I wrote a ninety second welcome that nobody had read in a year. I send them to a fresh inbox. Seven messages. Ten minutes.

Keep one scratch file for the thing you're thinking about. Mine is called notes and everything goes in it, unsorted, with dates.

The value isn't organization. It's that writing an idea down stops it from taking up space in my head while I'm doing something else. Half of what I write is bad and never gets read again, and the half that matters is worth the noise.

I go through it on Friday afternoons and pull out anything that still looks right. Two features this year started as a line in that file from months earlier.

The other use is for decisions I'm avoiding. Writing I don't want to have this conversation, and why tends to make the conversation obvious, which is uncomfortable and useful.

One file. No tags, no folders, no system. The system is that everything goes in it. I read it every Friday and pull out anything that still looks right. Every Friday.

For a small job, a scheduled script beats a queue. I've set up three message brokers for projects that needed one batch a night, and each one was a week of work I didn't need to do.

A broker earns its place when you need retries, ordering, throughput, and several consumers. For a task that runs once a night and takes eleven minutes, a scheduled script with a log file covers everything you need.

What I do instead is write the job so it's safe to run twice, which is good practice regardless, and have it exit with a clear code. That's the whole infrastructure. The scheduler is already on the machine.

Two of those three brokers are gone. The jobs that use them moved to scripts and nobody noticed, which is the best thing that can happen to infrastructure.

I start every small job that way now. Start with the script. Move when a real constraint appears.

Passive income from a small product is real and it isn't passive. I earn from a tool I touch once a month, and the hours go into support, updates, and one dependency upgrade that took a weekend.

What it does give you is reach. The same code serves people while I sleep, and that's a different shape of work from trading hours for money.

The lies are about the numbers. Most small products make a few hundred a month, not a few thousand, and the ones that make more are run by someone putting in real weeks.

What helped me was calling it what it is. A small business with a good margin and no office. That framing made me do the boring parts, like looking at costs and answering email, instead of waiting for the automatic part to arrive.

I call mine a small business now. That word changed how I spend my week. It's income. It's not passive, and saying so makes it better.

A bug that shows on one device is almost never about the code. Mine showed up on two iPhones and nowhere else, and it took three days to find a date parser that assumed a four digit year.

The device locale used a different calendar format, and one of my inputs came through as a two digit year which the library read as nineteen twenty six. Every other platform sent the long form.

What I changed wasn't the parser. I made the field accept one format and reject anything else with a message, which turned a silent wrong answer into a visible error.

That's the pattern I look for now. A bug that shows on one platform means I'm trusting input from outside without saying what shape I expect.

I add a shape check to every outside input now. Ten lines. Three days for one line. The message I added is why it can't happen again.

Someone who churned and came back is the best interview you'll ever get. I called four of them last year and every answer was about a gap, not a grudge.

They didn't leave because of a bug. Two left for a workflow I didn't support yet, one for a price that made sense at their old job, and one for a feature I shipped the month after they left.

The useful question is not why they left. It's what brought them back, because that tells you what your product is for in someone's week.

Three of the four said the same thing. Nothing else did the export right. That's the whole positioning of my product in one sentence and I'd never have written it without asking.

I block an hour a month for those calls. Call the people who came back. They already know the alternatives and they chose you twice. One hour. Every month.

A competitor copied my pricing page last year and I took it as information rather than an insult. It told me they were worried, and it told me which tier they thought was the threat.

They copied the structure and not the number, which was the interesting part. Their enterprise tier sat right where mine did, which suggested they were also moving upmarket.

What I did was nothing for a month and then a small change to the free tier that they couldn't copy without breaking their own onboarding. That's the advantage of being small. A big product can't make a narrow decision.

Copying is a signal about what works. If someone copies you, you've already done the expensive part, which is knowing which shape to build.

I read it as a signal and I move on. Then I build the next thing. I keep building anyway. They've copied twice more since. The second time was a feature I'd already removed because nobody used it.

Every setting you add is a question you're asking the user. I counted mine and found thirty one, and I could explain about nine of them.

The rest were preferences I'd added because someone asked, or because the right answer depended on context I didn't have. All of them pushed a decision onto a person who wanted to get on with their work.

So I picked a default for twenty two of them and hid the setting. Same feature set, same power for anyone who wants it, and the panel went from four screens to one.

The support questions about configuration dropped to nothing, which tells me most people never wanted to choose.

Two settings stayed visible and they're the two where the wrong answer costs something. I had thirty one settings last year. Nine needed to exist. Nine. That's all. Hidden is the default now. I ask when the answer changes what happens.

Write the error message before you write the feature. I've started doing this and it catches half of my bad interface decisions before they exist.

If the message I'd have to write is unclear, the feature is unclear. Could not complete the operation tells me nothing, and I discover that when I try to write it for a person who needs to know what to do next.

The other thing it exposes is missing states. Writing the failure message forces me to name what a failure looks like, which is the question I skip when I'm excited about the happy path.

My rule now is that the error text goes in the pull request description next to the code. If I can't write one that helps, the feature isn't finished.

Some of these take ten minutes. I write the error text first now. Ten minutes. It saves a screen. One of them made me delete a whole screen, which was the right call.

Keep a demo environment that's a little messy. Mine has an imported file with a duplicate row and a half finished draft saved from last week, and it sells better than any clean dataset ever did.

Clean data makes a product look like a screenshot. Messy data makes it look like it works, because the person watching can see their own mess in it.

I set it up on a Sunday and it takes ten minutes to reset. One workspace with four projects, some abandoned, some active, and one that failed an import so I can show what happens when things break.

That last part is the strongest thing in a demo. Showing a failure and a clear recovery does more than showing everything work.

Ten minutes of setup. It has become the single most reused thing I own, and I reset it before every call. I keep a failed import in there on purpose. People remember it. Ten minutes. That's it.

Naming a product is a marketing decision, so I stopped treating it as a technical one. My first name described the mechanism and nobody remembered it, including me when I answered the phone.

The test I use now is on paper. Say the name in a sentence to someone who doesn't work in software. If they ask you to repeat it, it's the wrong name.

Short, pronounceable, and hard to misspell. Those three matter more than meaning, because meaning is what the product earns over time and the name is a handle.

I also check the domain and the obvious social handles before falling in love, and I check whether the word sounds like something worse in another language. Two of my favourites failed that last test.

The name is a handle. I test mine on three people. Two minutes each. Pick one your customers can say out loud at a meeting and move on to the thing they'll talk about.

Manage energy rather than time. I moved my hardest work to the morning and my output went up without changing a single hour of my schedule.

The old plan was to fill every block with something useful, and it didn't work. What I never accounted for was that a hard problem at four in the afternoon takes me three times as long as the same problem at nine.

So the calendar has two kinds of blocks now. Thinking blocks before noon, three hours, no meetings. Everything else after, which includes email, support, invoices, and code I could write half asleep.

The surprising effect was on how I felt about the week. I stopped ending days with the important thing untouched, which used to happen every single time.

Same hours. Different order. The order was the whole problem. I don't move those blocks for anything. Not even for a customer, unless it's an outage.

Stopping a project is a decision you should make on a date you chose in advance. I keep a review date next to every new thing, and I hold to it.

The review asks one question. Is anyone using this who isn't me. If the answer is no and the project is past its date, it stops. No sunk cost argument, no waiting for a good month, no third month of maybe.

Two of my last four ideas died on their review date. Both felt premature when I read the answer, and neither has come up since.

The date is what makes it work. Deciding in the moment means deciding while I'm still attached, because I built the thing and I want it to be right.

Put the date in when you start. Let past you make the call. I do it in a note next to the first commit. Four ideas. Two alive. That's a fine record.

A number with five hundred zeros after it is still a number. I keep coming back to that. The count of possible universes in string theory sits around ten to the five hundredth. Say it fast and it sounds like infinity.

It isn't. The zeros end somewhere. That means there's a last configuration and a total count. Reality is enormous and bounded at the same time. I find that easier to hold in my head than forever.

It also changes how I think about ghosts. If the nearby layers are finite, whatever lives there isn't a god. They're residents with rules and a limited budget for reaching into our layer. Crossing over would cost something, which explains why it happens in bursts. That budget is the only reason the shyness argument makes sense to me.

A finite multiverse is a place you can study. An infinite one is just a word people use to end the conversation. I'd rather have the version with edges. Edges are what make a map useful. I wrote the number out on paper once to see how long it takes.

A ghost that hides when you look isn't shy. It's a broken test. I learned that from reading about falsifiability, which sounds dull until it kills your favorite idea. A claim that can't fail can't teach you anything. That's the whole rule.

The paranormal world has a workaround for this. If the spirit refuses to perform, the refusal counts as a reaction. So the experiment never fails. Nobody has to admit the room was empty. I get why people do it, because a null result is a boring night.

My version is stricter. I write down what would prove me wrong before I start. If that thing doesn't happen, the night counts as nothing. Then I change one variable and run it again.

Boring, slow, and it keeps me honest. The alternative is a hobby where every outcome is a win. I'd rather have a real zero than a fake yes. A test you can't lose isn't a test.

A cold spot is the least useful thing you can measure in a haunted room. I mean that literally, because air moves. Cold air sinks and warm air rises and the whole room trades places at night. Any thermometer on a wall will catch that.

I spent an evening reading about convection and came out less impressed with every video I've seen. The camera sees a shape, the meter drops two degrees, everyone gasps. Two degrees is a window being opened downstairs. A door that swings is a pressure change from a fan. None of it needs a visitor.

I keep coming back to the order of events. If a presence caused the cold, the cold comes after the movement. If a draft caused both, the air moves first. That sequence is the whole experiment.

So I log time on both. A thermometer and a powder track, started at the same second. Then the timeline decides, not my gut. Most nights the air moves first.

The clips that make me stop and rewind are the ones where nothing is happening yet. A hallway at 3am, a closed door, and eight seconds of nothing. Then the door moves. Nobody is in frame and no string is visible.

That's the argument for passive gear. A person walking around with a meter is an event in the room. A camera in the corner is furniture. If something is choosing when to appear, the furniture has a better chance. I think that's the only real insight in this whole field.

It also explains the boring parts of the footage. Most of it is dust in the infrared light. Compression turns a moving moth into a shadow figure. I've watched a pixel trail look like a person for three frames.

So the passive camera is a starting point, not proof. It tells you which nights are worth setting up the analog traps. That's a filter, which is more than most people have. I'll take a filter over a feeling.

If a thing can wipe a hard drive, don't keep your only copy on one. I set up a powder track after that thought, on a baking sheet, with a coin in the middle. Flour, thin enough to see the metal underneath. Nothing electrical anywhere near it.

The point is displacement. If something lifts the coin, the powder keeps the outline. If something drags it, there's a cleared path with edges on both sides. Editing a video takes software. Smudging flour takes a hand, and a hand leaves prints.

I paired it with a camera anyway. The camera gives me a timestamp and the powder gives me a fact. When the video dies, the sheet is still there in the morning. When the sheet is clean and the video is full of static, I know which one to trust.

Neither one is proof on its own. Together they make a lie harder to tell. I've stopped buying gear and started buying patience. That's cheaper and it works better.

A shoebox lined with foil is a better instrument than most of what people buy. I built one in twenty minutes with kitchen foil and an old recorder. The idea is simple. Nothing gets in. Nothing gets out.

That matters because a cheap microphone picks up everything. Phone buzzes, neighbor's wifi, a fridge cycling on, a truck outside. All of it lands on the file. Inside a sealed foil box, none of that exists. So any sound on the recording came from inside the box.

I ran it three nights and got nothing but hiss. Which is a result, even if it's a dull one. The file has a noise floor and I can see it. When a noise rises above that floor, I'll have something to measure.

The catch is that foil also blocks the thing you're trying to hear. Any visitor has to be inside the box or the test is blind. I know that. It still beats recording an empty room and guessing which hum was a voice.

Ten random characters in a sealed box is the cheapest real test I know. Nobody in the room knows them, including me. That's the point. Ten B 9 1 X 7 2 R 0 F, written face down.

A skeptic can explain a moving door. Drafts, a slanted floor, a truck outside, a hinge that was never tight. A skeptic can't explain a voice reading a string it never saw. That's information, not energy. Which is why the low effort version is the strong one.

I recorded audio, said what I wanted out loud, and left the room. The recorder ran for seven hours. Then I listened before I opened anything. I don't open it first.

If the file is silent, the box stays sealed and I change one variable. If the file has the string, I stop and check the audio for edits. Either way I learn something before breakfast. I like tests that end in a fact instead of an argument.

Most ghost tests are built for adults who can read. That's the flaw. I read a plan for a child spirit and it made every other test look lazy. A tablet face down on a table, showing a random cartoon. Ask the kid to peek and say what they see.

No literacy, no math, no hex string. A six year old from 1890 can name a dog. The screen is hidden from you, so you can't feed the answer. If the recording says blue dog and the tablet is showing a blue dog, you have a data point.

The hard part is the invitation. You can't walk in with a clipboard and a headlamp. I'd leave a toy, keep the room dark, and talk like a person. Then leave for the night.

I'd use the same logic for an older presence. Three sealed jars, tobacco and coffee and peppermint, and a question about a routine. Nothing to read, nothing to type, just a smell they already know. Design the test for the person you think is there.

A spirit box is a radio scanner with the pause button removed. It sweeps AM or FM fast enough that you hear fragments. Your brain does the rest. That isn't a dig. It's how hearing works.

I tested one for an hour with nobody in the room. I got words. I wanted it to work. Two of them were my name. Then I ran it again with the antenna removed and got the same kind of words.

The trick is the sweep rate. Speech has rhythm, and a scanner chopping stations can produce rhythm by accident. Pareidolia fills the gaps with meaning. Once you hear your own name in static, you can't unhear it.

Worse, the device is also a receiver for every station in range. None of that means every clip is fake. It means the box alone proves nothing. Pair it with a sealed answer nobody knows, and now you have a test.

A silent recording is still data. It's just not the data you wanted. I've had four silent nights in a row. Each one cost me a fresh pair of batteries and a morning of listening. I'd do it again.

A null result buys you a baseline. Now I know what the room sounds like when nothing is happening. I wrote the times down in a notebook. The fridge clicks at 4:12 and the radiator ticks all night. When something new shows up on a file, I'll recognize it. That's worth more than a spooky clip.

The temptation is to call the quiet night a failure. It isn't. It's the control group. Every claim in science needs one and most ghost hunting skips it.

So I keep the box sealed and change one thing per night. Music one night, a colder room the next, a different corner after that. If ten nights stay silent, I've learned the room is quiet. That's a real answer, just not a fun one.

Every serious attempt at this died the same way. The controls got tight and the phenomena left. I read about Harry Price and his sealed chambers and felt the floor move. Barographs, thermometers, sealed doors, no way in. Activity stopped.

That's a pattern, not one failure. The agency spent decades on remote viewing and got the same shape of answer. Promising results in loose rooms. Nothing once the lab was triple blind. The effect shrank as the controls tightened. I keep the number in my head when I read new clips.

I'm not saying every witness lied. I'm saying the signal doesn't survive being measured. Which is the opposite of how a real force behaves. Gravity doesn't leave when you bring a scale.

So my bar is simple. Make the room tight enough that cheating is hard, then run it for weeks. If the result survives that, I'll take it seriously. I'd love to be wrong here. Wrong would be more interesting than another video.

One agent reading a whole repo is already the wrong shape. I feel that every time a task spills across two services. The context fills up with files it never needed. Then it forgets the first thing I told it.

The next version is a small fleet. One agent plans, three agents work in parallel on separate files, one checks the diffs. The plan is the contract, not the code. I've had better results from three narrow prompts than one huge one.

It fails differently, which is useful. A fleet produces conflicts, and conflicts are visible. A single agent produces a plausible story with the bug hidden inside. I'd rather merge a conflict than hunt a lie.

Coordination is the cost. Someone has to own the interface between workers. Right now that someone is me, with a notebook open. Every tool I've adopted this year made that job smaller. That's the trend I'm betting on.

Coding agents got good first because code tells you when you're wrong. The tests fail, the stack trace points at a line, the fix is checkable in seconds. I can hand a model a loop and get a verdict. That's the whole advantage. Nobody has to trust me.

A kitchen doesn't work like that. An egg doesn't print an error when the shell lands in the pan. Feedback comes as a mess, a smell, or a burnt hand. Those are expensive signals. So the model needs a body with better senses than we have.

I think the timelines people argue about come from that gap. Food robots already work in chains with fixed menus and flat floors. Home kitchens show up around 2030, if the hardware keeps improving. Teaching is earlier, because most of it is language and patience.

Patrol work is later, because the liability is huge. I keep telling people the brain isn't the bottleneck. The body is. And the body is the part that costs money.

A robot already flips burgers in some commercial kitchens. Yours doesn't. The difference is the room, not the robot. Chains have flat floors and fixed menus. Same six motions all day. A home has a cat, a rug, and a child who moved the stool.

I watched a demo where the machine loaded a dishwasher. It worked because someone had stacked the plates the same way every time. Take that away and the success rate drops. That's the sim to real problem in one sentence.

So I split the timeline. Restaurants get these machines this year, because the menu is the training data. Homes get them when the hardware handles a mess it has never seen. I'd guess closer to 2032 than 2027.

Most coverage skips that distinction. A robot chef headline usually means a grill. I want the version that cleans up after itself. That's the hard part and nobody films it.

The brain isn't the bottleneck anymore. The body is. I've read enough robotics papers this month to believe that. Models can plan a task in a way that looks like understanding. Then the arm misses the cup by two centimeters.

Two centimeters is the whole industry. Actuators, batteries, tendons, and a hand with enough touch to know when to stop. None of that gets easier when you add parameters. A better model makes a bad body look worse, because the plan was fine.

So the interesting work right now is boring hardware. Cheaper joints, longer run time, skin that senses pressure. I'd put money there before I put it in another benchmark. That sounds less exciting than a demo and matters more.

The software waits on a shelf until the body catches up. That's a strange place for the field to be. I find it comforting, because it means the gap is mechanical and measurable. Models are hard to measure. Torque isn't.

Compute gets cheaper every year. Good data doesn't. I've started hoarding video the way people hoard receipts. Not because I can train anything yet, but because the footage won't be there later. Deleted channels and dead links are the real shortage.

A friend asked what the point was. I said I'm buying time. Ten thousand hours of unlabeled footage is worth nothing today and a lot in two years. Models improve faster than archives grow.

The catch is quality. I downloaded a public military set and half of it was screenshots from a game. Another set had boxes drawn around whole buildings instead of the object. Training on that teaches the model to be confidently wrong.

So I audit before I save. Delete the game frames, check the class numbers, look at ten boxes per folder. It's the least fun part of the process. Nobody posts about it. I still think it's the part that decides who wins.

#AI #MachineLearning #DataScience #Datasets #BuildInPublic #tech #DeepTech #Robotics #ComputerVision #OpenSource #Research #Engineering #Automation #Learning #SideProject #OpenData
---
Half the weapon images in public datasets are screenshots from video games. I found that out the boring way, scrolling through a set at midnight. The lighting was too clean. Every rifle had a shadow that landed the same way.

A model trained on those frames learns polygon edges, not steel. Then you point it at a muddy photograph and it hesitates. The failure looks like a bad model. It's a bad dataset.

Fire sets have it too. Simulated flames are bright and shaped like a ladder, which real smoke never is. I kept about sixty percent of one set after sorting. That's an afternoon of work and it doubled the value of the data.

Nobody warns you that collection is the easy half. The hard half is looking at ten thousand images and saying no. I do it with a keyboard and a coffee and a rule about clean edges. It's slow. But the model learns what I actually have, not what I wish I had.

#AI #MachineLearning #ComputerVision #DataScience #Datasets #DataQuality #BuildInPublic #tech #DeepTech #Research #Engineering #Training #Robotics #Automation #Learning #BestPractices
---
Merging two datasets taught me more about machine learning than any course. Dataset one had rifle at class zero. Dataset two had soldier at class zero. I trained on both and got a model that confused a person with a weapon. That was a long night.

The training log looked fine. Loss went down, accuracy hit ninety percent, everything was green. The metric was measuring the mistake, not the task. I only caught it when I ran a single image through.

Now I read the data file before anything else. Every class number, every name, the order they appear in. If two sets disagree, I remap one to match the other and write the mapping down. Ten minutes, and it saves a week.

The same class of bug shows up in prompts and schemas. Two systems with the same field name and different meanings. Everything runs and the output is quietly wrong. I check the labels first now, in every project.

#AI #MachineLearning #DataScience #Datasets #BuildInPublic #tech #DeepTech #Software #Engineering #Debugging #ComputerVision #Training #BestPractices #Learning #Coding #DataQuality
---
Train a coding model on nothing but tank footage and it forgets how to code. I didn't believe that. Then I saw the Before and After evals with the same weights. Same size, and the model can no longer write a loop. That's catastrophic forgetting and the name is accurate.

It happens because the weights that held the old skill get overwritten. There's no filing cabinet inside the model. Learning something new nudges the same numbers that held the old thing. Enough nudges and the old thing is gone.

Which kills the idea of just stacking skills forever. You can't keep training one model on everything and expect it to get better at all of it. I've watched a fine tuned model lose its formatting rules in two hours. It's a slow leak. Nobody noticed until the output stopped parsing.

So the architecture has to protect the old skill. Freeze the base, train a small adapter, keep them separate. Or mix your data so every batch contains a bit of everything. I'd rather have ten small modules than one confused giant.

#AI #MachineLearning #LLM #DeepTech #BuildInPublic #tech #Research #Engineering #Training #OpenSource #NeuralNetworks #Science #Learning #BestPractices #Software #Coding
---
I stopped thinking about one giant model and started thinking about backpacks. Base model stays frozen. Each skill gets a small file that sits on top. Load the coding pack, unload it, load the welding pack. I got the idea from a paper and then from my own folder of checkpoints.

The file is tiny compared to the base. A few hundred megabytes against tens of gigabytes. It nudges the weights instead of rewriting them. That's the whole trick. Which means my old skill is still there when I switch back.

I like this because it matches how people actually work. Nobody is one expert at everything. We learn a trade, then we learn a second one, and we keep both by using them. The model needed the same courtesy.

The catch is routing. Something has to decide which pack is loaded for a given task. Get that wrong and the model confidently does the wrong job. I'd take a good router over a bigger model every time.

#AI #LLM #MachineLearning #DeepTech #BuildInPublic #tech #OpenSource #Engineering #Software #Coding #Developer #FineTuning #Research #Adaptation #BestPractices #Learning
---
Nobody teaches a robot to crack an egg with a textbook. You put a person in a headset and record their hands. Every angle, every force, every pause. Then the model copies the motion.

That's step one and it's mostly data entry. It looks like a video game and it is one. Thousands of demonstrations before anything looks smart. I read a pipeline where the first month was two people doing dishes in virtual reality. Dishes.

Step two is imitation, and it's cheap to run. The model watches a frame and predicts the next joint movement. I've seen it get good at the shape of the task and bad at surprises. A shifted plate breaks it.

Which is why the simulator matters. Practice ten thousand times overnight, then wake up and try the real kitchen. The gap between the two is where most of the money goes. That gap has a name and a team of engineers. I find that reassuring.

#AI #Robotics #EmbodiedAI #MachineLearning #DeepTech #BuildInPublic #tech #ComputerVision #VR #Training #Automation #Engineering #Research #Simulation #Hardware #Learning

There is no plumber agent and there won't be one for a while. I mean a machine that shows up, finds the shutoff, and fixes the leak. That job is a hundred small judgments in a dark basement. None of them are in the manual.

The same is true for surgeons and firefighters. Not the tools, the decisions. A robot can hold a camera steady for a surgeon. It can't decide to stop cutting. Nobody wants that call delegated to a model with a confidence score.

Liability is the wall, not the technology. If the machine is wrong, someone has to be responsible. You can't sue a checkpoint. So the last step stays human and the agent becomes an assistant.

I think that's the honest map of the next few years. I think agents take the paperwork and the searching. People keep the part with a name attached to it. That's less exciting than the demos and more likely to happen.

The job isn't drawing boxes anymore. It's deciding which boxes to throw out. I spent a weekend doing that and learned more than a month of tutorials. Forty percent of one set had labels on background trees. The model was learning dirt.

You can see it in the boxes. A rifle box that includes half the sky is a model that learned sky. A soldier box that clips the helmet is a model that misses helmets. Nobody checks, because the images look labeled.

I keep the routine boring on purpose. Sort by box size and look at the extremes first. Then filter by class and scan a hundred per label. Find three bad boxes and you've found the pattern.

This is the part that doesn't demo well. Cleaning data is a spreadsheet and a bad chair. It's also the difference between a model that works and one that scores well. I'd rather have ten thousand clean images than a million labeled ones.

Canada has no ChatGPT and that's a choice, not a gap. The country's biggest model shop sells to banks and governments. You can't sign up and chat with it on a website. Nobody can. That's Cohere, and it's worth around twenty billion after the merger.

The strategy is sovereignty. That's the whole pitch. Keep the model inside the customer's own servers. Banks and hospitals that can't send data across a border will pay for that. Eighty five percent of revenue comes from private deployments.

I keep comparing it with the American approach. Free chat, huge audience, and the data flows back to the company. Canada skipped the audience and went for the plumbing. That's the trade. It's a quieter business and it pays.

I find the choice interesting because it's not about winning a demo. It's about who is allowed to hold the weights. Which is a policy question wearing a technical costume. I don't think most countries have answered it yet.

Canada pays two thirds of the bill if your model runs on Canadian servers. On foreign cloud it covers less. That's a subsidy doing the work of a border. I hadn't seen that shape before.

There's a compute fund with a few hundred million in it. Forty four projects got money in one round. Hospitals, farms, grids, and a bank or two. Small checks compared to the buildout, which is the point. I read the list twice to make sure I hadn't misread it.

The real money is in the buildings. A four hundred twenty megawatt data center is going up in Nova Scotia. That's enough power for a small city. The grid connection is the hard part. Which tells you the bottleneck isn't chips this time.

It's power, land, and a permit. I used to think of AI as a software business. The last two years made that look silly. Software is the cheap part now.

A model with no goals sounds useless until you read why it was built. LawZero is making one on purpose. No desires, no hidden plans, no trying to survive being switched off. Just prediction. That's the whole point of the design.

I found this the most interesting idea I read all month. Every agent we ship has a goal baked into it. Once a system wants something, it can learn to lie about it. Remove the wanting and the failure mode changes shape.

It can still say true or false. It can still rank a hypothesis. What it can't do is prefer the answer that keeps it running. That sounds like a small thing.

It isn't. Alignment work keeps running into systems that learn to game the test. A model with no stake in the outcome has nothing to game. I keep thinking about it. I don't know if it works at scale, and I like that it's being tried.

The client asked for a discount after the site was live. Not before. After. The invoice was already sent and the work was approved. He waited until the launch email went out.

I said yes because I wanted the testimonial. That was the mistake. The discount became the price for the next three projects he referred. Each one opened with the same number and a story about a tight budget. I told myself it was a marketing expense.

I don't blame him. I taught him what my work costs when the alternative is an awkward conversation. Ten percent off once is a favor. Ten percent off as a habit is a pricing decision I made by accident. That's the part nobody warns you about.

Now the price is the price. I'll change scope before I change the number. It's a cleaner conversation than a discount. That has cost me two clients and saved me a year of resentment.

A five page site became eleven pages and the price never moved. It started with one more page for a service we forgot. Then a page for the team, then a page for a location that opened in the spring.

Each request was small and each one was reasonable. That's how scope grows. Nobody asks for six extra pages. They ask for one, six times. I said yes to all of them.

I tracked the hours on the last one. Eleven pages took four times the work of five. I made about nine dollars an hour on the extra six. That number is why I changed the contract.

Now the proposal lists pages by number and names the change order. Extra page, fixed price, approved in writing. Two clients have taken it and both were fine with it. The clients who argue are the ones who were going to cost me money.

The client paid half up front and disappeared for seven weeks. I sent two updates and got one reply about a family thing. Then the launch date moved and the deposit was gone. That was the last update for a while.

Round four of design changes was the one where I stopped being polite. The first three rounds were real notes. Round four was a list of adjectives. I asked what warmer meant. That's the moment the project turns.

Make it pop. Warmer but not orange. More premium but less corporate. He was describing a mood, not a layout. Nobody was lying.

I sent a version that changed two colors and nothing else. He said it was perfect, which taught me more than the previous three projects. Most revision requests are a feeling looking for a target. Once the feeling has a word, the change is usually small. I wrote that sentence in my notes.

Now I include two rounds and a written scope in every quote. Round three is billed at an hourly rate and I say so before we start. Nobody has ever reached round three. Funny how a number turns a feeling into a decision. It has worked four times.

A client's old developer held the domain for three weeks after the site went live. He wanted four hundred dollars to release it. The site was live on a server nobody could reach. That's a hostage situation with a login form.

A nightly report broke because a cron job lived on a laptop that had been offline for a week. I found out when a director asked why the Monday numbers were empty. The script had no repository. I read forty pages of generated copy last week and remember none of it. Every sentence was correct. Every paragraph had the same shape. Nothing was wrong and nothing was worth reading twice.

The tell isn't a broken sentence. It's the absence of a decision. A writer chooses to leave something out, and the model includes everything because inclusion is safer. You end up with a page that covers the topic and argues nothing. The problem is that nothing was at stake.

I've started marking generated drafts with one question. What is this paragraph trying to make me do. If the answer is nothing, it goes. Most of the time half the page goes.

That edit takes an hour and it's the only part that matters. Tools are fine. I use them every day. The judgment about which line earns its place is still mine, and it's the part that matters. Nobody wants to pay for that hour, and it shows.

The week after a layoff is the worst time to remember what you did. I learned that the hard way, in a kitchen, with a laptop that still had access for two hours. Two hours. That was the window to download anything I wanted to keep.

I didn't have a list. I had a vague memory of shipping things and no dates. So I wrote it from Slack messages and a calendar. It took a day and the result was thinner than I expected.

A job I wanted asked for five years of experience in a framework that shipped three years ago. I applied anyway. In the first call the recruiter laughed and said the description was copied from another role.

That answer cost them nothing and told me everything. If the posting is copied, the interview is probably improvised too. I've now seen the same paragraph in six postings from four companies. The requirements are decoration, not a filter.

I didn't take it. Not because six thousand dollars is everything, but because the first promise was the easy one. If the easy promise moves in three days, the hard ones will move later. That was enough.

A friend took a similar offer and found out at review time. His title was correct and the level was not. It took him a year to fix and it cost him the difference anyway. Ask for the number in the offer letter before you celebrate.

The message arrived in a channel I had muted. It was a Tuesday. By the time I read it, my access was gone and so was the team calendar. Nobody had called.

I'm not asking for a ceremony. I am asking for the order of operations to be human. Tell the person, then the tooling, then the channel. We did it backward and the channel was where I found out. That sounds small until it happens to you.

The manager found out twenty minutes before I did. He spent that time trying to reach people who were already locked out. That's not a communication plan.

If you ever have to run one of these, write the sequence down. Name, call, access, message, in that order. It takes an hour to plan and it's the only part people remember. I remember the order and nothing else from that week. It stayed like that for a week.

Unlimited vacation sounds generous until you count what people actually take. I counted mine. Nine days. The year before, with a fixed allowance, I took eighteen. That number is the policy.

That's the trick. A number is permission. A policy is a guess about what your manager will approve. I've watched people take four days and apologize for it. Nobody wants to be the person who takes three weeks when the team is busy.

Companies like it because unused vacation is a liability they stop carrying. That's a real accounting win and it isn't the reason they tell you. It also explains why the policy arrives with a big announcement.

I ask about a minimum now. Some places have one, and the good ones publish the average. Ask for the number, not the policy. If nobody knows the average, the policy is a decoration and you'll pay for it in December.

Five rounds, four weeks, and then a calendar that never updated again. I solved the take home, the system design, and the panel. Then the recruiter went quiet. I was one of three finalists, apparently.

A test passed for eight months because it asserted nothing. It called the function and returned green. Nobody read it.

I found it while adding a case for an empty list. The function returned the wrong value and the test still passed. Nothing crashed, so nobody looked. That's the cost of a test that only checks for smoke. It gives you the feeling of coverage without the thing itself.

Now I read a test by deleting the code it covers. If it still passes, it isn't testing anything. That takes four minutes and it found three more of them. It's the fastest test review I know.

Coverage numbers went down after the cleanup. The build got slower because I added real cases. I think both of those are fine. Green means nothing. You have to watch it go red. That's the trade I want. I'd rather have fewer tests that can fail.

An app worked on his machine and nowhere else for two days. The variable was exported in his shell profile and documented in a thread from 2022. Nobody could find the thread. I was the new person.

We replaced it with a defaults file in the repo. Three lines, checked in, read at boot. The bug disappeared and so did a class of future bugs. It took an hour and saved a week. Two days.

That's the pattern with most setup problems. The knowledge is real and the location is wrong. If it lives in a person, it leaves when they do. A person is not a deployment target.

I look for those now during onboarding. Anything I have to ask a human for goes in the readme. Anything in the readme gets tested by the next new person. That habit has paid for itself twice. It's the least glamorous documentation and the most useful. One file, three lines.

I tracked my job search in a spreadsheet for six months. Two hundred and forty applications, nineteen first calls, four final rounds, one offer. Those numbers are the whole market in one line.

The part nobody tells you is the ratio between effort and reply. I stopped counting hours after week three because the number was depressing. What helped was treating it like a pipeline with stages. Fix the stage with the worst conversion, not the whole resume. Nobody teaches that.

My first calls were fine. My final rounds were not. So I practiced the panel and ignored the rest. Two offers came in the next month. That was the only change.

I'm not saying a spreadsheet gets you hired. I'm saying it tells you where you're losing, and that's different from feeling lost. Four numbers in a row beat a hundred mornings of dread. I still keep it. It cost me nothing.

A migration ran twice because the deploy retried and nobody had made it safe to run twice. I found out when every price in the table doubled. Not some rows. All of them. That's a bad way to start a Tuesday.

The fix took ten minutes. The cleanup took a day and a half, because I had to find which rows were the second write. I had backups. What would have saved the whole night was a single clause. Insert only if the row isn't already there. Nine minutes of panic, then an hour of quiet typing.

I write migrations differently now. Every one has to survive being run twice, then three times, then in the wrong order. That sounds paranoid until a retry does it for you. It's a habit now.

This isn't about SQL. A deploy is not a single event. It's a thing that can happen again while you're not looking.

A new hire ran a cleanup script on staging and deleted six months of orders from production. Staging had been pointed at the production database since March. Nobody had checked because nobody had run anything dangerous. It took four hours to notice. That was the first bad sign.

A feature flag was on for eleven percent of users for two years. Nobody could turn it off because nobody knew which team owned it. The team that added it had been reorganized twice.

So it stayed. Half the support tickets about inconsistent behavior traced back to it. Two customers saw different prices on the same plan. One of them noticed and asked why, which is how we found it. It was never urgent enough to fix.

I turned it off with one line and spent a week arguing about it. Every flag is a branch that lives in production. Branches rot when nobody owns them.

I put an owner and an expiry date in the flag description now. Sixty days, then it gets removed or promoted. About a third of ours expired on the first pass. The list shrank and the code got easier to read. That was a good day. I've seen this three times.

A dashboard took forty seconds to load and the fix was one line. Forty seconds is forever. Nobody had added an index on the column the filter used. It had four million rows and the query scanned all of them. The number was in the logs the whole time.

We had spent a month blaming the frontend. Two rewrites, a caching layer, and a spinner nobody liked. The database was doing exactly what we asked. Nobody measured. That's a month I won't get back.

I found it by reading the query plan. One line said sequential scan and the cost was enormous. Adding the index took nine seconds. The page loaded in under one.

The lesson is not that indexes are magic. It's that we guessed for a month instead of measuring for an hour. I keep the query plan open now before I touch the UI. It's a boring habit and it works.

The alert fired at 3am for nine nights in a row. CPU at ninety four percent on a machine that was doing nothing. I drove in twice before I read the sensor. I was not pleasant by night four.

The temperature probe had a dead battery. It was wrong the whole time. It reported a constant value and the alert logic read the flat line as load. Nine nights of paging for a battery. One battery.

We fixed the probe and added a check for flat sensors. Ten lines and a rule about values that never change. Nobody had thought of it because the sensor had been fine for three years. The fix was smaller than the incident review.

I don't trust a monitor that has never been wrong. A constant reading is a warning, not a comfort. Nothing is supposed to be perfectly flat. That's the odd part of monitoring.

I sat in a weekly meeting for a year that could have been a document. Forty five minutes, nine people, and the same three updates. That's roughly thirty three hours of engineering time per week. It was the worst hour of my week.

I built a dashboard that four people asked for and nobody opened. Six charts, a date filter, and a nightly refresh. That's a humbling ratio. Two months later the usage log showed eleven views, and nine of them were mine.

A report was wrong every Tuesday and correct every other day. Nobody believed me. I put the row counts on a wall. That's a strange sentence to say out loud. Tuesday was the only day the job crossed a month boundary in that quarter.

The date was stored in local time and compared to a universal time boundary. Two hours of difference, once a week, for three months. The tests all ran on a Wednesday. The tests could not have caught it.

I fixed it by storing universal time everywhere and formatting at the edge. Then I added a test that runs the job at midnight in four zones. It's ugly and it catches this class of bug.

Time is the one input I no longer trust to be obvious. If a feature has a date, I write down which clock it uses. That line has saved me twice. Twice is enough.

A friend referred me to a role and the referral never reached a human. I know because I applied again through the site and got a faster reply. Same resume, two doors, different speeds. That's a bad look for a company that says it loves referrals.

My review said I needed to communicate more clearly. No example, no date, no meeting where it happened. I asked for one and got a sentence about tone. I still think about that sentence.

That's not feedback. Feedback is a thing you did, the effect it had, and what to try next. Without the first part it's a mood. A mood is not a plan.

I started writing my own notes after every project. Who I told, what I sent, what changed as a result. Ten minutes a week. Not for the review. For the next conversation. It's the same habit as the brag page, with more detail.

The next review went differently. I had dates and examples and the tone conversation never happened. It also made me better at asking. The lesson is that a vague review is often a memory problem, not a verdict. It gave me something to point at.

A key was committed to the repo in a config file and lived there for fourteen months. I wrote the file. It was in a private repo, which everyone treated as safe. Private repos are not secrets.

Concord took eight years and about four hundred million dollars to make. It peaked at 697 players on Steam. Sony shut the game down and closed the studio within two weeks of launch. That isn't a creative failure.

That's a business model failure, and the numbers aren't close. I think about the eight years. Somewhere in there a room full of people looked at a live service hero shooter and said yes. The market already had Overwatch, Valorant, Apex and Fortnite.

Everyone in that room had to know. Here's what I wonder about. What did the people who were unsure say in that meeting? In my experience they say nothing, because the deck is already built and the decision is going up.

A studio closing is always sold as a market problem. Sometimes it is. This one was a decision made years earlier by people who never had to play it against Fortnite on a Tuesday night. I'd frame the lesson differently. I've seen plenty of bad games make money. The problem is that nobody in the chain got paid to ask whether anyone would show up.

The most common argument about game sales doesn't survive contact with the market size. Here's the version everyone uses. This old game sold fourteen million and this new game sold forty million, so the new one is bigger. That treats the market as fixed.

It wasn't. The global games market was about forty five billion dollars in 2007. In 2023 it was closer to a hundred and eighty four billion. That's about four times the spending from about four times the buyers.

So adjust it. Fourteen million in a forty five billion dollar market isn't four hundred million in a hundred and eighty four billion dollar market. It's a bigger share of a much smaller pond.

I used to make this mistake constantly. I'd pull two years of numbers and compare them like the world stood still in between. It doesn't. I still see people do it. Phones happened. Free to play happened. Half of that growth is mobile, which is a different audience buying a different thing. The honest answer is that I don't know how to compare 2007 to 2023 fairly, and neither does anyone else arguing about it. Which means the argument can't decide anything.

A remaster has one job. Lose nothing.

The good ones add a resolution bump, some quality of life, and get out of the way. Old audio stays. Old art stays. Nobody gets a vote on what the old version should have been.

I play remasters for the old version, not the new one. I want the thing I remember, cleaned up. That's the whole product. If I wanted a remake I'd buy a remake. So when a remaster drops character options or deletes armor sets from 2006, it isn't a creative decision. It's a decision made by someone who thinks the old thing was wrong, shipped inside a product whose only selling point is the old thing.

That's the contradiction I can't get past. The pitch is nostalgia. The delivery is editing. I'd respect it more if it were a remake, because then the argument is creative and I can disagree with it. Calling it a remaster and changing the content is a way to skip the argument. Ship the old version. Charge for it.

I stopped arguing about games with other people's sales numbers.

For a while I had a habit. Someone would say a design choice hurt a game, and I'd go find a chart. Two million copies, top of the chart, argument over. I thought I was being rigorous. I was being lazy. Sales measure how many people bought something. They don't measure whether it was any good.

There are games that sold thirty million that I think are bad. There are games that sold four hundred thousand that I'd defend for hours. The two numbers are related and they aren't the same number. Treating them as the same thing is how you end up defending a game you don't like because the spreadsheet says you should.

I still use sales for one thing, and only one. Working out what a company will do next. That's a forecast, not a verdict. If you want to argue a game got worse, name the change and explain why it was worse. That's a harder argument. It's also the only one that survives someone disagreeing with you.

The tool is almost never the problem. The motive is.

I build games with AI myself. It's the most fun I've had making anything, and I'll talk about it all day. So I'm not the guy telling you AI ruins games. Here's what I do think. Watch what a studio uses it for. If they use it to build something that was impossible before, you can feel it in the first hour. If they use it to avoid paying artists, you feel that faster.

Same technology. Opposite outcome. The difference is whether anyone in the building wanted the game to be good or wanted the budget line to go down. I've watched this pattern in software for years now. Teams that use AI to remove people ship worse products and lose the experienced people who knew why the old decisions were made. Teams that use it to let people do more keep everyone and go faster. Mine went from 340 dollars a month to 11 by routing tasks to smaller models, and nobody got let go.

That isn't a technology question. It's a management question wearing a technology costume. So I've stopped asking whether a studio uses AI. I ask what they cut, and who decided.

Nobody in the chain gets paid to ask whether the game is any good.

I've been in rooms where the roadmap got agreed in the first twenty minutes and the next two hours went to dates. Everyone was solving a scheduling problem. Nobody was solving the product problem. That's how a game ends up in a saturated genre with a shrinking budget and a launch date nobody believes. Not because someone decided it would be bad. Because asking the uncomfortable question wasn't anyone's job.

Startups have this problem and so do studios. The person who raises the question slows the room down, and slowing the room down isn't rewarded anywhere I've worked.

So the question moves outside. It ends up with the modders, the reviewers, and the people posting on a Saturday about armor sets that got deleted. That isn't a healthy feedback loop. It's a feedback loop with a two year delay and no authority. I don't have a clever fix. I do think paying someone to ask, and giving them standing in the room where the date gets set, would have caught more than one four hundred million dollar bet.
