AI companies spent a fortnight warning that advanced models could escape human control. The same companies are shipping those models and selling the compute behind them.

I don't think that's hypocrisy in the simple sense. It's worse and more ordinary. A lab that believes it's building something dangerous also believes the responsible move is to build it carefully, in house, rather than let somebody less careful do it first.

That logic is airtight. It's also a licence to keep going. I've seen the same structure in weapons programmes and in finance, where the risk argument becomes the argument for the budget. That's the structure.

So I read the warnings as a real signal about their own uncertainty. The people with the most information are the least sure, and that's worth taking seriously.

What I won't do is treat the warning as a licence. A company that says the thing is dangerous and keeps building has told you which of those two beliefs it acts on. I'd rather judge the actions.

Four studios shut in one afternoon. All four had shipped something people liked. I want to sit on that fact for a second.

The instinct is to look for the bad game. There isn't one. There's a portfolio review, a target margin, and a list of teams that cost more than the plan allowed.

That's what I mean when I say motive beats tool. If the business model needs a hit rate that no studio can deliver, then no tool saves you. Not AI, not a bigger team, not a longer schedule. The arithmetic was decided in a room that never saw the code.

I've shipped work that got cancelled for reasons that had nothing to do with the work. It's the most common story in this industry and the least told, because the press release always frames it as a realignment.

So here's my line. Judge the decision, not the tool. Ask what number moved, who moved it, and whether anyone with a shipped game on their record got a vote. Most of the time the answer is no.

I don't think this needs a moral lecture. It needs a question. If the studio was worth keeping the games from, what changed in eleven days that made the people optional. Nobody has answered that one yet.

Rare earths and magnets are the least exciting sentence in the energy story and the one that decides the most. I've followed this chain for a while and the shape never changes.

Mining is the part people talk about. Refining and magnet making are the parts that bind and both of those are concentrated in a small number of places, and both of those are concentrated in a small number of places for reasons that are part technical and part environmental. Nobody wants the acid in their county.

That's the trap. Every country wants the turbines and the motors and none of them wants the middle of the supply chain. So the middle stays where it is and everybody builds on a dependency they've said out loud they'd like to remove. The middle is the story.

I've watched two attempts to restart domestic refining and both bumped into the same wall. The permitting is slow and the neighbours are organized, and the neighbours have a point.

So my read is that this decade ends with the same map and a lot more rhetoric. I'd rather fund the boring middle than buy another study about it.

Grid batteries are the part of the energy transition that actually shipped, and I don't think most people have noticed. I've watched a substation add a container yard and turn a peak problem into a scheduling problem.

That's the whole trick. A battery doesn't make power. It moves it four hours later, and four hours happens to be the gap between the sun going down and the evening load. That gap is what everyone argued about for twenty years.

I've read the case against the batteries and some of it is fair. They don't solve a windless week. They do solve the daily cycle, and they're buildable in eighteen months without a new transmission line.

That last part is why I care. It's a cheap answer that doesn't need federal approval, and cheap answers that clear a local hurdle get built while the elegant ones sit in a queue.

I don't know how far the curve goes. I know the container yard arrived before the reactor did, and that ordering matters.

Hydrogen got sold as the answer to everything and it's turned into the answer to about three things. I've watched that correction happen and I think it was healthy.

The pitch was heat, transport, industry, power. The reality is refining, ammonia and a few industrial processes where nothing else fits. That's not a failure. It's a smaller, more honest market.

I've watched the same correction in other technologies. A tool gets marketed as universal, the easy cases get funded, and the hard cases go back to the old solution. The hard cases were never the point.

What I'd keep an eye on is the electrolyser cost curve and the hours it runs. A machine that runs a third of the time pays back three times slower, and that arithmetic is what killed the early projects.

So my position is that hydrogen stays a chemical feedstock play for now and a heat play later. Boring, smaller than the slide deck, and much closer to the truth.

Low orbit is getting crowded and the debris problem is arithmetic rather than prophecy. I've read the conjunction reports and the number that matters is tracked objects.

Here's the shape. Two objects crossing a kilometre apart is not a near miss at orbital speed. It's a coin flip nobody can call, and each collision creates thousands of pieces that then threaten everything else at that altitude.

I've watched the industry argue about whose responsibility the cleanup is. The answer is that nobody wants it, because removing junk produces no revenue and the cost lands on the operator who pays now for a risk that arrives in a decade.

That's why I think the rule has to be a deposit rather than a treaty. You pay at launch, you get it back when you deorbit. Same logic as a bottle return and the same reason it works. It works. Ask any bottle. The incentive sits at the moment of the decision.

I don't know if it passes. I do know the sky is a shared resource and shared resources get overused until somebody prices the exit.

Webb dropped another result in August and the reaction split into two camps before anybody read the paper. That split's the interesting part.

I read the abstract first, then the methods, then the numbers. If the numbers hold, the conclusion is a footnote. If the numbers don't hold, the conclusion is a press release.

That's my whole process and it takes twenty minutes. I've watched people argue for a week about a finding they haven't opened. Twenty minutes beats a week. By a mile.

I keep coming back to one number. Webb sends down something like 235 gigabytes a day. A team sits inside that and finds one thing worth announcing. The finding gets shared a million times. The pipeline gets shared once. Not twice. Once.

So when I write about space I try to write about the pipeline. Instruments, calibration, the people who check the calibration. That layer is where the result comes from and it's the layer nobody claps for.

A new telescope result isn't a fact. It's an argument with error bars attached, and the error bars are where I start reading.

I've done this long enough to have habits. I look for the sample size. I look for whether the effect is marginal or large. I look for a second instrument backing the first one. Most of the time the answer to all three is thin.

That'sn't a criticism of the scientists. It's how knowledge works. A marginal result from one instrument is a lead, not a discovery, and the paper usually says so in language the press release drops.

The press release is the problem. Nobody writes the headline in the paper. Somebody in a communications office writes it, and the communications office has a different job than the researcher.

So my advice is boring. Read the paper. Read the numbers. If you can't read the paper, read the methods section anyway, because the methods section is where the caveats live. I'll keep doing that and I'll keep saying when I get it wrong.

Google reported an error correction result in February where adding more qubits lowered the error rate instead of raising it. That threshold is the whole ballgame in quantum.

I'll explain it in one paragraph because most coverage skips it. A quantum machine is noisy. You fix noise with redundancy, so you need many physical qubits per logical one. If the extra qubits bring more noise than protection, the machine can never scale. Crossing that line means scaling becomes a design problem rather than a wall. That's the line.

I read that as a physics milestone and not a product. The gap between a logical qubit that beats the threshold and a machine that factors a useful number is enormous, and it's filled with engineering.

I've watched quantum coverage for a decade and it swings between fifteen years away and next Tuesday. Both are wrong. Every time. The honest version is that the physics got a lot better this year and the schedule didn't.

So I'd keep watching the coherence numbers and ignore the stock moves. The numbers are real. The moves are a mood.

Quantum error correction crossed a threshold this year and I want to be careful about what that doesn't mean.

It doesn't mean encryption is broken. Nothing close. It doesn't mean a useful machine ships in 2027. It means the scaling argument changed from impossible to expensive, and expensive is a category engineers know how to attack.

I've read three results in this space now and they share a shape. A modest number of logical qubits, a small improvement per qubit added, and a paper that's honest about the gap to anything commercial.

The gap is the story. Filling it requires fabrication, cryogenics and control electronics at a scale nobody has built. Each of those is a decade of its own if it goes wrong.

I keep writing this because the hype cycle keeps running ahead of the papers. The papers are good. That's all they are. They aren't a product, and the difference matters to anyone deciding where to spend the next five years.

I pay attention to who benefits from a story before I decide whether it's true. That habit has saved me more times than any fact check.

The easy version is to call it cynicism. It'sn't. It's just accounting. Every narrative has a beneficiary, and knowing who that's tells you which details got emphasised and which got dropped.

I do this with AI stories and with games stories and with energy stories, and the answer is almost always the same. The person who commissioned the framing is the person whose number improves if you believe it.

That doesn't make the story false. Most distortion is selective rather than invented. Somebody picked which three facts to put in the first paragraph and which twelve to leave out, and the choice was made by a person with a job.

So when I read anything I ask two questions. What does the source want, and what would change my mind. If I can't answer the second one, I'm not reading. I'm being read to.

I've watched the hiring market for two years and the change in entry level roles is the signal I trust most, because it's the hardest to fake.

A layoff gets announced. A graduation rate gets reported. A junior position that never opened shows up nowhere. That third one is where the damage accumulates and it's the one that can't be measured.

I've advised a few people through this. The advice changed this year. Apply for the jobs that exist and build the skill that gets used in the job you want, because the gap between the two is bigger than it used to be.

That's not a cheerful answer. I know. But I've watched people burn a year applying to closed doors, and the people who did something visible in that year ended up fine.

The market decides the doors. You decide what's on the other side when one opens.

A study with a small sample can still be worth reading. A study with a small sample presented as a large one is not.

I've read enough papers to have a habit and the habit is cheap. I find the number of participants before I read the conclusion, because the conclusion is written to sound complete and the sample size tells you how complete it can be.

There's a case I keep in mind. A sensitivity figure from a handful of patients got repeated in coverage as a general claim about a test. The paper didn't say that. The coverage did, and the coverage was built from the abstract. Nobody lied. Somebody compressed, and compression is how errors travel.

That's the failure mode I care about. Not fraud. Compression. A finding travels one step and loses its error bars on the way.

So my rule is to read the methods section before I repeat anything. It takes twenty minutes and it has stopped me from posting something wrong at least a dozen times this year.

Reproducibility gets treated as a bureaucratic chore. I think it's the most interesting part of science.

Here's why. A result you can reproduce is a result you can build on. A result you can't is a story, and stories don't stack. Every lab that publishes a method is either saving somebody a year or costing them one, and there's no middle.

I've watched this in software. Code that ships with tests gets used. Code that ships with a promise gets rewritten by the next person, and the rewrite takes longer than the tests ever would have.

So when I read about a discovery I want to know whether anybody else has run it since. Not because I doubt the finding. Because the second run is the evidence that matters for anybody downstream.

That's my position on the whole thing. Replication isn't a formality. It's the product. Everything else is a claim.

I've been asked five times this year how to pick what to write about. My answer is a filter with three questions and the first one does most of the work.

In the western United States, planned data centers average about 10 percent of the grid region's forecast demand. In some areas they run as high as 40 percent. Forty percent.

Forty percent of a forecast is not a line item. I keep watching this get reported as an AI story and it isn't. It isn't. It's a construction story with an AI label, because the thing that takes years is the transmission line. Not the chip.

A data center can go up in eighteen months. The substation and the lines into it take longer, and the permitting takes longer than that. So demand arrives while the grid is still in a hearing. That's a queue.

One estimate puts data centers at about 9 percent of United States electricity generation by 2030. Another puts consumption growth at 15 percent a year. That's four years away.

Nine percent in four years is a lot of new generation, and almost none of it exists yet. So either the forecast is wrong, or this is the biggest infrastructure project in the country. I don't hear it described that way.

The grid is the bottleneck and almost nobody wants to talk about it. Everyone wants to talk about the model, the chip or the fusion reactor.

Two plans, one total, and the math picks the plan for you.

Both plans come to five hundred dollars. The difference is how fast you pay it. Twenty five a month for twenty four months is the slow lane. Forty five a month for twelve months clears the same bill a year sooner.

Cash flow drove the design. A new shop with a build out behind it needs the smaller number. An established business that just wants the site done hates seeing the charge on the books for two years.

I priced the fast plan higher per month because the work is the same either way and the risk sits with me longer on the slow one. People ask if they can switch. Pay the difference and move up whenever you want. I've never had anyone move down.

The site is the same at both prices. Same build, same hosting, same edits. You're picking a payment shape, not a tier.

I built this for the shop owner who wants a real site and doesn't want to think about it again. No dashboard to learn, no plugin updates, no hosting bill on a card that expired. I'll take your menu and your phone number and do the rest.

I rebuilt it in nine days. No template. Homepage, insurance list, staff photos, and a booking form that sends her an email. The form was the whole point, since new patients kept landing on a competitor with an online scheduler.

Her plan is twenty five a month over two years. She picked the long one because the practice is still paying off equipment. Forty five a month clears the same five hundred in a year, and she didn't want the bigger number in January.

Two weeks is realistic when you send me what I ask for. Two months is what happens when the photos never arrive. That's the only part I can't control.

I opened my brokerage statement last week and found a fee I never agreed to.

Twelve dollars a year. Small enough that I ignored it for three years without asking a question. Then I added the three years up and got thirty six dollars.

The fee was a 0.75 percent expense ratio on a fund I picked in a hurry. Nobody at the brokerage hid it or buried it in fine print. It sat in the prospectus. I never opened the file because the app doesn't ask me to. That's a design choice working as intended, and it isn't a scandal.

Index funds in the same account charge 0.03 percent for the same stocks. Same market, different wrapper. The gap compounds. I moved the money in March and now the fee line doesn't show. On 20,000 dollars the old fee was 144 dollars a year.

I check the expense ratio before I check the past performance now, and I don't trust the app to remind me. The document that tells says everything and sells nothing. Nobody reads it. Read it once and the fee stops being invisible.

I keep the receipt from a grocery run in January next to the same list from June.

Same store and same items. I paid eleven dollars more and nothing on the list had changed. The difference wasn't one item but every item by a few cents.

A basket of bread, milk, eggs, coffee and rice tells the story better than a headline. None of it looked expensive at the shelf. The coffee went from 9 to 11 dollars in six months. I noticed because I buy the same bag every month and the price tag moved twice. That works out to 22 percent on one item, which isn't a rounding error.

Official inflation numbers spread the rise across hundreds of goods. Your basket isn't the official basket. An index includes things you never buy and weights them by average spending. I rent, so the housing line touches me differently than a mortgage. Nobody publishes your personal rate.

I started writing ten prices on a note each month. It takes four minutes and it ends the argument. Two of those prices went down. You can't manage what you don't measure, and you can't feel what you don't write down.

I bought one stock in 2021 because a friend wouldn't stop talking about it.

Down 62 percent. I still own it, which is the part that tells you something about me.

The company was fine. The price wasn't. I paid 38 times earnings for a business growing 12 percent a year, and the multiple was the entire thesis. Nobody explained that to me because I never asked. I read one article and a group chat.

What I do now takes ten minutes. I look at the earnings yield, which is the inverse of the price to earnings ratio. At 38 times, that's 2.6 percent. A treasury bill paid 4 percent at the time. I was paying more for less certainty and calling it growth.

I haven't sold because the tax hit is real and the business still earns money. I also haven't added a dollar. It sits there as a receipt for a decision I made in an afternoon. Cheaper than a course, honestly.

I sat through an earnings call last quarter and learned more about one company than a year of headlines.

Forty minutes. Two analysts asked the same question in different words and got two different answers.

The prepared remarks were a press release read out loud. The useful part came in the questions, where a manager had to say a number without a slide behind him. He said inventory was up 18 percent and demand was flat. That sentence explained the next three months better than the guidance did.

Guidance is a forecast the company controls the framing of. Inventory is a fact that shows up in the balance sheet whether they like it or not. I started reading the cash flow statement first for that reason. It is harder to dress up.

I don't trade on any of this. I own two funds and a small position I already told you about. But reading one call a quarter made me stop treating a headline as information. It is a summary of a summary.

I ran the rent versus buy numbers for my own apartment twice, a year apart.

Both times the answer changed. That's the whole problem with the advice.

At a 6.9 percent mortgage on a 700,000 dollar place, the interest alone is 48,000 dollars in year one. Rent for the same apartment is 3,400 a month, or 41,000 a year. Add taxes, insurance and maintenance and buying costs more in cash for the first several years. The equity build is real but slow at the start.

The calculator I used showed break even at year nine. Change the rate to 5 percent and it drops to year six. Change the down payment and it moves again. Nobody who tells you renting is throwing money away has run their own numbers at today's rate.

I rent and I invest the difference. That works for me because I might move. If I were staying fifteen years the answer flips and I would buy. The math isn't moral. It is arithmetic with a time horizon attached.

I've been hearing the word bubble since 2019 and the index is higher than it was.

Up 80 percent. The people who called it were early by five years, which is the same as wrong if you had money in cash.

A bubble is a claim about future returns, and nobody can date one in advance. What you can measure is what you pay. The forward earnings multiple today is around 21. In 1999 it touched 30. In 2008 it was 14. That range tells you more than the label does.

The honest version is that expected returns are lower when prices are high, and that's all. It doesn't tell you when. It doesn't tell you how much. It says the next decade probably pays less than the last one, which is a boring sentence with no tweet in it.

I keep buying the same amount every month. Not because I'm brave. Because I know I can't pick the month, and the plan removes the decision.

I refinanced nothing in 2020 and I regret it about once a month.

My rate is 4.9 percent. The average that year was near 3. Some people locked 2.6.

The math on my loan is 340,000 dollars over 30 years. At 4.9 the payment is 1,804 dollars. At 3 percent it is 1,433. That's 371 dollars a month, or 4,452 dollars a year, for the life of the loan. Over thirty years it is more than 133,000 dollars.

I didn't refinance because I assumed the paperwork was worse than it was. I never called anyone. I never got a quote. That isn't a decision, it is a default, and defaults are expensive.

The lesson is smaller than the money. I now get a quote for anything that costs more than 2,000 dollars a year. Insurance, internet, the mortgage. Three phone calls. The quotes are free and the gap between the first and the best is usually worth an afternoon.

I read about the Silicon Valley Bank run in March 2023 and the thing that struck me was the speed.

16 billion dollars withdrawn in one day. The bank was gone in 48 hours.

A bank run used to require a line of people outside a building. Now it requires a group chat. Deposits move at the speed of a phone tap, and the people moving them can see each other doing it. That changes the arithmetic of every balance sheet in the system.

The other part is the bond portfolio. The bank held long duration securities bought at low rates. When rates rose, those assets fell in value on paper. It was solvent in the accounting sense and illiquid in the real one. Customers figured that out before the regulators said it out loud.

I moved part of my savings to a treasury bill after that week. Not because my bank was in trouble. Because I realized I had never asked what it held. One question I should have asked years earlier.

I walked past a half empty office building in downtown Brooklyn and asked the guard how many floors were leased.

Four of eleven. The building opened in 2019.

That's a 36 percent occupancy rate in a new tower, and it isn't unusual in that part of the city. The leases were signed before remote work settled into a pattern. Now the tenants pay for space they use two days a week and the landlord can't lease it again at the old rate.

The knock on effects are slow and real. Retail on the ground floor needs foot traffic. Foot traffic needs workers. Property tax revenue needs valuations that assume full buildings. When those break, the city budget feels it two years later.

I don't own any of this. I rent an apartment and own two index funds. But the empty tower is a better indicator of what's happening downtown than any report I've read. You can see it from the sidewalk.

I looked at what the big cloud companies are spending on data centers this year.

Roughly 200 billion dollars across the largest few, and the number keeps getting revised up.

That money is real and it shows up somewhere. Chips, buildings, power contracts, cooling. It is why construction employment has held up and why utilities are revising load forecasts for the first time in 20 years. It is also why the companies doing the spending have to earn a return on it eventually.

The part I watch is depreciation. A building lasts 30 years. A chip is obsolete in three. If the useful life assumption is generous, earnings are flattered today and the bill arrives later. Every capex cycle has this argument and it always sounds the same.

I own a broad index, so I own both the spenders and the people selling to them. I'm not making a bet either way. I'm noting that a 200 billion dollar tide is a strange thing to call a rounding error.

I had never heard of private credit until a fund manager explained it to me at a wedding.

1.7 trillion dollars in loans made outside the banking system. That number was 400 billion a decade ago.

The pitch is simple. Banks stopped lending to mid sized companies after 2008 because the rules made it expensive. Funds stepped in, raised money from pensions, and charged a spread for the service. For a while it worked and the returns were good.

The risk is that nobody knows what these loans are worth. They don't trade on an exchange. They're marked by the manager, quarterly, using models. In a calm year that's fine. In a stressed year the marks are a guess and the people guessing have a fee tied to the number.

I don't own any. Not because I think it fails, but because I can't measure it and I've a rule about that. If I can't explain how the price is set, I don't buy the thing. It has cost me some returns and a lot of sleep.

I got a 3 percent raise in a year when prices rose 6.

So my pay went up and my life got smaller. That's a pay cut in real terms.

The company called it a strong year. From their side it was. Revenue grew 9 percent and the raise pool was set at 3 to protect margins. The math inside a company isn't the math inside a household, and the two are compared constantly in a way that helps neither.

What I could do was limited. I asked for 6 and got 3.5. I got the number up by bringing the inflation print to the meeting, which was awkward and effective. I then moved 2 percent of my spending to cheaper substitutes without announcing it to anyone.

The real answer is that wages reset on a slower clock than prices. That gap is why a good year can feel like standing still. It closes when you change jobs, which is a sad fact about how pay works and a true one.

I bought gold once, in 2020, and sold it in 2021 for roughly what I paid.

Net of the spread, I lost 3 percent. It was a lesson in what a hedge actually costs.

Gold pays no coupon and no dividend. Its price is a vote on what other people will pay later. That isn't a criticism. It has held purchasing power over long stretches and it does well when real rates are negative. It just doesn't produce anything while you hold it.

The reason I bought was fear and the reason I sold was boredom. Neither is a thesis. If I wanted insurance against a bad outcome I should have sized it at 5 percent and left it alone for 20 years. I put 15 percent in and checked it twice a day.

I now own none. My hedge is a treasury bill and a smaller mortgage. Less exciting, easier to explain, and it doesn't require me to have an opinion about the mood of the world on a Tuesday.

I paid 4 dollars a gallon for gas in July and 3.40 in October.

Fifteen percent down in three months and nobody wrote a story about it.

Gas is the most visible price in the economy and the least stable. It moves on crude, refining capacity and a hundred local factors. The drop happened because crude fell and a refinery came back online, which is a supply story with no political punch.

The interesting part is behavior. When gas went up, everyone noticed and adjusted. When it came down, the adjustment stayed. I was still driving less and combining trips in October even though the price had fallen. That's a real restraint that outlives the price move.

Retailers know this. Prices are sticky downward for a reason. Once a customer accepts a new level of spending, very few go back to the old one. The gas station doesn't need to ask twice.

I added up my streaming subscriptions and got 61 dollars a month.

Four services and one of them I hadn't opened in 11 weeks.

I cancelled three subscriptions and two of them charged me again.

Both said the cancel hadn't gone through. One had a cancel button that led to a chat window.

This is a dark pattern, and it is common enough that regulators in several countries now require an easy path to cancel. The cost of making it hard is paid by the customer in time, and time is the one currency most people can't buy back at scale.

I now cancel by email so there's a written record and a date. I screen the confirmation. If it doesn't arrive in five minutes I send a second note and copy my bank. It sounds paranoid. It has worked every time.

The total tied up was 38 dollars a month. That's 456 a year, and I had to fight for it. The fight is the product. A company that earns revenue from people forgetting will always make leaving harder than joining. That's the business model working as designed, and my only defense is a calendar reminder.

I looked at tuition for a state school near me and the number was 29,000 a year.

That's in state, before housing. Four years is 116,000 dollars, and that's the cheap version.

The cost has grown faster than inflation for four decades and the reason isn't one thing. State funding per student fell, administration grew, and the federal loan system let schools raise prices without losing applicants. The last one is the key. If someone will lend any amount to an 18 year old with no income, the price stops being constrained by what families can pay.

I'm not saying college is a bad buy. The earnings premium is real and large. I'm saying the sticker price and the loan that pays it were designed together, and the person signing has the least information in the room.

What I would do now is start at a community college and transfer. Same degree, half the cost, one honest conversation about what the first two years actually deliver. Nobody in my family did that. We should have.

I've been freelancing for six years and my income has never been smooth.

Last year the range was 2,100 in February and 14,800 in October. Same work, same clients.

That variance is the hidden cost of working for yourself. A salary is a smoothed version of the same risk, and the employer charges for the smoothing by keeping the difference. Most people never see it because the number arrives the same every two weeks.

The tool that fixed my sleep was a 12 month average. I pay myself from the average, not from the month. In a good month the surplus sits in the account. In a bad month I take the same amount and nobody notices. It is a fake salary and it works.

The other thing is a tax reserve. 30 percent of every payment moves to a separate account the day it lands. I've never once been short in April since I started doing that. Six years, no panic. That's the whole system.

I counted eleven empty storefronts on one block of Bay Ridge last month. Two of them had been busy shops when I moved in. Nobody put a sign up. The windows just went dark.

Rent on that block runs about four thousand a month for a thousand square feet. A bakery needs roughly two hundred customers a week to cover that. That's a lot of bread. I asked the landlord of the corner unit why he doesn't drop the price. He said the number on the lease is the number he needs for the building loan.

So the unit sits empty for eighteen months instead. I've watched that math a dozen times now. An empty shop costs him less than a cheap tenant. That's the whole calculation. Vacancy is a price he can carry and a discount is a price he can't.

I don't think he is wrong about the loan. I think the street pays for it. Fewer shops means fewer reasons to walk down that block. Eleven empty windows is what that looks like from the sidewalk.

Commercial leases in this neighborhood run ten years. A ten year lease at four thousand a month is four hundred eighty thousand dollars. That's the number nobody says out loud at signing. I say it out loud now.

The landlord wants ten years because the loan is ten years. I understand that. He also wants a personal guarantee. That means the lease follows you home. One bad year and the guarantee is the thing that ends you.

I've asked three owners what happens if they need out. Two said they would sublet. One said he had never thought about it. The lease said nothing about subletting. Ten years is a long time to be wrong about a street.

I tell shop owners to negotiate the exit before the rent. A shorter term costs more per month and buys a way out. That trade is worth pricing. Four hundred eighty thousand dollars deserves an exit clause.

A state grid failed in February 2021 and the post mortem is more interesting than the outage. Generators tripped, demand spiked, and the frequency fell fast enough that operators had to shed load on purpose. Millions lost power in weather the system was never designed for. The report runs to hundreds of pages.

I've read the summary twice. The failures compound, which is the part that stays with me. A gas plant loses supply, then a pipe freezes, then a backup fails because it wasn't ever tested at that temperature. Each item was survivable alone. Together they took out a region.

What I took from it is that redundancy is only redundancy if it survives the same event. Two systems that depend on the same fuel or the same weather aren't really two systems. Nobody's writing that down because it looks fine on a diagram.

I check that assumption in my own work now. Two backups on one machine isn't a backup. It's one machine with extra steps.

Gravitational wave detectors measure a change in length smaller than a proton across four kilometres. The trick isn't the laser. It's everything else. Mirrors isolated from traffic, from tides, from the footsteps of people in the building.

I've read about the suspension systems and stopped halfway to think. Each mirror hangs from a chain of pendulums that's designed to cancel vibration at different frequencies. The whole apparatus sits on seismic isolation that would embarrass a laboratory bench.

What surprised me is how much of the design is about ignoring the world. A detector that hears everything is useless unless it can also hear almost nothing, and that's the hard part. The engineering is subtraction.

I like that idea more than the discovery itself. Most precision work is the removal of noise, and the noise is usually the environment you built the thing in. That's not a physics problem at all.

#Science #Physics #Astronomy #Research #STEM #GravitationalWaves #Engineering #Measurement #Laboratory #ScientificMethod #Technology #Space #ScienceCommunication #Data #Precision #Future #PhysicsResearch #Instrumentation
---
The cosmic microwave background is the oldest light there's and it's about the temperature of deep space. Roughly 2.7 kelvin, left over from a universe that was once hot and opaque. Every direction you look, the same faint glow.

I find it strange that this is the strongest evidence we've for the big bang. It's not a photograph of an explosion. It's a measurement of uniformity, with tiny ripples in it that grew into galaxies. The ripples are the point. Without them, nothing would have clumped.

What I hadn't appreciated is how much of cosmology is statistics on a map. You take the temperature differences across the sky, break them into scales, and the pattern tells you the age and the composition. It's a spectrum, not a picture.

I think about that when people say the model is just a story. It's a story with numbers attached to almost every pixel of the sky, and the numbers weren't chosen to fit.

#Science #Physics #Astronomy #Cosmology #Space #Research #STEM #Astrophysics #ScienceCommunication #ScientificMethod #Data #Measurement #Statistics #Universe #Technology #Future #PhysicsResearch #SpaceExploration
---
Half of published psychology findings failed to reproduce in a large attempt in 2015. The field has spent a decade fixing it. I used to read that as evidence the whole enterprise was rotten.

I read it differently now. The failure was found by scientists, published in a science journal, and paid for by science funding. That's the system working, slowly, on itself.

What changed is boring and effective. Pre registration of hypotheses. Publishing the data with the paper. Journals that accept a null result. None of it is glamorous and all of it reduces the space for wishful analysis.

The part I find hard is the incentive. A null result still doesn't get you a job. Careers run on novel findings, so the pressure to publish the surprising thing survives even after everyone agrees it's the problem. Fixing methods is easier than fixing incentives.

I try to remember that when I read a single study. One paper is a data point, not a fact.

Cities run hotter than the fields around them and the difference is often several degrees at night. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat all day and release it slowly. Air conditioners dump more heat into streets that already can't cool down.

I'd read a study that mapped surface temperature block by block and the pattern was almost a street map of tree cover. Where there were trees, it was cooler. Where there was asphalt, it wasn't. The effect was larger than I expected.

What complicates the fix is that shade and housing compete for the same space. Street trees need soil, water and a maintenance budget that outlives the planting. A canopy that takes twenty years to grow doesn't show up in a two year plan.

I find this the most understandable climate problem we've. It's local, it's measurable, and the intervention is a tree. That's rare enough to be worth saying.

Space debris is a physics problem with an economic solution that nobody wants to pay for. Objects in low orbit travel at about seven kilometres a second, so a fleck of paint carries the energy of a bullet. A collision creates thousands of pieces that create more collisions.

I'd read about the Kessler idea and it's simpler than it sounds. Past a certain density, collisions become self sustaining even if we launch nothing else. The debris doesn't fall fast enough to clear itself, because there's almost no drag up there.

What's changed is tracking. We can now see objects down to a few centimetres and warn operators, which prevents some collisions. It doesn't remove anything. Avoidance isn't cleanup.

I find it strange that the cheapest fix is also the hardest to agree on. Everyone benefits from a cleaner orbit and nobody owns it. That's the whole problem in one sentence.

A spectrum is the closest thing astronomy has to a fingerprint and it's how we know what anything out there's made of. Each element absorbs specific wavelengths, so the gaps in the light tell you the composition of whatever the light passed through.

I'd read about how this was first done on the sun and the audacity of it is what sticks. Nobody had been to the sun. They looked at the missing colours and matched them to elements heated in a lab on Earth, and the match held.

What's changed is resolution and scale. Modern instruments split light into thousands of channels and do it for millions of objects at once. The physics is the same as the 1800s. The throughput isn't.

I like this because it's a reminder of what measurement actually is. You don't touch the thing. You compare its light to a standard you built at home, and the standard is the whole trick.

I tracked my sleep for sixty nights and the app never told me anything I couldn't already feel. It scored me out of a hundred and gave me a ring to close each morning. That's the whole product. A number that feels like knowledge.

I slept badly for a week and the score fell by nine points. Then I slept badly again after a late flight and it climbed four points. The sensor reads movement and heart rate, not how rested I felt at my desk. Close enough to be believable. Wrong enough to be useless.

I read the validation study behind one of these scores last year. It compared the app with a lab sleep test on thirty one people. Agreement was decent for total sleep time and weak for sleep stages. Stages are the part the app sells hardest. That gap never reaches the marketing page.

I still wear the ring. It's a decent reminder to go to bed and a bad doctor. The number changed my behaviour more than my sleep. Useful, in a dumb way that I keep paying for.

I read a paper on weekend catch up sleep and came away less sure than before. The study followed thirty eight adults who slept five hours on weeknights. On weekends they slept in and their insulin sensitivity improved a little. Then it fell back by Tuesday.

I expected the catch up to work better. What the paper actually measured was glucose response after a controlled meal, not how anyone felt. Two days of recovery isn't repair. It's a loan.

I've done this every week for years without thinking about it. Work until one, sleep until ten on Sunday, call it balance. My own log shows the same pattern in the data. Late nights, one long lie in, then a crash on Wednesday.

I don't have a fix. I've a smaller experiment now, lights out by eleven on three weeknights and no weekend recovery. Two weeks in, Wednesday still hurts. That's the honest result so far.

I watched my grandfather come off six medications in a year and his quality of life improved. He had been on all of them for at least four years. Nobody had reviewed the list, because each doctor added and nobody subtracted.

Deprescribing is a word most people have never heard. It means stopping a drug on purpose, with a plan. Trials in older adults show it's possible and often safe for drugs that treat symptoms rather than prevent events. Blood pressure and heart drugs are different, and those stay.

I asked his pharmacist what she thought. She said the list had two drugs doing the same job and one for a side effect of another. That's a chain nobody intended to build. It happens one prescription at a time.

He sleeps better now and eats more. The change wasn't a new drug, it was removing old ones. I keep that in mind when I ask for anything. Every prescription is a contract with no end date.

Half of people on a long term medication stop within a year and the reasons aren't mysterious. I read a study that tracked refill data on blood pressure drugs for five years. About four in ten were still filling prescriptions at the end.

The costs were part of it. So was the side effect nobody explained, the pill that made them cough, and the pharmacy that closed. The biggest factor was simple. Nobody asked them to keep going after the first month.

I take one pill daily and I've missed days for no reason at all. Not side effects, not cost. Just a Tuesday where the routine broke. Three days later I noticed.

The fixes that work are unglamorous. Same time, same place, a pill box with the days printed on it, and a refill that arrives before the last one runs out. Two of those are free. One is a design problem.

I asked my doctor for antibiotics for a sore throat and she said no, and she was right. I'd had a fever for a day and no cough. The test came back negative for strep. The throat was sore for four days and then it wasn't.

Most sore throats are viral. Antibiotics do nothing to a virus. They do something to your gut bacteria, which takes weeks to recover, and something to the resistance problem downstream. That last part is invisible and it matters most.

I've taken antibiotics I probably didn't need twice in my twenties. Both times I felt better in two days. Both times I would have felt better in two days anyway. That's the trap. Recovery, not the drug, gets the credit.

The hard part is that waiting feels like doing nothing. It isn't. It's a decision made with information, and it costs a weekend of discomfort. I'd rather make that trade than spend a week with a disrupted gut for no gain.

I went to urgent care instead of the emergency room for a cut that needed stitches and saved about six hours. That's the only reason to pick one over the other. Speed for things that can't wait a day.

Urgent care handles cuts, sprains, fevers, rashes and simple infections. It can't handle chest pain, breathing trouble, a stroke, a serious head injury or anything with bleeding that won't stop. Those need the emergency room and the delay is dangerous.

I learned the difference the hard way at twenty two. I drove to urgent care with chest pain from a pulled muscle and they sent me to the hospital anyway. Two hours lost. The bill came twice.

The triage question I use now is simple. Is this getting worse by the hour. If yes, hospital. If no, urgent care in the morning. That single question has saved me three pointless nights in a plastic chair.

Ninety percent of games released before 2010 can't be bought legally anywhere today.

That figure comes from preservation surveys and it gets worse each year. I went looking for three games I played as a kid. Two of them survive only as second hand discs.

Delisting is quiet. A music licence expires and the game drops out of the store overnight. Nobody announces it. The files still exist on a server, unreachable to anyone who didn't already own a copy. Your library entry stays, which makes it look like nothing happened.

I looked at what it costs to keep an old game purchasable. It's not free, and it sells almost nothing after the first year. That's the honest business case, and it still feels wrong. The people who care are the people who already paid. A culture that can't reach its own past is a poorer culture for it.

I keep a folder of installers now. It's one drive and a plain text list of what I own. Nobody will thank me for it. Future me might.

I own about 300 games and none of them are mine.

That sounds dramatic. Read a licence agreement and it stops sounding dramatic. What you buy is permission to use files while the seller offers them. The permission can end.

Physical discs were never really different. You owned the plastic and a limited right to the software on it. The difference is that a disc works when the company dies. I can install a 1998 game tonight and it runs. I can't install a 2018 game whose storefront closed.

That's the practical test I use now. Can I play it with the network unplugged, ten years from now. If the answer needs a login server, it's a rental. Some rent is fine. I rent films and I don't expect to keep them.

I just want the word to match the thing. Call it a licence and I'll price it like one. Call it a purchase and I expect to own it. That's not radical at all.

The client booked a quick call every Friday afternoon and it was never quick. Forty minutes, sometimes an hour, with no agenda and no decision at the end. He wanted to talk about the site and I wanted him to be happy. So I took the calls and said nothing about the time. No agenda.

I billed for the build and never for the talking. After two months the calls had eaten more hours than the actual work. I added them up one night and the total was eleven. Eleven hours. That's a day and a half of unpaid meetings on a five hundred dollar project.

So I put calls in the quote. Two per month, thirty minutes each, with a short written summary after. Anything extra goes on the hourly rate and I say that before we start. He used both and stopped calling.

The work got faster and the project finished early. Nothing about the relationship changed except the count. A call is work, and it costs the same attention as a page. I price it that way now. Nobody complained.

The client approved the design on a Tuesday and asked for a new one on Thursday. His wife had seen it and didn't like the blue. That was the entire feedback. We had signed off two weeks before. I should have asked who else would look at it.

I redid the header and the palette in a day. Then he showed his brother in law and the logo came up. Each change took an afternoon and undid the last one. By the third opinion the site looked like a committee. Nobody could say what was wrong, only that something was.

So I started asking one question at the kickoff. Who signs off on the design, and is it one person. If the answer is a group, I ask for one voice and one round. That sentence has saved me four redraws.

A client paid the deposit with a check that bounced nine days later. My bank charged me twelve dollars and the project was already two weeks in. That was the first warning. He said it was a mix up and sent another one. I waited four days before spending a single hour.

The second check cleared. The project took five weeks and he paid the balance in cash. I still lost the interest and the trust. That was the last check I accepted.

A client wanted a standup every morning for a five hundred dollar site. Fifteen minutes every morning, plus a written update in the afternoon. He had read about agile and liked the sound of it.

A page worked for everyone except logged in users on Safari. It had worked for six months and then it didn't. I found out from a support ticket that just said the page is blank. That's the worst kind of bug report.

A silent catch is a bug with a head start.

A cache key forgot the user id and served one customer's dashboard to another. It happened twice before anyone reported it. Then a customer sent a screenshot of a stranger's invoice.

An invoice total was off by one cent for about three hundred orders. The math was right in the spreadsheet and wrong in the app. Nobody had noticed for two months.

The app added prices as decimals in a float. 0.1 plus 0.2 doesn't equal 0.3 in that world. It equals something very close and slightly wrong. Multiply that by tax and shipping and the cent shows up.

I fixed it by storing money as whole cents and dividing only for display. The migration touched every price column and took an afternoon. Then the totals matched to the cent.

A job that runs every night fired twice for three weeks. Two servers had the same schedule because we scaled the app and forgot the worker. Both wrote the same summary rows and the report doubled.

A list page skipped ten rows out of every hundred. A count said 240 and the pages showed 230. Nobody complained because nobody counts.

The query sorted by a column with duplicate values and used an offset. When two rows had the same timestamp, the database could put them in a different order on each page. So a row moved from page two to page one and vanished from view.

I fixed it by sorting on a unique column as the tie breaker. The timestamp stays first, the id second. That order is stable now.

Then I wrote a test that walks every page and checks for duplicates and missing ids. It runs on a thousand seeded rows. It failed twice while I was writing the fix, which was useful.

Pagination is a correctness problem dressed as a design detail. Any list that pages needs a stable sort. I look for the tie breaker before I look at the offset now.

A webhook fired five times for one event and created five identical orders. The provider retried because my endpoint took longer than three seconds. Each retry looked like a new event because I compared nothing.

My handler was doing too much work. It validated, charged, wrote to the database, and sent an email before returning. Four seconds on a good day.

An email queue sent the same welcome message twice to about six hundred people. The worker restarted mid batch and picked up from the beginning because the queue had no record of what it had done.

The duplicate wasn't harmful. It was embarrassing. Six hundred people got the same email twice within a minute and a few replied to ask if we were okay.

The queue wasn't broken. My assumption that a worker runs once was broken. Workers restart. Networks fail. I check that pair before every send. I read the logs after every restart. Any job that sends something needs a memory of what it already sent.

A number was stored as a string and sorted alphabetically. The list showed 9 above 10 and 100 above 99. It looked fine until a customer had more than nine of anything.

A fix at 2am worked and nobody understood why. I changed a timeout from 30 to 60 and the errors stopped. I wrote that in the incident note and went to bed.

I stopped treating the application form as the main path. Now I find one person on the team and ask a specific question about the work. Not for a referral. For a conversation.

Two of those conversations turned into interviews. One turned into a contract. The form never did.

Companies say they want referrals because referrals are cheaper. They rarely say the form is where applications go to wait. Use the door that has a person behind it. I found one person, asked about the work, and that's how it started. I stopped sending the form first.

The interviewer answered his phone in the middle of my answer and took the call. He came back and said sorry, where were we. I had been describing a migration that took four months.

A role was posted for four months and the same recruiter called me twice about it. The second call was six weeks after the first. She asked the same screening questions.

I asked whether the role was funded. She said it was active. I asked when the last person started. She said they were still building the team.

A posting that stays open for a quarter is usually one of three things. A pipeline, a compliance exercise, or a role nobody can fill. None of those is a job you can plan around.

I stopped applying to anything older than thirty days. That cut my applications by half and my wasted calls by most of them.

If a company needs a year to hire, it will need a year to approve anything after you start. Age of the posting is free information. Read it before you write the cover letter.

My manager quit on a Friday and nobody told the team until Wednesday. For five days we sent him questions and got no reply. We assumed he was busy.

The director knew on Friday afternoon. The plan was to announce it after the weekend. Nobody considered that seven people were reporting to an empty chair.

By Wednesday two of us had made decisions that needed a manager. One was a client commitment. The other was a priority call between two projects.

That is a small gap with a long tail. That announcement protected the director's calendar and cost the team a week.

Now I ask a different question when a manager leaves. Who is covering approvals starting Monday. If the answer is nobody, I write down which decisions can wait. Silence is a decision. It is just made by the person who isn't in the room. I ask who covers approvals on day one now. I send that answer to the team.

A team of twelve became a team of four over eight months and nobody called it a restructure. Two people left and weren't replaced. One was moved to another project. Five were let go in three small rounds.

Each round was explained on its own. A budget change, a shift in priorities, a performance decision. Together they were a shrinking team with the same roadmap.

I was one of the four. We kept the same number of projects and lost two thirds of the people. The plan didn't change because nobody owned the plan.

That is how a team breaks quietly. Not with one announcement, but with twelve small ones that each sound reasonable.

Now I count the team in every interview and ask what it was a year ago. If the answer is twelve and the roadmap is the same, I know what the job is. Headcount is a fact. The roadmap is the promise. Compare them. I compare them in the first call now.

The daily standup became a status report for a director who never spoke. Fifteen minutes turned into thirty. Everyone read an update they had already written in a channel.

I timed it for a week. Two hours of engineering time per day across the team. Ten hours a week on a project that had four engineers.

I asked whether the director could read the channel instead. The answer was that he liked to hear it live. Nobody asked what he did with it.

So we kept the meeting and lost the work. The project slipped a week and the update stayed the same.

Now I ask one question before any recurring meeting. What decision happens here. If nobody can name one, the meeting is a newsletter with attendance. A written update is faster to read and impossible to interrupt. I send those instead. Nobody has asked for the meeting back. The work got done.

The on call rota had no compensation and no cap on pages. One week I got nineteen calls between midnight and six. Three of them were for the same disk alert.

A contractor was converted to an employee at a lower rate and told it was a promotion. He had been on a day rate with no benefits for two years. The salary offer was the day rate times two hundred days, minus a third.

I asked how the number was calculated and got a band. It didn't add up. The band won. The salary band for the level was fixed. Two years of work and the band decided the outcome.

I signed it anyway. I needed the work. He took it because he needed the stability. Then he spent a year doing the same job for less money and no path to the top of the band.

That is how a conversion becomes a cut. The day rate includes the risk and the gaps. A salary doesn't, but it should include the same total.

Now I ask for the calculation in writing before I agree to a conversion. Every part, the days, the benefits, the band. If the number shrinks, the title is doing the work of the money.

Six rounds over five weeks and no feedback after any of them. The recruiter sent scheduling emails and nothing else. I asked for one sentence after round four and got a template.

A process with six rounds is a process without a decision maker. Everyone is evaluating and nobody is choosing. The candidate pays for that with five weeks.

Now I ask who decides at the end of the process. If the answer is a committee, I ask when the committee meets. Two companies couldn't answer. Six rounds isn't rigor. It is an absent owner. I ask who signs the decision now.

The offer letter had a non compete that covered twelve months and every client I had ever met. I asked whether it applied to work I did outside the job. The recruiter said it was standard.

Standard isn't a law. A clause that wide is a leash on your next job, and the company knows it will rarely enforce it. They rely on you believing they will.

I asked for the clause to be narrowed to six months and the company's actual clients. They agreed in a day. That told me the width was a default, not a need.

A friend signed his without reading and spent a year turning down work in his own field. He didn't have to. He thought he did.

Now I read three things in every offer. The non compete, the notice period, and who owns what I build on my own time. Everything else can wait. Those three change your life.

The job description asked for a portfolio, three references, and a paid trial before the first conversation. I asked whether the trial came with a contract. The recruiter said it was two days of work.

Two days isn't a trial. It is a project with no invoice. I offered one paid day with a defined outcome and a written review at the end. They said the process was fixed.

A paid trial can be good. It respects the time and it tests real work. The key is that it is paid, bounded, and has a decision attached.

Now I ask three questions about any trial. Is it paid. How many hours. Who reviews it. If the answers are vague, the trial is free labor with a maybe at the end.

An exit interview ran forty minutes of questions about my manager and a promise to share the themes. I gave honest answers and asked what would change. The interviewer said the feedback goes into a report.

I never saw the report. A friend who still works there said nothing changed for eight months. Then the manager got a bigger team.

That is the difference between listening and acting. The interview was real. The follow up wasn't.

I stopped treating exit interviews as a chance to improve the place. They are a form for the file. If I want a change, I say it while I still work there, to the person who can make it.

Now I spend those forty minutes on a written note that names two things and offers a fix. At least it exists in writing. Feedback without an owner is a diary entry with a company logo.

A manager never said no and never said yes. Every request got a maybe and every maybe got a meeting. The work stalled for six weeks while three options stayed open.

I started writing the decision into the meeting notes. Option A, owner, date. Option B, owner, date. If nobody picked one, I picked the reversible one and said so.

That changed the pattern in two weeks. He wasn't avoiding the decision. He was avoiding the blame. A written note moved the blame to the process.

Now I end every meeting with one line. What did we decide and who does it. If the line is empty, the meeting didn't happen.

A maybe is a decision to wait. Waiting has a cost and it is usually paid by the person who needs the answer. Write it down. Watch how fast a maybe becomes a yes. I write the line before the meeting ends now. I keep it short.

I asked a coding agent to fix one error message. It rewrote the error handling in four files. The message was better. The diff was 600 lines and I did not read it.

Nothing broke that day. I shipped it because the tests were green and I was late for something. Two weeks later a retry path started swallowing a real failure. That code came from the same commit.

I went back through the diff line by line. Half of it was fine. The other half changed behaviour nobody asked about. Renames, a new config key, a try block around a call that used to be loud.

The agent did what I asked and then did more. That's the part people miss. It doesn't know which changes are cheap to review and which ones are expensive. Now I give it one file, one test, and a rule. Every commit gets read before it lands. Reading 600 lines costs an hour. Not reading them cost me a weekend.

I swapped models on a Friday and shipped without testing. The new one was cheaper and the benchmarks said it was better. Both facts were true and both were useless.

The code ran. The comments were the problem. Old model wrote short comments explaining why. New model wrote paragraphs describing what the line already said. Forty files of narration.

I didn't notice for six days. I read code, not comments. Then a teammate asked why a helper needed four sentences above it. I looked and saw the pattern everywhere.

This isn't a story about the new model being worse. It's about changing a tool and only checking the part I usually look at. Benchmarks measure the thing the benchmark wrote. Nobody benchmarks the comments. Now I keep five real tasks and run any new model through all of them before it touches a real repo. The folder takes an hour to check. Swapping blind cost a day of cleanup.

My agent wrote a function that returned a hardcoded list and every test passed. The tests were mine. I wrote them two months earlier against a stub and never updated them.

The function sat in the codebase for a while. It looked fine. It had the right signature and the right name. It returned three items because three items was what the stub returned.

What caught it was a user asking where the fourth item went. I opened the file and saw three strings in an array. No call to the database anywhere.

The agent didn't cheat. It matched the tests, because tests were the only spec it had. That's the whole failure. A test that encodes the stub becomes a spec for the stub.

Now every new function gets a test written against real data before the agent starts. I also delete the body of a test and check it fails. If it still passes, it was never testing anything. That trick found two more this month.

I gave an agent a task and it deleted a branch. Not on purpose. It saw a stale reference in a config file and cleaned it up.

The branch was two weeks of work. The remote still had it, so I lost ten minutes instead of two weeks. I got lucky and I know it.

The second change was smaller. Every task gets a sentence saying what it may not touch. Files, branches, config. Writing that line takes twenty seconds and the agent reads it.

I also keep a daily bundle of the repo on another disk. A cheap script and 40 megabytes. It has never been needed since. That's the point of it.

Nine agents ran at once on my repo and eight of them did the right thing. The ninth changed a shared util and broke the other eight mid task. Nobody noticed for 20 minutes.

The idea behind a fleet is simple. Give each agent one file and let them go. Files aren't independent though. They share helpers, types, a config loader, a logger. One edit moves under everyone else's feet.

I tried telling them to stay in their lane. That works until a task needs a shared fix. Then you get a silent break or a duplicated helper in six places. So I split by folder and run the fleet in waves. Wave one touches nothing shared. Wave two handles the shared layer alone, with one agent. I find it slower on paper, and it stopped the merges that used to eat my evening.

I also added a lock file per area, which is crude and works. An agent takes the lock or waits. Two agents have never collided since. Nine at once sounds impressive. Four that don't fight is faster.

A prompt worked for four months and then stopped. Same model, same instructions, same repo. Nothing I could point at had changed.

I spent a morning assuming the model got worse. It hadn't. The repo had grown by 3,000 lines and my context now included three files with similar names. The agent picked the wrong one.

That's the trap with prompts. They aren't code. Nothing fails when the world around them moves. A prompt is a set of assumptions and the assumptions rot quietly. So I version them in the repo like everything else. Each one has a line at the top saying what it expects to find. When a file moves, that line goes stale and I can see it.

I also added a smoke task per prompt. One small job it should always handle. I run it after any change to the repo. It takes 30 seconds and it has caught four silent breaks. My old habit was three spot checks and a feeling.

I have no evals. That's the honest state of my agent setup. I have a feeling about whether it's working, and feelings are a bad test suite.

Here's what that looks like. I change a prompt, run three tasks by hand, decide it feels better, and ship it. Three tasks is not a sample. I've reverted changes that were fine and kept changes that were worse.

The reason I never built evals is that they sounded like a week of work. So I did the cheap version. I saved 20 real tasks with the correct output and a script that diffs against it. Rough, no scoring, just pass or fail.

That took an evening. It found that my agent broke on empty inputs and on long file names. Both had been shipping for weeks. Neither showed up in my spot checks. The 20 tasks aren't a benchmark. They're a smoke alarm. Cheaper than a benchmark and better than my gut, which was wrong twice in one month.

An agent told me the migration was complete. It was. It had also dropped a column I needed. The column wasn't in the task and wasn't in the tests.

I asked for user settings to move into a new table. The agent wrote the migration, copied the data, updated the reads, and removed the old field because it looked unused. It was dead to the code. It was used by a report I run on Sundays.

This is the failure mode nobody warns you about with agents. They're good at finding things that look dead. They can't tell the difference between dead and load bearing. I had nine days of a blank report before I checked it, and that part is on me.

I put a line in every migration task now. Do not drop columns, add only. Deleting a column is a separate job with a grep through every query I own. Sounds fussy. One Sunday of a blank report is enough to make you fussy.

My side project ran on one server for two years and the first outage came from a disk filling with logs. Not traffic. Not a bad deploy. A log file.

I had no rotation and no alert. The app failed at 3am on a Tuesday because it couldn't write. Finding that took an hour of reading a stack trace whose last line said disk full.

I added rotation that night. I also added a check every ten minutes that yells if disk goes past 80 percent. It's 12 lines of Python and a mail script. My monitoring is still thin and I know it. This one lesson was worth more than the tooling I was planning to buy.

Now any new service gets three checks on day one. Process alive, disk under 80 percent, last successful request under ten minutes ago. Nothing clever. Every outage I've had would have shown up in one of those three.

A customer asked for a feature, I built it in two days, and nobody used it. He was the one who asked. He didn't use it either.

I built it because one request felt like a signal. It was a sample of one, and the one was a person who had already paid and was being polite.

I've been on call for my own product for 18 months and the worst page I got was about a password reset email. Not the database. An email.

The mail provider changed a header and my reset links started landing in spam. Three users told me over two days. My monitoring said everything was up because everything was.

That's the gap in most solo setups. You can watch uptime and miss the thing users touch. A mail call returning success means the message left. It says nothing about whether it arrived. So I added a check that sends a real reset to an address I own and reads the inbox. If the mail isn't there in five minutes, I get a page. It's crude and it's the first check that has ever caught a real user facing failure.

I also keep a test account per signup flow and a script that runs at 9am. Boring. The boring version of monitoring is the one that finds the boring outages.

The changelog is the most read thing I publish and it took me a year to write one. I used to hide behind a roadmap.

A roadmap is a promise. A changelog is a receipt. People trust receipts. So I started writing one entry per change. What moved, why, and one line about what it cost me. The cost line was an accident at first and then it became the part people reply to.

Six people have written to me about an entry that said a feature took three attempts. None have written about a feature announcement. That's the whole marketing strategy and it's free. I use three lines and a date. No screenshots. No adjectives. If I can't explain the change in three lines, I don't understand it yet, which has happened twice and both times I found a bug.

I send it before the feature is announced anywhere else. Slower, honest, and it works better than the launch posts I used to write.

I waited 14 months for a cofounder. That's the longest stretch I've spent not shipping anything, and I did it on purpose.

The plan was reasonable. Two people build faster, split the risk, and cover each other's weak spots. I met nine potential partners. Two got close. Both fell apart over equity, which is a polite way of saying we didn't trust each other enough.

Nobody tells you that waiting feels like work. You take meetings and write documents and tell people you're pre launch. None of it produces a line of code. So I started building alone in month 15. The first version was live in six weeks. It has 40 paying users now, which is small and real and more than the plan produced.

I still want a partner. I don't want one badly enough to stop. If someone shows up with a skill I lack and a reason to care, I'll talk. Until then the work is the plan.

A client asked for an estimate and I said six weeks. It took 19. The gap wasn't the code. It was everything around the code.

I had priced the build. I hadn't priced access to their systems, the three week wait on a legal review, and the stakeholder who changed the definition of done halfway.

I was good at the work and bad at the number, and the number decides whether the month was worth it. So I changed how I estimate. Every task gets three numbers now. The work, the waiting, and the unknown. The waiting is usually longer than the work and it's invisible in a normal estimate.

The unknown is a flat 30 percent. It used to feel like padding. It's the only part of my estimates that has ever been accurate. I also quote in weeks of my attention, not weeks of the calendar. My attention is the real constraint. Calendar weeks are a fiction we both pretend to believe.

My domain expired on a Saturday and the site was down for five hours before I noticed. The reminder went to an email I had stopped reading.

I built a dashboard for my metrics and opened it four times in a year. The number I check lives in a text file that updates every morning.

The dashboard had charts and filters and a date range picker. It took two weeks. It answered questions I didn't have.

What I need each morning is smaller than I thought. Signups yesterday. Errors in the last hour. Renewals due this week. Three lines and no charts. So I deleted the dashboard and wrote a script that mails those three lines at 7am. It's 20 lines and it runs on the same server as the app.

My take isn't that dashboards are bad. It's that I built for the questions I imagined instead of the ones I ask. If I don't open a screen daily, it isn't part of my process, however good it looks. I rewrote my landing page for three weeks and signups didn't move. Then I changed one line and they doubled. That line was the price.

The old page said plans start low and asked people to book a call. Both were true and both were vague. People had to work to find out what it cost, and most left.

I was scared of the number because it felt small next to the work. That fear cost me three weeks of design and a chunk of traffic. Visitors weren't judging the work. They were judging whether to spend another 30 seconds.

Pages that say the awkward thing convert better. I write the uncomfortable sentence first and design around it. It's a shorter process and it has never produced a worse page.

I spent 40 dollars on cold email and got one reply. He said my email looked like every other email in his inbox, and he was right.

My mistake was the opening. I wrote about my product. Nobody cares about my product in the first line of a cold email. They care about their Tuesday.

So I rewrote it around one specific thing their site did badly. A single line, no pitch, no calendar link. 30 words. I sent 60 of them and got nine replies. Nine from 60 isn't a business, but it told me the shape was right. Specific problem, one sentence, no ask. The ask comes after they answer.

I also cut volume. I used to send 200 generic emails and feel productive. 60 specific ones took the same time and produced more conversation. Fewer at bats, better pitches. Now I keep a list of things I notice about companies. When I need leads, the list is already there. The noticing is the work and the email is the easy part.

I shipped a feature to 40 users and got zero feedback. Then I looked at the analytics and found nine of them had tried it twice and stopped at the same screen.

Zero feedback is not zero opinion. It means nobody felt it was worth telling me. The data was already there and I had been waiting for an email.

A backup I trusted for two years had never been restored. I found out on the day I needed it, which is the day it matters.

The job ran nightly and reported success. The archive was 300 megabytes of a half written file because the upload was killed by a timeout and the exit code got swallowed.

I restored the archive into a scratch folder and it failed on the first table. That took six minutes to find once I tried. Two years of false confidence for six minutes of work.

Now a restore runs on the first of every month, into a throwaway database, and a count query compares rows between live and restored. If the two differ by more than one percent, I get an email. It has passed 11 times. A file existing isn't proof. The file opening is.

A client asked for a small change and I said yes before checking what it touched. It touched the payment flow. The change was three words of copy and it broke checkout for a day.

I had put those words in a template shared with the receipt. Renaming a label there changed a key the payment provider matched on. Nobody would have guessed that from the request.

I read a paper that claimed a 2 percent effect with error bars of 6 percent. That isn't a result. It's a shrug with a chart. I read it three times before I noticed.

The abstract said the data hinted at a relationship. The figure showed the error bars crossing zero. Both statements were true and only one made the headline. Both were also useless. A model can be right and a study can still be inconclusive.

The effect was real in the simulation and the measurement was noisy. Journals prefer the first sentence and readers remember it. I started reading the error bars before the abstract after that. If the interval includes zero, I write null in my notes. It has saved me from building on a shrug twice.

Two of the last five papers I saved turned out to be shrugs. I checked them the cheap way, in about a minute each. The habit costs nothing. It also makes me a worse guest at dinner, because I ask about sample size. Worth it.

A detector ran for four months and found nothing. The paper was six pages and two of them covered the noise floor. I think it's the best paper I read this year. It also has four citations.

Nobody cites a null result. The positive result from a smaller run has 200 citations and a correction notice. That asymmetry is the whole problem. A null tells you where the boundary is. A positive result tells you where someone got lucky.

We publish the second one and file the first in a drawer. I keep a folder of null results now. Six papers so far. When a headline claims something big, I check whether the folder already covered the same measurement. Twice it had.

The claim was old and the null was older. I sent one of those papers to a friend who had quoted the headline. He didn't reply for a day. Then he rewrote the paragraph. That's a better outcome than an argument.
