I spent a weekend running a public dataset again and could not get the published number. I got something 30 percent off. Then I read the methods section properly. The dataset had been updated twice since the paper.

The paper used version two. The link on the page served version three. Two rows had been corrected and one column renamed. Nothing announced it. That's the least glamorous failure in science and probably the most common.

A result depends on a snapshot of data that nobody froze. Six months later the snapshot is gone. I hash every download now and note the date. It takes ten seconds. If I share findings, I share the hash too.

Two people have written to me about my numbers. Both of them were on a different version. Neither of us was wrong. That's the part people miss about reproducibility. It isn't about lying. It's about drift.

A signal showed up in three separate analyses and vanished when someone checked the time zones. All three used the same broken pipeline. That isn't three confirmations. That's one bug counted three times.

I have made this mistake in my own work. I ran the same query three ways and called it a cross check. It wasn't. Same source, same assumptions, same blind spot. Real confirmation needs a different instrument or a different team.

Repeating yourself isn't replication. Now when three studies agree, I look for the shared dependency. Datasets, software, calibration, even the same reviewer. The question isn't how many analyses agreed. It's how many independent ways of being wrong got ruled out.

That reframing has changed what I read. I stopped counting papers and started counting methods. A field with 50 papers on one dataset has one dataset. I wrote that line in a note and it keeps being true.

I stopped trusting a model because it fit the data too well. The residual was flat. No structure at all. Real data almost never looks like that.

The cause was a smoothing step in preprocessing. It removed the noise the model was supposed to explain. So the model predicted something that had already been cleaned for it. Two weeks of work gone. I had measured my own filter.

The plot looked great. I was pleased for a week. The result meant nothing. Now I fit the raw data first, badly, and look at the residuals. If they look like a mess, that's expected. If they look like nothing, I go looking for the step that ate the noise.

It's a cheap check. It has caught three versions of the same mistake since. One of them was in a tool I wrote and trusted. Trust is the wrong word for a thing you never tested.

A referee rejected my favourite paper in four sentences and every one of them was right. I was angry for a day. Then I rewrote the introduction.

The objection was that I claimed a mechanism without ruling out the obvious alternative. I had a sentence saying the alternative was unlikely. Unlikely isn't ruled out. That's the difference between a good idea and a result. Ideas survive on plausibility.

Results survive on what you excluded. I had spent 40 pages on the first and one sentence on the second. Now I write the alternatives section before the discussion. Every explanation I can think of, and what would show it wrong. Half the time I can't answer.

Then the claim shrinks. That's the point. A smaller claim I can defend beats a bigger one I can't. I have applied the same rule to product launches since. If I can't say what would prove the idea wrong, it's a wish with a budget.

I got access to a lab notebook from 1997 and it explained a discrepancy four papers had blamed on the instrument. The entry was three lines. A cable was swapped. A note said it would be fixed Monday.

It was fixed. Nobody updated the calibration file. So every measurement from that month carries a bias nobody has looked for. Data outlives its context. A number stays in the archive and the reason stays in a drawer.

Twenty five years later the two are in different buildings. I keep a file next to every dataset now, called what happened. Four lines on how it was collected and what was wrong with the instrument that week. It isn't science.

It's the thing that makes the science checkable. I watched it save a colleague a month last year. He found a gap in a series that had been quoted in two papers. That gap was in the notebook, not the data. Nobody had read it because nothing suggested they should.

A telescope proposal of mine was rejected twice for the same reason. I only understood it on the third read. The reviewer said the science case assumed the result. He was right.

I had written it as if the measurement would work. No plan for a weaker signal. No plan for a follow up. No statement of what a null would mean. It read like a request to confirm something.

I checked the units on a colleague's calculation and found a factor of 1,000. Kilometres and metres in the same column. The result had been in a draft for three weeks.

It was just believable. I nearly missed it too, and I was looking at the column. Now every calculation I write prints its inputs with units and asserts on the order of magnitude. It's five lines. It has caught two of my own errors. One was in a chart I had already shown to people.

I did not enjoy that email. Fixing it took ten minutes. Apologising took longer. Unit checks aren't glamorous and they aren't optional. A number without units is a rumour.

An exoplanet disappeared last year. It had been in a catalog for six years. A reanalysis found the signal was the star's own pulsation.

The original team wasn't careless. They had one instrument and no way to tell. That's the honest state of a lot of discovery. You find a signal and you can't separate it from the thing that made it. Time and better instruments do the separating.

I have watched a planet go away before, on paper. I read the retraction and thought about product metrics. A number moves, everyone builds a story. Six years on, it was the calendar. I keep that retraction in a folder now.

I now ask what else could produce this pattern. Not in general. Specifically. Which other process would look the same, and how would I tell them apart. If I can't answer that, I have a hypothesis and not a finding.

A famous radio signal turned out to be a microwave oven in the building. Two decades of papers cited it before that. The lesson isn't that the astronomers were fools. It's that nobody checked the kitchen.

The team found it because they started testing in a different building and the signal stopped. That's a good experiment. Change one thing and see if the signal follows.

I try to apply that to my own work. When a metric changes, I change one thing on purpose and watch. New query, same data. New data, same query. If the number follows the tool, the tool was the cause. I have done that with a cache.

Almost every weird result I've had in the last year was my own kitchen. A different time zone, a stale cache, a filter I forgot. The signal was real. I know that feeling. It just wasn't the universe.

I read a claim that a telescope saw the earliest galaxy yet. Two paragraphs down, the paper said the redshift was a guess from one photometric point. That's not a measurement. That's a strong maybe.

This is the gap between a press release and a paper and it is usually four words long. Candidate, probable, tentative, possible. Those words carry the whole uncertainty and they get dropped in the headline.

The paper was fine. The authors were careful. The problem is the chain between them and me, and every link drops a caveat because caveats are boring.

I stopped at possible and closed the tab and moved on. Now I read the abstract's verbs. Detected means one thing. Suggest means another. Found a candidate means the instrument sneezed and nobody knows why. If the headline verb is stronger than the paper verb, I stop reading the headline and read the paper.

I built a small pipeline to check a published table and it disagreed with the paper in 14 rows. I assumed I was wrong. I was wrong about being wrong.

The paper had sorted a column as text. Values like 9.5 landed above 10. The sorting didn't change the statistics but it changed which point was labelled the outlier, and the conclusion leaned on that label.

One line of code, one wrong conclusion, and nobody caught it in review because the table looked fine. That is the class of error I find most often. Not bad math. A type that quietly changed what the math was looking at.

Now I check the dtypes before any analysis. Numbers stored as text, dates stored as text, empty strings instead of nulls. It takes a minute and it has changed the answer twice. I trust my own pipeline a bit less now.

A grant funded the boring part and that's why the result held. The instrument was already built. Most of it went on calibration, a second detector, and a person to check the analysis. None of that makes a good abstract.

I read two papers on the same question with opposite conclusions and both were right. They measured different things and used the same word for it.

One defined recovery as a return to baseline. The other defined it as no further decline. Those aren't the same claim, and the press covered it as a fight.

Most disagreements that look dramatic are definitional. The measurement is fine, the construct is fuzzy, and two teams sliced it differently. Nobody is lying and the argument is unwinnable. I checked both papers twice.

That is why I write the definition before the result. Not after. If the number changes meaning when I move the line, I don't have a finding. I have a choice of lines. The same habit has saved me in product work. Churn means three things depending on who is asking. Writing the definition first turns an argument into a decision.

I tried to replicate a simple result three times and got three different answers. Same code, same data, different seeds. The published value sat inside the spread and my first run happened to hit it.

That was the day I stopped reporting a single number. I was annoyed. Those three runs weren't close. A single run of anything stochastic is an anecdote with a decimal point. The honest output is a range and the honest figure is the distribution.

So my analysis scripts run 20 times and print the interval. It takes longer and the plots are uglier. It also ended an argument with a colleague in one message because we could see we were both inside the noise.

The other thing it changed was my reading. When a paper reports one number from one seed, I ask how lucky it was. Not because the authors cheated. Because the number is a draw and the paper shows one draw.

An old dataset got released again with better calibration and the effect got smaller. Not gone. Smaller. The original authors published the update themselves, which almost nobody does.

That kind of correction is the healthiest thing in a field and it gets no attention. A result that shrinks under better data is still a result. It means the direction was right and the size was optimistic.

I have started tracking effect sizes across versions when I read a topic. First paper says 30 percent. Reanalysis says 12. Better instrument says 8. I watch the direction survive and the number decay. That decay curve is more informative than any single paper. I ask for the date now, every time.

If I only read the first paper I'd think the effect was 30 percent. Nobody publishes the decay in one place, so I keep it in a note. Four topics so far and every one shrank.

A model predicted a value before the measurement and got it right. That is the kind of prediction that counts. Everything else is a fit wearing a lab coat.

Most claims I read are retrodictions. The model was built on the data and then asked to explain the data. It does that by construction. The interesting test is the next measurement, and that is often in the future and not in the paper.

This is why I care about writing predictions down in advance. Writing the prediction down before you look is the way anyone can tell a forecast from a story.

I do a small version of this with my own guesses. Before I check a number, I write what I think it is. The file has 60 entries now. I'm right about half the time, which is worse than I assumed and better than nothing. I was wrong about half of them.

The most cited paper in a field I follow has a correction that nobody cites. The correction halves the main effect. Papers still reference the original number.

Citations propagate errors because citing is social. You cite what everyone cites. Checking the correction takes one click and nobody does it because the number is already in your draft.

I have done this. I cited a figure for two years that had been revised. A reader emailed me and was polite about it. I fixed the post and felt bad for a week.

Now I open the paper, not the citation, before I use a number. And I look for a correction notice on the publisher page. It's 30 seconds and it separates quoting a result from quoting a rumour. Reading the actual papers also made me realise how many of my confident claims came from a summary of a summary. That was uncomfortable and useful.

I asked a researcher why her field ignored a null result and she said because a null doesn't get you the next grant. That's the whole mechanism in one sentence. I wrote it down.

The incentive isn't fraud. It's selection. You run 20 analyses, one of them is interesting, and that's the one you write up. Nothing dishonest happens at any single step and the literature ends up wrong.

That is the same shape as a growth team reporting the campaign that worked. Twenty tests, one winner, and the deck says the strategy is validated. The 19 failures are in a spreadsheet nobody opens.

The fix is boring and it works. Report the number of attempts. Every time I show a result now I add a line saying how many things I tried. It makes the finding smaller and it makes it true. That line has never made a claim useless, and it has stopped me believing two of my own.

A friend in a lab spent nine months on an experiment that failed because a filter was installed backwards. No result at all. Fixing it took two minutes.

Nine months is not unusual. Most experimental time goes into finding out that the apparatus was doing something you didn't know about. That failure isn't the data. It's that the failure is invisible in the output.

I think about this when someone asks why a feature took so long. My answer is usually a backwards filter. A dependency, an environment, a permission, a config that was right in staging and wrong in production. None of it is on the roadmap and all of it is the work.

I check the physical layer first now. Is it plugged in. Is the filter facing the right way. Is the data the data I think it is. Half of my debugging time has been spent skipping that step.

A survey of the sky found 400 objects and 60 of them were the same object counted twice. The catalog had no deduplication step. Two observations, coordinates a few arcseconds apart, both kept.

That seems like sloppiness and it's the normal condition of messy data. Coordinates have uncertainty. Two points three arcseconds apart could be one source or two. The decision needs a rule and the rule needs to be written down.

I hit this with user records all the time. Same person, two emails, different capitalisation. Same company, three spellings. Every analysis I run starts with a dedupe step now, and I write the rule in a comment.

The number of duplicates is also a finding. 60 out of 400 is a 15 percent error in every count that follows. That isn't a detail. It's the headline, and the paper reported the count without the rule. I check the count before the result.

Two measurements of the expansion rate disagree by more than their error bars and both teams are careful. That tension has been open for years and it's the most interesting thing in the field.

What I like about it is that nobody has been able to find a mistake. Both groups checked. Outside groups checked. The disagreement survived every audit, which means either one measurement has hidden systematics or the model is incomplete.

That is what a real problem looks like. Not a scandal. A gap that persists after everyone competent has tried to close it. I read the updates every few months and the gap is still there, slightly smaller, still significant.

The honest position is that we don't know which one is wrong. I find that more useful than most confident claims, because it tells me where the next discovery is likely to come from. I keep reading.

A student found a bug because the answer was 10 to the power of 40 and the expected answer was 1. She didn't know the field well enough to assume the big number was fine.

Expertise is a filter that removes surprise. You see a result in the expected range and you stop looking. A newcomer sees a number that seems absurd and asks why.

I try to keep one naive question per review. What is this number in plain terms. If a growth chart says conversion is 0.04, someone should ask whether that means 4 percent or 4 per hundred of a hundred. Half the time nobody agrees.

The other habit is asking the newest person on a project what confuses them. Their confusion is data. It points at the part of the system with an undocumented assumption, which is usually the part that will break. I wrote it down.

I built a checker for a paper's arithmetic and it passed. I was pleased with myself for a minute. Then I counted. Then I noticed the table had 11 rows and the dataset had 12. One row had been dropped and the text didn't say why.

Dropped rows are where conclusions go to hide. A missing value, an outlier, a participant who didn't finish. Each exclusion can be justified and the sum of them can change the answer.

The result held without the row, which is the good outcome. I only know that because I counted the rows. Nobody counts the rows.

Now the first thing I check in any dataset is the count. Rows in, rows out, and the difference explained. It's the cheapest audit there is. It has found three unexplained exclusions in work I was about to quote, and one of them flipped the sign of the effect. I counted twice.

---
A claim survived 20 years because everyone repeated it in the introduction. Nobody had run the original experiment again. When someone did, the effect was half the size.

Introductions are where facts go to become folklore. You cite the number because the last paper cited the number. It isn't dishonest. A citation is cheaper than a replication and the incentive points the wrong way.

I catch myself doing this in writing. A statistic feels familiar, so I use it. Familiar isn't verified. The ones I've checked, I remember, and there are maybe nine.

Now I keep a file of numbers I have verified with a link and a date. It's small and it's the set I let myself state without hedging. Everything else gets I read that attached, which is a weaker claim and an honest one. I checked one of them last month and it was half the size.

#Science #Research #Citations #Lessons #Tech #BuildInPublic #Skepticism #Writing #Methodology #AI #Data #Learning #Thinking #Statistics #Publishing

I read a blog comment that explained a result in four lines. It pointed out that the effect was the same size as the instrument's known drift, and it linked a calibration paper.

That comment did more than the peer review. Reviewers check whether the analysis is sound. They rarely check whether the signal is bigger than the instrument's own wobble, because that knowledge lives in a different subfield.

I have started reading the comments on papers I care about. Not the rude comments. The ones from someone in another field who knows the hardware. Twice they have saved me from quoting something.

The broader point is that review isn't the same as checking. A paper can pass review and still be wrong about the world. Checking happens after publication, in public, by people with nothing to gain. That's the part that works. I saved the comment and the link.

I put my phone in another room for a week and the first thing I noticed was how often I reached for it. Forty times on day one. I counted because I started writing a mark each time. That number is the whole problem.

None of those reaches were urgent. Most were between two sentences of work. A small gap opened and my hand filled it before I had a thought.

I didn't become more productive in any way I could measure. I did become less tired at 4pm, which I didn't expect and can't fully explain.

Now the phone lives in a drawer during the morning block. I check it at lunch and again at six. I miss nothing that matters and I answer the same messages an hour later. Nobody has complained. I have stopped counting the reaches. I built a whole system for this once, with apps and rules. The drawer works better.

I reviewed my own code at 1am and approved a change that dropped a foreign key. The next morning I read the same diff and saw it in three seconds. Same eyes. Different brain.

That is the argument for not shipping late and it has nothing to do with discipline. Tired review isn't review. You read the lines, you feel competent, and the part that checks meaning is offline.

I used to think late nights were my best hours because the interruptions stopped. They were quiet and they were bad. The work I produced after midnight needed a rewrite about as often as the work I produced before nine.

Now I stop at 10pm, even mid task. I leave a note saying where I am and what I was about to do. Picking it up in the morning takes four minutes. Fixing a 1am decision took a day last time.

Every good idea I have had at 3am turned out to be average at 9am. Not wrong. Average. The gap between the two versions is the interesting part.

At 3am the idea arrives with its own certainty attached. It feels complete. By morning I can see the two hard parts I hadn't solved, and the certainty is gone.

I started writing the 3am ideas down without acting on them. The note says the idea and the time. I read it at breakfast. About one in five survives, and the ones that do are usually small and specific.

That filter has saved me from three bad pivots and one very bad domain purchase. The energy at 3am is real and useful. It's just not evidence. It's a mood that writes things down. I keep the notes in one file. I read them on Sundays, which is the only time I trust my own judgement.

I had 41 tabs open and could not tell you what nine of them were. I closed them all and the work didn't slow down. That was uncomfortable.

Tabs are a to do list I never read. Each one is a small promise that I will get to it. Forty one promises is a pile of guilt with a memory cost. I counted first. Nine were from a project I finished in March. Nobody needs 41 tabs.

I now keep three tabs open at a time. The rest go into a note with a line each. If I don't miss it in a week, I delete the line.

The thing I didn't expect was the change in how reading felt. With three tabs, I finish the article. With 40, I skim four and keep none. The number of things I read has gone down and the number of things I remember has gone up.

It works maybe half the time. The other half I come back with milk and no answer. The half that works is worth the twenty minutes, and the milk is a bonus. My best debugging tool is a pair of shoes. I have stopped feeling guilty about the walk. It's part of the job now.

I turned off every notification for a year and missed nothing. That sentence is doing a lot of work, so here is the detail. I missed three things and none of them mattered by the next day. Nobody noticed either.

The fear before I did it was that someone would need me and I wouldn't answer. What actually happened is that people emailed or messaged and I replied within a couple of hours. The world has a second channel for anything urgent.

What mattered was the badge. A red number on an icon is a small alarm that fires in the background of every thought. Removing it did more than removing the sound. That's the whole change.

I drank coffee at 3pm for years and wondered why I couldn't fall asleep at 11. The half life is about five hours. Nobody had told me, and I never looked.

Doing the arithmetic myself was humbling. A 3pm cup leaves a quarter of the caffeine in you at 1am. Not enough to feel wired. Enough to shave an hour off deep sleep that you never notice losing.

I moved my last cup to before noon. The first week was rough and the second week was fine. What changed was the mornings. I wake up before the alarm now, which has not happened since I was 25.

I'm not going to pretend this is a wellness journey. I just wanted to stop feeling like a tired person. The fix was arithmetic and it cost me a coffee at 3pm. I sleep through the night now. That sentence sounds small and it changed my year.

My back hurt for a month before I changed anything about my desk. I assumed it was age. It was a chair with a broken gas lift that sat four inches too low.

I found out because I worked from a kitchen table for a week while travelling and the pain went away. That is the entire story of most physical problems in this job. The cause is boring and the fix is a measurement.

Now I check three things. Screen at eye level, feet flat on the floor, elbows at 90 degrees. That isn't a setup. It's a checklist, and it takes five minutes.

The other thing I do is stand up every 40 minutes. Not for fitness. Because sitting still for three hours makes my shoulder do a thing that costs me two days. I set a timer and I ignore it half the time. The half I don't ignore is the difference.

I read a book about attention and then did the opposite of everything in it for a month. The gap between knowing and doing is the whole field of health.

The book said to protect a two hour block. I scheduled one and filled it with email because a client needed something. Then the next day the same thing. By Friday the block was a slot for other people's work.

What changed was the calendar name. I stopped calling it deep work and called it a meeting with myself. That sounds silly and it worked, because a meeting is a thing I don't move.

I have kept the block for 11 weeks. It has been moved twice and cancelled once. Both times I noticed the week felt worse, which is the only data I have. The name is stupid and the block is real. I moved the block twice. It survived both times.

I read 60 books last year and remembered four. I can tell you the covers of the other 56 and almost nothing inside them.

That is a reading problem I created by optimising for count. Counting is easy and it turns reading into a collection. Books I remember are the ones I argued with, took notes on, or tried to apply.

So I stopped counting. Now I read fewer and write a page about each one. Each page has to say what I disagree with. If I can't find anything to disagree with, I didn't understand it well enough to keep it.

The result is nine books this year and I can explain all nine. Nine is a smaller number than 60 and a much larger number than four. The count was never the point. I read slower now. I also read a page twice and I don't count that as cheating. That's fine.

I answered a call while writing a function and both came out wrong. The function had a bug I would have caught and the call got a version of me that was half there. Nobody said anything. That's the problem with multitasking, it fails quietly.

I used to believe I could listen and work. What I was doing was switching fast enough that neither side noticed the gaps. The other person notices. They just don't tell you.

Now I take calls standing up, away from the screen, with a notebook. It's worse for my step count and better for everything else. I remember what was said. I hear the thing under the question.

The rule is one channel at a time. It sounds obvious written down. It took me a decade to actually do it, and the calls got shorter because I stopped asking people to repeat themselves. It's a good rule.

I worked 90 hours in a month and shipped less than the month before. I have the commits to prove it. That was the most expensive lesson of my year.

The extra hours went into fixing things I broke during the extra hours. A deploy at midnight, a rollback at 2am, a morning spent reading logs. The loop felt like effort and produced nothing.

Nobody made me do it. I was scared a competitor would ship first. The competitor shipped a feature I had already built and nobody cared, which is usually how that fear ends.

Now I track hours and output in the same note. When hours go up and output goes flat, I stop. That rule has fired twice. Both times I took a day off and came back to find the problem in an hour. Tiredness is expensive and it bills you in rework. That rule is cheap to follow.

I got a headache every afternoon for two weeks before I noticed the pattern. It was the screen, and it was the distance. I had moved my monitor to fit a second one and ended up 20 inches from the glass.

The fix was free. Push it back, raise it, look away every 20 minutes. I set a timer that walks a small dot across the screen and I hate it. I also stopped getting the headaches.

The eye strain thing is not abstract. Your focus mechanism has a muscle and it gets tired like any other. Mine was tired by 3pm every day and I was reading that as a motivation problem.

I still forget to look away. The timer is annoying enough that I listen to it about half the time. That half is the difference between a headache and no headache. That's been true for about a year now.

My wrist hurt for three weeks and I kept using the same trackpad. It went away in four days when I switched to a mouse. Four days.

I had decided the pain was from typing and spent money on a keyboard. My keyboard was fine. The trackpad was the thing my hand was doing 600 small movements an hour on.

I diagnosed by vibes. I picked the most visible tool and blamed it. The cause was the thing I used without thinking about it, which is always the hardest to see.

Now when something hurts I change one input for a week and watch. Mouse, then keyboard, then chair height. It's slow and it works. The body is a system and guessing at it costs more than testing it. I swap one input for a week and keep a note. That's it. No app and no specialist. It's boring and it works.

I stopped answering email first thing and started with the hardest file. Three weeks later the backlog was smaller, which makes no sense until you look at why.

Email creates more email. Every reply I send produces a question or a task. Starting there meant I spent the morning generating work for the afternoon. The hardest file produced a commit and no new input.

That is the asymmetry nobody tells you about. Reactive work multiplies. Deep work terminates. One of them fills the day and the other ends.

Now I answer everything after lunch in one pass. The volume of mail has dropped by about a third. Not because people like me less. Because my replies are shorter and I stopped opening threads I didn't need to be in. I wrote the rule on a sticky note. I moved it to the monitor. Nobody has asked me to go back. It works.

I wrote a to do list every morning for a year and finished about half of it. Then I noticed the half that got done was always the same kind of task.

Items that got done were small and specific. Rewrite the error message. Add the missing index. Everything else was vague and large. Improve onboarding. Think about pricing.

Vague items are not tasks, they are moods. They sit on the list for weeks and make everything else feel unfinished. The list grows and the useful part shrinks.

Now every item has to start with a verb and fit in an hour. If it doesn't fit, it becomes a note and gets broken down later. My list is shorter and I finish about 80 percent of it. The other 20 percent moves to tomorrow, which is fine, because it's a real thing and not a feeling. I do this on paper now. I like the crossing out.

I read a breakdown of AI capital spending against AI revenue last week and the gap is not subtle. Spending is in the hundreds of billions. The revenue that anyone can point at is a rounding error on that.

That doesn't mean the spending is wrong. Railroads were built before anyone could pay for a ticket, and the people who built them mostly went bankrupt. Infrastructure outlived the companies that paid for it.

What I can't figure out is the timing. A railway takes a decade and the demand arrives eventually. A data centre needs to earn money in three to five years or the depreciation eats the operator.

So I stopped trying to predict which model wins. The more useful question is who holds the debt when the build finishes and the price of a token has fallen 90 percent. My guess is the answer matters more than any benchmark. I don't know the answer. Nobody does. It's a guess with a deadline. Fine by me.

Inference got about 10 times cheaper in 18 months and every product I use stayed the same price. That gap is going to be the story of the next few years.

Cost is the most reliable thing in the field. Same quality, less money, every quarter. It happened to bandwidth and storage and it's happening here faster.

What that means for a builder is that anything priced per token has a shelf life. Your margin is a bet against a curve that keeps falling faster than you can plan.

I priced my own tool per seat for this reason. The model cost is a line item that shrinks. The seat is a relationship that doesn't. I'd rather sell the thing that gets more valuable as the compute gets cheap. I price against that curve. It's the only forecast I trust. Nobody else seems to. So far, so good. It held.

Chip export rules get written by people who have never rented a GPU and they still work. That surprises me every time I read about a new restriction.

The reason is that the bottleneck isn't the chip. It's the fab, the packaging, the memory, and the 40 other things that all sit in three countries. You can design around a rule and you can't design around a supply chain.

I used to think controls were theatre. Then I watched the lead times on a specific accelerator go from six weeks to nine months and stay there. The policy did something and the something was expensive.

What I find interesting is that the workaround is the same. Build a worse chip, buy more of them, and spend the difference on power. Constraints produce ugly engineering, and ugly engineering is where most of the industry lives. I have no idea what the next rule is. I watch lead times instead. They tell me faster than any announcement. Nobody asks me anyway.

I have used four models this month and I could not tell you which one wrote most of the code. That is the commodity problem arriving on schedule.

When the output is good enough from three vendors, the model stops being the product. The product becomes the thing around it. Your data, your workflow, your support, the 400 small decisions that make it fit one industry.

Most AI startups I read about are a model call with a pricing page. That's not a company. It's a wrapper with a burn rate, and the wrapper gets thinner every quarter as the base model absorbs the feature.

The uncomfortable version of this applies to my own work. If the only thing I add is a prompt, I should assume it gets built into the tool by next summer. So I try to add the part that requires being in the room with the customer. I have been on the wrong side of this. I built the wrapper. It was fine for a year.

An agent startup raised a large round and their demo was a browser clicking through a checkout. I asked what happens when the site changes and got a slide about robustness.

Robustness is the whole product. Anyone can automate a flow that worked yesterday. The job is automating a flow that will be redesigned in six weeks by someone who has never heard of you.

The teams that will survive are the ones who treat the site as a moving target. Fallback paths, detection, a human in the loop when confidence drops. That is unglamorous and it's where the money goes.

I have built three scrapers in my life and all three broke. The third one broke on the day a client demoed it, which taught me more about reliability than any talk I have watched. Now I assume the target moves and I build the alarm first. I have been that demo. It's a good feeling. It lasts a quarter. Then the site changes.

A benchmark result is marketing until someone publishes the harness. I learned that from a table where the winning model had a different prompt format than everyone else.

The comparison was real in the sense that the numbers were measured. It was meaningless in the sense that the measurement favoured one contestant. Nobody lied. They just tuned the thing that made them look good.

This is the same problem as a startup publishing a conversion rate without the denominator. The number is true and the frame is the argument.

Now I read the harness before the table. Prompts, temperature, retries, how many attempts count as a pass. If those are missing, the ranking is a preference. I have stopped quoting benchmark numbers in my own writing unless I ran them, and my writing got shorter. I read the harness before the table. That's the whole method. It's not clever. It works though.

A data centre near me is being built on farmland and the local argument is about water, not chips. That is where this whole thing lands.

The numbers are strange when you read them. A large facility draws what a small city draws, and it draws it all day. The grid was not planned for a customer that never sleeps and can move in 18 months.

I don't think the answer is to stop building. I think the answer is that power becomes the product constraint and the companies that solve it win. That means gas, nuclear, geothermal, and a lot of ugly contracts.

What interests me is the second order effect. If power is the limit, then efficiency is worth more than capability. A model that is 30 percent dumber and 5 times cheaper starts to look like the right engineering choice. I have no numbers to back this up. I read the local minutes instead. Nobody does. It's early. I ran a 7 billion parameter model on a laptop and it wrote a better SQL query than the hosted model I paid for. It was slower and it was offline and it was enough.

That result changes what I think the next few years look like. Most tasks don't need the biggest model. They need a good enough model that runs where the data already is, with no per call cost and no network.

The hosted labs will keep winning the hard problems. The local models will take the boring ones, which is most of the volume. Nobody writes a funding announcement about that work.

I have started designing for the small model first and treating the big one as an upgrade. It makes the product cheaper and it makes me honest about how much of my value is the prompt. I shipped it as a joke. It's now the default in my tool. Still is.

---
Open weights won the argument and nobody announced it. Every serious tool I use now has a local model in the settings, and half of them default to it.

This was never about ideology for me. It was about what happens when a vendor changes a price or a policy and my product stops working. A weight file is a business continuity plan.

Counter argument is that open models lag by six months on the hard tasks. That's true and it has been true for two years, and the gap hasn't closed or widened. A constant gap is a stable market, not a temporary one.

I use both. The hosted model for the thing that needs to be right, the local one for everything that needs to be cheap. What interests me is that the split keeps moving toward local, one task at a time. I have been running both for a year. The split moves every month. It's not close. I checked.

---
A hospital near me still faxes discharge summaries. I read that and stopped worrying about whether AI is ready for healthcare.

The bottleneck was never the model. It's the 40 year old system that nobody can change, the compliance review, and the nurse who has 90 seconds to enter the data. A model that saves 20 minutes of typing is worth more than a diagnostic tool that nobody trusts.

The companies doing well in this space are unglamorous. They do prior authorisation, coding, scheduling, and transcription. Paperwork. The stuff that has a number attached and a person who hates doing it.

I think that's where most of the value lands in the next decade. Not in replacing the doctor. In removing the 40 percent of the job that is reading and retyping. Cheaper to sell and easier to prove. I have watched two deployments stall there. Nobody writes about the paperwork. It's where the money is.

I hired a junior developer in 2019 to write basic endpoints and I would not hire that role today. Work still exists and the shape of it changed.

The junior used to learn by doing the boring parts. Now the boring parts are generated in 20 seconds, which means the learning path is gone. You can't get good at reviewing code if you never wrote any.

Teams I see doing this well pair the junior with a real problem and a senior who has time. The junior's job becomes reading, testing, and asking why. That is a harder job and a better one.

I don't know what entry level means in five years. I do know that every senior I respect learned by breaking something small and fixing it. If we remove that, we save money now and pay for it in a decade. I have hired four juniors over the years. Two are seniors now. Both learned by breaking things. Nobody planned it. That's the path.

---
Consulting gets eaten before product does and I think people have the order wrong. A consultant sells a deliverable. A model can produce a draft of that deliverable in an hour.

What doesn't get automated is the room. Knowing which document matters, who needs to agree, and what the client actually means when they say integration. That is 80 percent of the job and it is invisible in the invoice.

So the smart consultants I know are selling the room and giving away the document. Drafts are free. Judgement about which draft and why is the fee.

I have been on both sides of this. The work I get paid for now is mostly deciding what to build, and the building takes a fraction of the time. My rates went up when I stopped charging for the typing. I have sold both ways. The room pays better. It's also more fun. Every time.

An enterprise pilot I know of has been in evaluation for 14 months and has processed 400 documents. Contracts are worth more in press releases than in revenue.

That is the normal shape of enterprise AI right now. Buying is slower than the technology cycle. By the time the security review finishes, the model has been replaced twice.

Vendors that survive sell into a budget that already exists. Not a new AI line item. Same line that paid for the old vendor, with a better number on it.

I have stopped being impressed by pilot announcements. The number that matters is production seats after 12 months. I have asked three companies for that number and all three changed the subject. I ask for it every time now. It's the only one I trust. Nobody has it. Still nothing. That tells me something. It's not a buying problem. It's a proof problem.

Per seat pricing breaks when the software does the work of three people. I have watched two companies hit this and both handled it badly.

Customers look at the bill, see one seat doing the job of a team, and ask why they pay per person. Vendors have no good answer because the value isn't in the person, it's in the outcome.

My fix is to price the outcome, which sounds smart and is much harder to sell. Buyers want a number they can forecast, and outcome pricing looks like a bet.

I price my own work on the result for this reason. It's scarier and it aligns the incentives. If the thing doesn't work, I don't get paid, which is the only honest way to sell a tool that claims to save time. I have not solved this. I just charge for the result. It's uncomfortable and it works. Ask me in a year.

---
Latency is the product now and almost nobody markets it. A tool that answers in 400 milliseconds feels like software. One that answers in four seconds feels like a form submission.

I moved a feature from a hosted model to a local one and the quality dropped about 10 percent. Users liked it more. They said it felt faster, which it did, and that beat the better answer.

This is an old lesson that the AI era keeps relearning. People don't measure quality in the abstract. They measure how the thing feels while they wait. A spinner is a product decision.

I now treat response time as a feature with a budget. Anything over a second needs a reason and a progress indicator. The reason is usually that I was too lazy to cache. I have stopped trusting the number. I watch the graph now. It tells the truth. That's new.

Evals are becoming a product and I think that's the most underrated business in the field. Everyone can build a demo and nobody can tell you whether it got worse.

The gap is measurement. A team ships a prompt change, the demo looks better, and three weeks later a customer finds the edge case that used to work. Nobody has the 200 cases that would have caught it.

The companies selling this are boring and they are growing. Test sets, scoring, dashboards, the ability to diff two versions. It's the same business as software testing with a new vocabulary.

I built my own version because I'm cheap. Twenty tasks and a diff script. It found bugs that three months of manual checking didn't, and it took an evening. That is the whole argument for the category. I have measured this wrong for years. A stopwatch is enough. It's cheaper than a rewrite. Try it.

I forgot what my assistant knew and spent an hour explaining a project it had already seen. Context is the product and nobody has solved it.

The window got bigger and the problem got worse in a way. More context means more chances to include the wrong file, the stale doc, the version from March. The model answers confidently from the wrong page.

What works for me is boring. A short file at the top of every session that says what this project is and what not to touch. Six lines. It beats 100,000 tokens of retrieval.

I think the winners here will look like filing systems, not magic. Good defaults, obvious state, a way to see what the model is looking at. The hard part is not the window. It's knowing what belongs in it. I have used that line twice. It ends the meeting. Nobody argues with it.

I fine tuned a model for a week and got a 4 percent improvement that a better prompt matched in an hour. That was an expensive lesson in ordering.

Fine tuning is the thing everyone wants to do because it feels like engineering. It's also the thing with the worst return per hour for most problems. Data cleaning and a clear instruction beat it almost every time.

Where it does work is style and format. A model that has to output your schema, your tone, your 40 fields. That is a pattern matching job and training helps.

I now do the boring steps first. Prompt, then examples, then retrieval, then training. I have only reached step four twice, and both times the data was the reason, not the model. I have watched this twice. Both teams lost the deal. The price was the reason. That's the pattern. Every time. It's why I stopped selling seats.

The GPU rental market looks like a bubble and the tell is the contracts. Three year commitments signed by companies that have been alive for 18 months.

I don't say that with any confidence about the timing. Bubbles can run for years and the people calling them early have been wrong since 2023. What I can say is that the structure is fragile.

What interests me is what survives. Compute gets cheaper, some providers consolidate, and the applications that needed cheap tokens get a windfall. An infrastructure crash is somebody else's cheap input.

I have no position and no prediction. I keep my own costs on a review each month so a price change doesn't end the product. That's the only bubble insurance available to someone my size. That's it. Nothing clever. It's dull work and it has saved me twice. The first time was a logging bill from a service I had forgotten about. I recommend it.

A compliance review added six weeks to a launch and removed nothing from the product. I used to think that was waste. Now I think it's the moat.

Anyone can build the feature. Very few teams can document the data flow, the retention policy, the model provider, and the human review step in a form a bank will accept. That work is dull and it is the reason the deal closes.

The regulation is also a filter. It raises the cost of entry and rewards the companies that were already organised. Small teams can pass it, they just have to start earlier than they want to.

I now write the data flow diagram before the first line of code on anything that touches personal data. It takes an afternoon and it has saved me two weeks twice. Boring is a competitive advantage when everyone else is in a hurry. So far.

If code gets cheap, the expensive part becomes deciding what to build and proving it works. Both of those are human and neither scales the way people hope.

I have watched a team generate 40,000 lines in a month. They spent the next month deleting most of it. The volume was never the constraint. Knowing which 4,000 lines matter was.

The teams that will do well are the ones with strong taste and strong tests. Taste picks the right problem. Tests catch the machine's confidence. Neither comes from a model.

I keep coming back to the same conclusion. The tools got better and the job got harder, because the job was never typing. It was judgement, and judgement is the one thing you can't generate on demand. I have watched this happen twice. Both teams shipped faster. Both had to fix it later. That's the trade. Nothing new.

I tripled my rate in one email and lost half my clients. The other half didn't blink. Revenue went up 40 percent that quarter. I expected a slow month and got a waiting list.

I cancelled in month five and spent 300 dollars on a technical audit. The audit found 40 broken pages and a duplicate title on every post. Fixing those did more in three weeks than the links did in five months. Boring beats clever. The traffic came back in July. It took four months. The site is fine now. I check it each month.

I invoiced a German client in dollars because that's what my template said. The exchange rate moved 8 percent between the quote and the payment. I lost 640 dollars on an 8,000 dollar job.

Nobody argued. The client paid exactly what the invoice said. The bank took its cut and the rate did the rest. I found the gap when I reconciled the month and the number didn't match the quote. It was a quiet loss, which is the kind that lasts.

Now the currency is in the contract and the rate is locked for 14 days. If it moves past that I reissue the invoice. It sounds fussy until you do the math. On a year of international work the difference is a holiday. I read the contract now. I check the rate first. It moves fast. I should have known better. I do now, and I ask for the rate in writing.

I offered a 5 percent discount for payment ahead of the date. One client took it every month and still paid on day 29. He called that ahead. The invoice said 30. The margin was already thin.

I dropped the discount and raised the base rate. He stayed. The discount was teaching him that the price was negotiable and the scope was soft. Both were my fault. Now the window is five days, and it is written above the total. He paid on time after that. The extras stopped. I learned that the hard way. I won't do it again, not for any client.

I had a good year and a 26,000 dollar tax bill I hadn't planned for. It was in the account in December and gone in April. I paid it and started the next year with nothing set aside.

Nobody warns you that a good month feels like profit. It isn't. It's revenue with a bill attached. I was spending the whole number on tools and trips and calling the leftovers savings. The leftovers were never enough. I found that out in a bank branch, which is a bad place to learn math.

Now 30 percent of every payment goes to a separate account the day it lands. I don't look at it and I don't count it as mine. The first year I did this the tax bill was boring. Boring is the goal. The account is called tax. I set it up in May. It still works. It is boring.

The curriculum had 60 hours of video and 200 exercises. Each exercise had a solution one click away. Students who clicked through finished in a month. Students who tried to solve them took three. Both groups got the same certificate.

The job guarantee had a clause. You had to apply to 10 jobs a week and accept any offer within 30 miles. Two people got jobs. One was already working in IT. The other went back to his old job in a call centre after 11 weeks.

I stopped teaching there. A bootcamp can teach syntax. It can't teach the 300 hours of confusion that make someone employable. Selling the shortcut is easy. Delivering it is not. I asked for a refund. I got one after three emails.

A university recorded its lectures in 2019 and never updated them. Students in 2026 were watching a man explain a tool that had been shut down. I was one of those students.

Our library cut its hours to save two staff jobs. It now closes at 4pm on weekdays and is shut on Sunday. Study room is empty by 5.

I used that library to study for a certification. I work during the day, so the new hours meant I lost my desk. My next library is 11 miles away and closes at 6. I did the math and it added 90 minutes of driving each week.

Our council said the cut saved 84,000 dollars. They didn't count the people who stopped coming. Nobody counted them. A library is not a shop with a till. Its value is in the quiet hour after school and the warm room in winter.

I still go on Saturday. Staff are kind and the shelves are the same. It feels smaller now, not in size but in what it promises. A service that closes at 4 is a service for people who don't work. It was quiet. I miss it.

A boy was labelled gifted at age seven and never lost the label. By 14 he had stopped doing homework. Teachers kept saying he was bright, which meant they didn't ask why the work was missing.

I taught him maths for a year. He could do the problems in his head and refused to write them down. The label had taught him that effort was for other people. When the work got hard in year nine, he had no habit to fall back on.

His parents believed the label. They had been told he was special for seven years. Every teacher who suggested otherwise was wrong. That is a lot of weight for a kid to carry.

I don't think the label is evil. I think it is sticky. A test at seven is a snapshot, and a snapshot should not be a life sentence. I started telling parents that the label describes a moment, not a child.

I don't know if group work teaches collaboration or teaches people to free ride. I learned to pick the team. I know the free riders in my group are now managers. They learned the lesson the project was teaching.

A plagiarism tool flagged a student for a quote in quotation marks. It was a quote from a book on the reading list. That tool had matched it against a study guide.

I fixed it in 20 minutes. Resubmission took the student a week and a half. She rewrote a paragraph that had been fine and made it worse. Her final grade dropped by four points.

I bought a supplement that claimed to be third party tested. That test was on the website as a file. That file was a certificate for a different batch.

I don't think supplements are all fake. I think third party tested is a phrase with no standard behind it. Anyone can test anything. The question is who paid for the test and what happened to the batch that failed.

I don't think the office is lazy. I think a process with six steps and no clock is a process that works for the office. I keep the appeal letter on my phone now. I attach it to every appeal.

An asteroid passed 3,000 km above the ground. It was 1 metre across. Astronomers found it 7 hours before closest approach.

I read the alert the next morning. That object came from the direction of the sun, which is the blind spot. It would have burned up in the atmosphere and no one would have noticed. The 3,000 km number is close in space terms and far in human terms.

The survey that found it has 4 telescopes and a budget of 8 million dollars. It is looking for the big ones. A 1 metre rock is not a threat. A 30 metre rock is a city block and we find about half of those.

I don't think we are doomed. I think a 7 hour warning is a number that tells you how much of the sky is unwatched. I follow the survey now. It finds something most weeks.

I don't think the organiser failed. I think one telescope for 200 people is a scheduling problem, not an astronomy problem. I bring binoculars now and I look for the person who knows the sky. They are usually at the back with a flask.

A rocket launched at 6:12am and I watched from a beach 8 miles away. That sound arrived 40 seconds late. That ground shook in my chest.

I had set an alarm for 4:30 and driven 90 minutes. There were 300 people on the beach. A man next to me had a scanner and a notebook. He had seen 74 launches. He said this one was a small one.

The rocket went up and the plume caught the sunrise. It looked like a candle in a dark room. Then the sound came and people cheered. The whole thing lasted four minutes and the drive home took two hours.

I don't think it was worth the drive. I think it was worth the alarm. I would do it again for a bigger rocket and a later launch. The sunrise was the best part and that was free. I would do it again.

A good first issue sat open for two years. It was a typo in the docs. Twelve people said they would fix it. None did.

I fixed it in four minutes. That pull request took 11 days to merge because the maintainer was on holiday. The issue had a label that said help wanted and a comment from a bot welcoming contributors.

The project had 200 good first issues and 4 active maintainers. The label was a promise the project couldn't keep. New contributors got excited, opened a request, and waited. Half of them never came back.

I don't think labels are bad. I think a label that says good first issue on a project with a two week review time is a filter for patience. I look at the merge time before I contribute now. If it is over a month, I send a patch and move on. I look at the merge time before I contribute.

A pull request had 400 comments and no decision. That change was 30 lines. The discussion covered naming, scope and a rewrite of the module.

I was the author. I wanted to fix a bug. By comment 100 the thread was about whether the project should support an old version. By comment 300 someone had proposed a design document. The bug is still open.

I closed the request after five months. I maintain a fork with the fix and 12 users. The original project has 9,000 users and the same bug. Nobody has complained because the bug only shows up on a specific input.

I don't think consensus is bad. I think a 30 line fix that needs 400 comments is a project with no decision maker. I ask who can say yes before I write code now. If the answer is everyone, the answer is nobody. I ask who can say yes before I write code.

I forked a project with 2,000 users. That fork died in eight months. I learned more from the death than the launch.

That original maintainer had stopped responding. I announced the fork with a roadmap and a Discord. Two hundred people joined. Twelve sent code. Three stayed for more than a month. The rest wanted a fix and left.

The hard part was not the code. It was the releases, the security reports and the support. I had a full time job. The project needed 15 hours a week and I had four. I archived it in March and pointed users back to the original.

I don't think forks are a failure. I think a fork is a company with no employees and no revenue. Before you fork, count the hours, not the stars. I count them now and I have not forked since. I count the hours before I fork.

A bug report said the app was broken. It had no version, no logs and no steps. That title was "doesn't work". I closed it and asked for details.

That reporter came back with a screenshot. That screenshot showed an error from a version released two years earlier. He was on an old build because his company pinned it. That bug had been fixed in 2023.

I reopened the issue and added a template. The next 40 reports had a version and logs. The time I spent triaging dropped by half. One person had been doing support for a year without a template because nobody had asked.

I don't think users are lazy. I think a form is a kindness to everyone. I add a template to every repo now. It is four fields and it saves a conversation. The bug was real and it was in his build. I add a template to every repo now.

A sponsor paid 5 dollars a month for a project used by 4,000 companies. He was the only sponsor. That project had 3 million downloads.

I saw the sponsor page because I was looking for a dependency to replace. That maintainer had a note that said "if this saves you money, sponsor me". That note had been there for two years. Those companies using it had a combined revenue of 2 billion. Nobody paid.

I emailed one of them and asked if they sponsored. The reply said they used the community edition and had no budget for it. The company had 300 engineers and a coffee budget of 40,000 a month.

I don't think companies are evil. I think open source is invisible in a budget until something breaks. I sponsor three projects now, 20 dollars each. It is not enough and it is more than the companies with 300 engineers.

A maintainer deleted his package from the registry and broke thousands of builds. He was 24 and had been maintaining it for free for six years. He had 200,000 dependents.

I was affected. My deploy failed at 9am with a 404. I found the package had been unpublished. The maintainer's blog said he was tired of companies making money from his work and not contributing.

He restored it 11 hours later. The damage was done. Builds failed for a day. Three companies posted about it and one offered to fund him. He accepted 4,000 dollars a month and hired a second maintainer.

I don't think he was wrong to be angry. I think deleting was the only lever he had and it hurt the wrong people. I pin versions and vendor critical packages now. I also sponsor the ones I can't replace. I pin versions and vendor what I can't replace.

A docs page was wrong for four years. It said the function took two arguments. It took three. I found out when a user opened an issue with a stack trace.

I had copied the example from the docs and shipped a bug. The docs were generated from a comment that had not been updated. The comment was from 2019. The function changed in 2021 and the test was updated and the docs were not.

I fixed the page in 10 minutes. It had 40,000 views in the previous year. I don't know how many people copied the example. I know one did, because he was polite about it.

I don't think docs are secondary. I think a test proves the code works and the docs prove a person can use it. I add a docs test now that runs the example. It is a script and it catches this every time.

Our build pipeline cost 900 dollars a month. I found out when the card expired and nobody noticed for a week. That pipeline ran 4,000 builds a month and 3,800 were the same test.

I looked at the logs. A scheduled job ran the full suite every hour on a branch that had not changed. The job was added in 2021 to catch a flaky test. The test was fixed in 2022. The job stayed.

I deleted the job and the bill fell to 210 dollars. Nobody complained. One person asked if the night builds had stopped. I said they had never been used. He said he liked seeing them green in the morning.

I don't think CI is waste. I think a pipeline is a place where old habits get a credit card. I review the schedule every quarter now. It takes 20 minutes and it paid for a holiday.

A contributor rewrote the whole project in a weekend. He opened a pull request with 14,000 lines changed. That message said "cleanup".

I was the maintainer. That rewrite removed two features, changed the public interface and dropped support for an old runtime. It also fixed a bug I had been chasing for a year. Two things were true at once.

I asked for the change split into 40 requests. He said that was busywork. We argued for a week and he closed the request. The bug is still there. I fixed it myself in 30 lines six months later.

I don't think big changes are bad. I think a 14,000 line request is a demand for trust that a stranger has not earned. I ask for small changes now and I explain why. The good contributors understand. The others were never going to stay. I review the schedule every quarter now.

A maintainer merged a change without running the tests. That change broke the build for 200 users. He merged it at 11pm and went to bed.

I was one of the users. My deploy failed at 7am. I found the broken commit and bisected it in 20 minutes. That fix was a missing import. I opened a request and it was merged in an hour.

The maintainer said he had been awake for 18 hours and the change looked fine. He had a policy that said tests must pass. The policy was in the contributing guide. The button was green because the test job had been skipped for a docs change and the skip applied to the whole pull request.

I don't think he was careless. I think a green check that can be skipped is a green check that means nothing. I require the test job on every change now. It is a setting and it takes a minute.

A security advisory was disputed by the vendor for 18 months. That issue was a token that never expired. That vendor said it was a feature. Three projects shipped a workaround.

I reported it. Those vendor's response said the behaviour was documented. That documentation said the token could be configured to expire. That default was no expiry. The default was the problem.

The advisory was published without the vendor's agreement. It got a score of 7.5 and 40 projects patched within a month. The vendor fixed the default in the next release and never mentioned it in the changelog.

I don't think vendors are always wrong. I think a default is a decision and a decision can be a vulnerability. I check the default token lifetime in every library now. If it is infinite, I set it. I require the test job on every change, with no exceptions at all.

---
A dependency upgrade broke production for 40 minutes. That changelog said "minor fixes". That upgrade changed a date format from local time to a global standard.

I was on call. That error was a timestamp that was 5 hours off. Those logs looked fine because the logs used the new format. The database had the old one. Two systems disagreed and neither complained.

We rolled back in 20 minutes. The upgrade had been auto merged by a bot because the tests passed. The tests didn't check the date. Nobody had written one because the format had been stable for six years.

I don't think minor releases are safe. I think "minor" is a promise about the version number, not the behaviour. I read the diff now for anything that touches dates, money or ordering. It takes 10 minutes and it is the whole job. I check the default expiry in every library.

A repo had 900 open issues and 4 maintainers. I wanted to help and asked where to start. That reply was a link to the issues page.

I picked a bug with a reproduction. I fixed it and opened a request. It sat for three weeks. I asked for a review and got one comment about the test style. I fixed that and waited two more weeks.

The issue was closed by a bot as stale. I reopened it. The maintainer merged it a month later and said thanks. The whole thing took 11 weeks for a 12 line change. I have not contributed since.

I don't think the maintainers are rude. I think a project with 900 issues is a project that can't say yes. I look at the closed issue rate before I contribute now. If it is lower than the open rate, I send money instead. I read the diff for dates and money.

A company used an open source project in its product for six years. It contributed nothing. Then it hired the maintainer.

I know because I was at the company. That maintainer had 40,000 users and no income. That company had a support ticket that took three weeks to fix. The engineering manager did the math and offered him a job.

He joined and spent half his time on the project. The company paid his salary and got a faster fix cycle. It was cheaper than the outage. The calculation was obvious once somebody made it.

I don't think companies are villains. I think the value of a dependency is invisible until you add up the support tickets. I ask for a line item now when a project is critical. If nobody can name the maintainer, that is the risk. I sponsor the projects I depend on every single month.

A foundation took over a project and added a 40 page governance document. That release cadence dropped from monthly to twice a year. That project is still alive.

I was a contributor. That foundation brought a code of conduct, a technical steering committee and a budget. That budget paid for two developers. That committee met every two weeks and approved the roadmap.

Those releases slowed because every change needed a vote. The security fixes kept shipping because they had an exception. The community split into people who liked the process and people who wanted the old speed. Both were right about different things.

I don't think foundations are bad. I think a project with a company behind it and a project with a committee behind it fail in different ways. I read the governance before I depend on a project now. It tells you how fast it can say yes.

A package name was squatted by a person who published an empty module. That name was one letter off a popular library. It had 40,000 downloads a month.

I found it in a dependency tree. That module did nothing. It was a placeholder published in 2018 by someone who wanted the name. The popular library had a typo in its docs for six months and people copied it.

The squatter had no malicious code. He had a readme that said "this is not the library you want". Nobody read it. The downloads came from lockfiles that nobody audited.

I don't think squatting is harmless. I think a name is a namespace and namespaces need rules. I check the package name against the official one before I install anything. It is a habit and it has caught two more. I read the governance rules before I depend on any project.

A build needed 8GB of memory and a machine with 16 cores. That project had 200 contributors. I tried to build it on a laptop with 8GB and it swapped for an hour.

I asked why. That answer was that the build compiled everything in parallel and the CI machine had 32 cores. That CI was donated by a company. The company's machine was not the machine a contributor had.

I added a flag to limit the jobs and documented it. The build took 14 minutes on my laptop instead of an hour. Three contributors said it was the first time they had built the project locally.

I don't think fast builds are bad. I think a build that only works on the biggest machine is a build that excludes people. I test on a small machine before I call anything done. It is a slow habit and it finds real problems.

A contributor licence agreement was 8 pages and assigned copyright to a company. I read it before I signed. I did not sign.

That agreement said the company could relicence my contribution under any terms. That is the standard for some projects and it is a lot to ask. The project was a tool I used every day. The bug I wanted to fix was small.

I opened an issue instead and described the fix. A maintainer implemented it in a week. My name is not in the commit. The bug is gone. That was the trade I chose.

I don't think these agreements are evil. I think they are a business decision and a contributor is allowed to say no. I read the agreement before I write code now. If it assigns copyright, I ask if there is another way. I test on a small machine before I call it done.

A project had no release in three years and 200 open issues. That maintainer said it was stable. Users said it was abandoned. Both were true.

I used it in production. That last release worked. The issues were mostly feature requests. The security reports were fixed in the main branch but never tagged. That was the problem. A fix in the main branch is not a fix for anyone using a release.

I asked for a tag. The maintainer said tagging was a hassle and people should use the main branch. I pinned a commit and wrote a note in my repo. Six months later a new maintainer took over and shipped 4 releases in a month.

I don't think stable means abandoned. I think a project without releases is a project without a promise. I check the last release date before I depend on anything now. If it is over a year, I look for a fork.

A bot closed 500 issues in one night. That message said "stale, please reopen if still relevant". That project had 900 open issues and 4 maintainers.

I had an issue in that batch. It was a crash on a specific input. I reopened it and the bot closed it again 30 days later. I gave up. That crash is still there.

That maintainer added the bot to reduce noise. It worked. The open count fell to 400. The number looked healthy and the bugs were still open. The bot had moved the problem from a list to a memory.

I don't think automation is wrong. I think a bot that closes without a human is a policy that says silence is resolution. I look at the reopened count now. If a project closes 500 and reopens 200, the bot is a broom. I check the last release date before I depend on it.

A read me file promised a feature that was never built. That feature was in the roadmap, the docs and the landing page. That code had a stub that returned an error.

I built a product on that promise. I found the stub in week three. That error message said "not implemented". The issue had been open since 2021 with 200 upvotes. The maintainer said it was coming soon.

I should have checked the code. I checked the docs because the docs are supposed to describe the code. The docs were written by a marketing person and never reviewed by an engineer. That is a sentence that explains a lot of software.

I don't think read me files are contracts. I think a stub is the truth and a promise is a plan. I read the source before I build on a feature now. It takes 10 minutes and it has saved me two products.

A laptop screen replacement was quoted at 480 dollars. A new laptop with the same specs was 600. That repair shop said the panel was special.

I found the panel online for 90 dollars. It took 40 minutes to fit and needed a 12 dollar tool. That shop was not lying about the panel. It was lying about the word special. The panel was a standard part with a connector.

I fixed it myself and gave the laptop another three years. The shop had a 70 percent margin and a queue of people who didn't know a panel costs 90. That is not a scam. It is a service with a price.

I don't think repair shops are evil. I think a repair that costs 80 percent of a new device is a design decision, not an accident. I check the part price before I agree to anything. The number is public and it changes the conversation.

A phone battery replacement cost 60 dollars and lasted four months. That shop used a battery with a fake label. I found out when the phone shut down at 40 percent.

I opened the phone and looked at the cell. That label said 3,200 mAh. That cell underneath said 2,200. That connector was taped. The shop had a 90 day warranty and my failure was on day 120.

I bought a genuine battery for 35 dollars and fitted it myself. The phone lasted another two years. The shop is still open and still advertising genuine parts. I left a review with a photo. It has 40 helpful votes.

I don't think every shop is dishonest. I think a battery is the easiest part to fake and the hardest to check. I ask to see the part before it goes in now. If they say no, I go somewhere else.

A graphics card cost 1,600 dollars in 2021. That list price was 700. I bought it because I needed it for work and the wait was six months.

I paid 900 over list. That card mined for a year before I got it. That seller had 40 of them and a photo of a warehouse. That card worked and the fans were worn. I replaced them for 30 dollars.

The shortage ended in 2023. The same card sells for 300 used. I lost 1,300 dollars on a part that was worth 700. I made the money back in 4 months of work. That is the only reason it was not a disaster.

I don't think the seller was a villain. I think a shortage is a transfer of money from people who need a thing to people who have it. I buy last generation now. The 20 percent performance gap is cheaper than the 100 percent price gap.

A chip factory took five years to build and cost 20 billion dollars. It opened and produced wafers at 40 percent yield. That plan said 80 percent.

I read the earnings call. That yield problem was a process step that needed 200 more engineers. That company had hired 1,000 and lost 300 to competitors. That building was on time and the people were not.

A fab is not a building. It is a building plus 3,000 people who know how to run it. The concrete takes two years. The knowledge takes ten. The company knew that and the timeline did not.

I don't think the project was a failure. I think a five year plan that ignores the ten year part is a press release with a foundation. I ask about the team before the building now. It is the same question in every industry. I ask about the team before the building.

A single board computer had a 12 month wait and a 3x price on the secondhand market. It cost 35 dollars new. Resellers wanted 120.

I needed six for a classroom. I bought three at list price and waited. That other three came from a reseller and two were dead. That dead ones had burn marks near the power input.

The shortage was caused by a factory that made one component. That factory had a fire. The board maker could not get the part and would not redesign. The design was five years old and the part was cheap.

I don't think the maker was lazy. I think a 35 dollar board with one supplier is a miracle with a single point of failure. I keep two spares now and I buy the version with a socketed part. It costs 5 dollars more and it sleeps better. I keep two spares now.

A solid state drive died after 14 months. That warranty was 12 months. That drive had 40 terabytes written and the rating was 600.

I checked the health before it died. It said 98 percent. That controller failed, not the memory. That drive went from working to not detected in one reboot. I lost 200 gigabytes of photos.

That drive was a cheap brand with a good rating. That rating came from a test that measured speed in the first hour. Nobody tests the controller for a year. The reviews were written on day one.

I don't think cheap drives are all bad. I think a rating is a snapshot and a backup is a decision. I keep two copies now, one local and one off site. The drive failure cost me a weekend. The backup costs 6 dollars a month. I keep two copies of every photo now. It works.
