A printer refused to print because a cartridge was "not genuine". That cartridge was genuine. The printer's firmware had been updated and the chip was now rejected.

I called support. They said the update improved security. They offered a new cartridge at 20 percent off. The cartridge I had was 40 dollars and had 60 percent ink left. The printer was 90 dollars.

I bought a chip resetter for 12 dollars and it worked for a year. Then the printer needed another update and the resetter stopped. I gave up and bought a laser printer from a different brand. It has no chip and costs 3 cents a page.

I don't think all printers are a scam. I think a printer that checks the ink is a subscription with a motor. I check the cost per page and the cartridge lock before I buy. It is a 5 minute search that saves 200 dollars a year.

A right to repair bill was debated for four hours. That opposition said it would damage innovation. That bill covered phones and farm equipment.

I went to the hearing. A farmer testified that he could not fix a tractor without a dealer. That dealer was 90 miles away and charged 200 dollars an hour. That tractor was down for two weeks during harvest.

A manufacturer's lobbyist said the software was proprietary. He said opening it would let people bypass emissions controls. The farmer said he did not want to bypass anything. He wanted to replace a sensor.

The bill passed the lower house and died in committee. The same bill had died three times. I don't think the vote was about repair. It was about who owns the thing after you buy it. I write to my representative now. It is slow and it is the only lever. I write to my representative now.

I bought a soldering iron for 12 dollars. It had a dial, a stand and a pointy tip. I fixed a monitor and a lamp with it. I still use it.

A friend bought a 90 dollar station with a digital display. He uses it for the same jobs. He said the temperature is stable. Mine drifts by 20 degrees and I have learned to compensate. Those joints have held for four years.

The expensive station is better. It is also not the thing that made the difference. The difference was learning to tin a tip and clean it. That took an hour on a video and 20 failed joints.

I don't think tools are a waste. I think a beginner buys the station because it feels like progress. I tell people to buy the cheap iron and spend the 78 dollars on parts. The parts are where the learning is.

I called support and asked for an exception. They said the policy was the policy. I asked if I could pay the difference for a better panel. They said no. I used the monitor for two years and the pixel stayed green.

A server had a 10 year old processor and 32 gigabytes of memory. It ran a service with 4,000 users. That replacement quote was 12,000 dollars.

I looked at the load. That processor was at 12 percent. That memory was at 60 percent. That disk was the bottleneck. A 200 dollar drive would have fixed the problem. The vendor wanted to sell a whole machine.

I replaced the drive and the service ran for another two years. The vendor's engineer admitted the quote was a standard config. He said nobody asks for the load data. The company had been about to spend 12,000 on a problem a drive could solve.

I don't think vendors are dishonest. I think a quote is a default and a default is a guess. I ask for the bottleneck before the quote now. It is one command and it has saved six figures across three jobs.

A 40 dollar cable failed after two months. A 6 dollar cable from a bin has worked for three years. That expensive one had a braided jacket and a brand.

I cut the expensive one open. Those conductors were thin and the shielding was foil. That cheap one had thicker wire and no shielding. The shielding mattered for the video signal and the thickness mattered for charging. The brand mattered for the price. It worked.

I now buy cables from a company that publishes the wire gauge. It costs 9 dollars and it has lasted two years. The braided jacket was a look and the wire was the thing.

I don't think price signals quality. I think a spec sheet signals quality and most cables don't have one. I check the gauge and the rating before I buy. It is boring and it is the only thing that predicts whether a cable works.

A laptop fan failed and the machine shut down every 20 minutes. That replacement fan was 18 dollars. That repair shop wanted 140 to fit it.

I ordered the fan and watched a video. That job took 30 minutes and needed a tiny screwdriver. That hardest part was a cable with a fragile connector. I broke the first connector and had to order a second fan.

The laptop worked and ran cooler than before. The old fan had been failing for a year and I had ignored the noise. The shutdowns were the fan's last message. I had blamed the software.

I don't think repair is always easy. I think a 30 minute job is worth attempting before a 140 dollar quote. I check the part price and the video before I decide. If the video is over an hour, I pay someone. I ask for the old part back. Every time.

A repair shop swapped my motherboard for a used one and told me it was new. I found out because the serial number did not match the box.

That shop replaced a charging port. That port is a 20 dollar part and an hour of work. That invoice said a new board at 220 dollars. The board in the machine had a different serial and a scratch near the memory slot.

I asked for the old board. They said it had been sent for recycling. I asked for the recycling record and got silence. I disputed the card and got 160 dollars back. The shop is still trading.

I don't think every shop does this. I think a repair is a trust exercise with no receipt for the parts. I ask for the old part back before I pay now. A shop that refuses is a shop that has something to hide.

A motherboard had a bad capacitor and the machine would not boot. That capacitor was 40 cents. That board was 200 dollars. I replaced the capacitor with a cheap iron.

I found the bad cap by looking at the top. It was bulging. A forum post said it was a common failure on that model. I bought 10 capacitors for 4 dollars and replaced three. That board booted and ran for four more years.

That repair took an hour and the risk was a burnt trace. I practiced on a dead board first. The first attempt lifted a pad and I had to run a wire. The second worked. The third was clean.

I don't think everyone should solder a board. I think a 40 cent part is a fact that changes the decision. I look for the bulging cap before I replace anything now. It is the cheapest diagnosis in hardware.

A router stopped getting firmware updates after two years. It still worked and it had a known vulnerability. That vendor said the model was end of life.

I found the vulnerability in a mailing list. It let an attacker on the network read the admin password. The vendor had fixed it in a newer model and not backported it. The router had 400,000 units in use. It still worked. Nobody patched it.

I installed open firmware and the router worked for another three years. The process took an hour and required a serial cable. Most users would not do it. They would keep the router and the vulnerability.

I don't think vendors should support hardware forever. I think two years is a warranty, not a lifetime. I check the support window before I buy a router now. If it is under five years, I look for one that can run open firmware. I check the support window before I buy. Five years is the floor.

I don't think the researchers were malicious. I think a security claim travels faster than a correction. I wait for a second source and a version number now. A 404 page said "page not found" and nothing else. No search, no links, no way back. I had followed a link from a search result.

I was looking for a recipe. That site had reorganised its URLs and not redirected the old ones. The 404 was a dead end. I went back to the search results and picked a different site.

That site had 4,000 old URLs without redirects. The traffic to those URLs was 12 percent of the total. The fix was a redirect map. It took two days and recovered most of the traffic in a month.

I don't think 404 pages are an edge case. I think a 404 is a door that should lead somewhere. I add a search box and the top links now. It costs nothing and it keeps the visit. I add a search box and the top links now. It costs nothing.

Returns cost more than the sale on about a fifth of online orders. I ran the numbers for a small shop last year. Twenty two percent of orders came back. The average return ate 14 dollars in postage, repacking and staff time. That was before the refund.

So the product was never sold. It was rented, at a loss.

We tried a restocking fee. Sales dropped 8 percent in a month. So we removed it. Then we photographed every item against a ruler, from four angles, in the same ugly lighting as a customer's hallway. Returns fell to 15 percent. No fee, just honesty about how it looks in real life.

Six accounts were returning nine or more items each. They were not stealing. They were buying three sizes because the size chart was wrong. We fixed the chart and two of them stopped.

I used to think returns were a customer service problem. They are a photography problem, a sizing problem and a copy problem. The refund is the cheapest part.

Eye level is the most expensive shelf in the shop and the least useful one.

Brands pay for it because that's where the eye lands. I doubt the number holds up. We swapped our best margin products down to knee height for a month, just to see. Sales barely moved. What moved was the number of people who asked staff for help, and that went up.

Turns out reaching down makes people stop and think. Thinking makes them talk. Talking sells more than a display ever did.

I have watched shops rebuild entire fixtures around a planogram drawn by someone who never stood in the aisle. Twelve thousand pounds of shelving to put a cereal box 40 centimetres higher.

Try the dull experiment first. Move the thing. Count for two weeks. You will learn more than the supplier deck will tell you. Retail keeps buying certainty. Shoppers aren't certain. They are tired and in a hurry and mostly looking for a reason to leave.

The greeter at the door is the cheapest theft deterrent and the most ignored job in the store. We had a man on the door for a year. He said hello, asked if they needed help, and did nothing else. Shrinkage fell by a third in that period. Same stock, same cameras, same staff count.

I don't think he was catching anyone. I think being seen is the whole mechanism. A person who looks at you is a person who might remember your face.

Then the store cut the role to save hours. Shrinkage climbed back over two quarters. Nobody connected the two things, so they bought more cameras instead. Cameras record. They do not greet.

The job got automated with a sensor that plays a recorded welcome. It fools nobody. Customers can tell a recording in under two seconds, and so can a shoplifter.

If I ran a store again, I would hire for the door first and stock the shelves second. Hard to measure, easy to feel, and the numbers eventually agree.

---
Self checkout didn't remove the cashier. It moved the labour to the customer and added a queue for help.

I timed it. Six tills, one assistant. Average wait to get a bag override was 90 seconds. The old staffed line moved faster on a busy Saturday because a cashier fixes a problem without leaving the till.

The shop saved two salaries and lost the impulse aisle. Nobody buys a chocolate bar while wrestling a screen that says unexpected item in bagging area.

Then there is the honesty problem. Self checkout shrink runs higher, by most estimates, and the gap isn't teenagers. It is ordinary people who scan the cheap item and pocket the expensive one because no one is watching and the machine is already annoying them.

I am not against the machines. I am against pretending they are free. They buy speed for the shop and cost trust at the counter. Put one person on four tills, not six. Staff the help button harder than the till.

Music tempo controls how long people stay, and almost nobody tunes it on purpose.

We ran a slow playlist for a fortnight. Same shop, same stock, same week of the month. Dwell time went up 11 percent and sales went up 4. Then we ran fast music. People moved quicker, bought less, and the queue was shorter at closing.

The fast playlist made the shop feel busy. The slow one made it feel calm. Neither was better. They were different shops.

The trick is matching the tempo to the job. A lunch counter wants fast. A bookshop wants slow. A pharmacy wants whatever gets people out without feeling rushed.

Most shops hand this to a streaming service and never think about it again. That's a decision, just not a deliberate one. I would rather pick 30 songs by hand and know why each one is there. It costs an afternoon and it's the cheapest mood control you will ever install. I still run both playlists on a Tuesday. I have no idea which one is right.

---
Prices ending in 99 still work, and I resent how well they work.

We tested identical products at 19.00 and 18.99. The 99 version sold 9 percent more. Same margin, basically. Same product. The only difference was a digit that made the number look smaller than it was.

I know why it happens. The eye reads left to right and stops at the first digit. Nineteen is a different number from eighteen in the part of the brain that decides fast.

But there is a cost. If everything ends in 99, the whole shop reads as a discount shop, and discount shops are expected to discount. We had to break the pattern on the expensive lines. Round numbers signalled quality, somehow, to the exact same customers.

So now we use 99 on the cheap things and whole pounds on the good things. It is arbitrary and it isn't. People read the shape of a price before they read the value. I don't like it. I use it.

Loyalty cards collect data for the shop and give the customer a discount they were going to get anyway.

I signed up for four of them last year to see what the offers looked like. Three sent me a birthday voucher for something I had never bought. One sent me a coupon for the exact thing I buy every week, which is the only useful one.

The rest were a data harvesting exercise with a plastic card attached. And they cost the shop money twice, once in the scheme fee and once in the discount.

What actually worked in our shop was remembering people. The woman who buys the same bread on a Friday. The man who asks for the thick cut bacon. No card, no points, just a person who knows.

We couldn't scale that past one shop. I know. But the lesson scaled fine. Use the data to be useful, not to be seen collecting it. A loyalty scheme that rewards the habit you already have is just a rebate with extra steps. I keep mine in a drawer.

---
Free shipping over 40 pounds doesn't increase basket size. It increases abandonment just under 40 pounds.

I watched the funnel for six months. The threshold pulled a few people up. It also created a cliff. Baskets at 37 pounds died, and so did baskets at 34. People would rather leave than pay 5 pounds of postage to reach a number that felt invented, because it was.

We moved the threshold down to 30 and the cliff moved down with it. Same shape, different number. That is when I understood it was not about the number at all.

What fixed it was showing the postage cost early. Small text under the price at the top of the page. No surprise at checkout. Conversion went up 6 percent and the average basket didn't move.

The honest version was cheaper than the clever one. That keeps happening to me. Postage is not a marketing lever. It is a cost. Show it and stop pretending. I would show postage on the first line of the page.

Abandoned cart emails work, and most shops send the worst possible version of them.

The bad one arrives 20 minutes after you leave and says you forgot something. I didn't forget, I decided. Now I feel nagged and slightly judged.

The good one arrives the next morning, shows the item, and says the size you picked is down to two. That is information. It reopens a decision instead of questioning it.

We changed the copy and the timing together. I sent one email two days later, and no discount at all. Recovery went from 3 percent to 7. When we added a 10 percent code, recovery went to 9 and margin went down. Not worth it.

The lesson is boring. Say something true about the thing they wanted. Don't say come back. Do not say we miss you. Nobody misses me, I left four hours ago. One email. Real reason. Then stop.

---
When an item is out of stock, the substitute you offer decides whether the customer stays.

We used to show a grey button that said out of stock. That is a dead end dressed as information. The customer leaves, and the shop has paid for the visit and learned nothing.

Now the page shows the next best thing, with one line explaining why it is close. Same size, different brand, one pound cheaper. Conversion on those pages went from 4 percent to 13.

The mistake I made first was offering whatever had the most stock. That is the shop's problem, not the shopper's. People can smell a push.

Offer the closest match, say what differs, and name the thing that is missing. If nothing is close, say so and offer to email when it returns. That list is now our best source of demand data. Empty shelf, full signal. Most shops just show the emptiness. I would rather show nothing than the wrong thing.

---
The box is bigger than the product because shelf space is rented by the centimetre.

I bought a tube of cream last month. The carton was three times the volume of the tube. Inside was a plastic insert holding air in a very specific shape. Somebody designed that insert. Somebody approved it. It exists to make the thing look like more.

I get the logic. A bigger box gets more facings. More facings means more chance the eye lands. But the customer pays for the box twice, once in the price and once in the bin.

We cut our packaging by a third and put the saving into a clearer front panel. Returns from damaged goods dropped, postage dropped, and nobody complained that the box looked small. They complained about the old one.

There is a version of this that is just greenwashing. Don't slap a leaf on it. Shrink the box and show the numbers. Retail has been optimising for the shelf for 40 years. The shelf isn't where the decision ends.

#Retail #Packaging #Ecommerce #Sustainability #Design #SmallBusiness #Costs #Shipping #ProductDesign #Waste #ShopFloor #Operations #StoreDesign #CustomerExperience #Conversion

One queue for all tills beats a queue per till, and shops keep getting this wrong.

I watched a bank branch and a supermarket solve the same problem in opposite ways. The bank had six windows and six lines and everyone in the wrong one. The supermarket had one line feeding 12 tills and almost no anger.

The maths isn't subtle. With one line, the wait is average. With six, it is random, and people remember the one time they picked badly. Ten minutes in a single line feels fair. Ten minutes behind a person with a full trolley feels like a personal insult.

We changed ours in a weekend with some tape and a sign. Complaints about waiting dropped by half. Actual waiting time didn't change.

Fairness is a feature. It is cheaper than speed. If you cannot do one line, at least tell people which till is fast. Information beats hope.

#Retail #Queues #StoreDesign #CustomerExperience #Operations #SmallBusiness #ShopFloor #WaitingTime #Psychology #Service #Ecommerce #Conversion #Merchandising #Sales #Checkout

Mirrors near the till aren't there for vanity. They are there to make you feel watched while you decide.

I noticed it in a clothes shop first. A mirror at the end of the aisle, angled so you can see yourself and the door behind you. You stand up straighter. You put the thing down or you buy it. Either way you stop drifting.

The effect is real and slightly grim. Being observed changes behaviour, even when the observer is you. Some shops use it to prevent theft. Some use it to make the space feel bigger. Both work, and both are the same trick.

What I wouldn't do is put one where it startles people. We had a mirror in a corner that made customers jump because they caught movement in it. Two complaints, one refund, mirror gone.

Use it at the threshold, not in the dark corner. Light the space and let people see themselves decide. I moved ours twice before it worked.

I read 200 reviews of the same kettle and learned more about the shop than the kettle.

Star ratings were useless. Everything averaged four point two. The text was where the truth lived. One line kept appearing in different words. It boils fast and the handle gets hot.

That is a design flaw, stated 40 times, hidden behind a number that rounds it away. So we changed how we read reviews. We stopped sorting by helpful. We started searching for the word hot, or loud, or broke. The complaints cluster, and the cluster is the product.

The other thing I learned is that a shop with zero bad reviews isn't good. It's filtered. Five one star reviews with calm replies built more trust than 300 perfect ones. People are looking for evidence that you handle problems, not evidence that none exist.

Sort by pain, not by praise. The pain is specific and specific is actionable.

A wishlist is a confession. A cart is a decision. Shops treat them the same and lose both.

We had 4,000 wishlist items and 900 carts. The cart got three recovery emails a week. The wishlist got nothing, ever, because it was filed as browsing.

But a person who saves a coat in October is telling you a date. They are waiting for a sale, a payday or cold weather. That's the most predictable signal in the shop and we were ignoring it.

We started one email, sent when the saved item dropped in price. Open rate 44 percent. Conversion 11. No discount invented, just the news that the thing they wanted got cheaper.

The carts got quieter too. Fewer emails, better timing. Stop treating intent as noise. A save is a slow yes. I would send that email the moment the price moved, and never twice in a week.

A two hour delivery window is a promise. A same day delivery is a bet the shop makes with the customer's evening.

I paid for same day once. The courier arrived at 21:40, after I had given up and gone out. The parcel sat behind a bin. Nobody was lying. The shop just promised something it did not control.

Two hour windows are boring and they work. People plan around them. The courier has slack. It looks reliable instead of fast. Fast is a feature you can only sell once. Reliable is a feature you sell every week.

We stopped advertising speed and started advertising the window. Orders did not fall. Refund requests did, by more than half, and the support inbox got quiet enough that one person could handle it.

There is a version of speed that is just optimism with a tracking number attached. I have run that version. It does not end well.

Click and collect works best when the shop admits it is a warehouse with a door.

The launch was a mess. Customers ordered, then queued at the till behind people buying milk, while a teenager went to look for the parcel. Ten minutes, sometimes twenty.

Then we moved the collection point to a shelf by the entrance with a screen and one person. Average handover, 40 seconds. Complaints stopped.

The deeper fix was stock accuracy. Half the delays were items the system said were in stock and weren't. We started counting the click and collect lines every morning before opening. Fifteen minutes of work, and the failed collections went from 12 percent to 2.

Nobody praises a collection that works. They only notice when it doesn't. If the shelf and the system disagree, the customer finds out at the worst moment. Count first, promise second. I still check that shelf at 8am.

Coupons should not stack, and every shop learns this the expensive way. We ran a 20 percent off code and a free shipping offer in the same week. Somebody combined them and bought a 60 pound order for 41. Then they told the internet.

The fix was not a rule. The rule was already there in small print. The fix was making the checkout say no before the customer felt cheated.

So we built a single field. One code, clearly stated. If a second one arrives, the page explains why it didn't apply. Apologies, but the price is the price.

Discounts are not the problem. Silent discounts are. The customer who finds a loophole is not a villain. They are doing what you would do.

I would rather run fewer promotions and make each one legible. Ten percent, one week, clearly dated. It converts about as well and it doesn't produce a thread on a deals forum. I now write one code a quarter.

Refunding to store credit is a trick, and customers know it's a trick.

We did it because the payments processor kept the fee either way. Two pounds on a 40 pound order, gone, whether the item came back or not. Store credit kept the money in the shop.

The cost was trust. People asked for a refund and got a voucher, and their face changed. One man said, so I have to spend it here. He did. He never came back.

We switched to cash refunds and the return rate went up slightly. The repeat purchase rate went up more. It turns out people come back to a shop that gives money back without a fight.

The maths is close and the feeling isn't. A refund is the last thing a customer remembers about you. Give the money back. Keep the customer. Not the other way round. I would do it again.

Fitting room lighting is the most expensive lie in fashion retail.

I tried on a jacket in a shop with warm light and a mirror at a slight angle. I looked excellent. I bought it. I got home and the bathroom mirror said something else entirely.

The shop didn't lie on purpose. It just used the light that made the room feel nice. But the result is a return, a refund and a customer who now trusts the shop less.

We changed ours to something closer to daylight and put a plain mirror in, straight on. Returns fell 9 percent. Sales in the room fell too, for about a month, and then recovered.

The honest room sells fewer jackets and keeps more of them. Most chains won't do this. The dishonest room converts better this quarter and costs more next quarter. Someone is measuring the wrong window. I have never gone back to the warm bulb.

The impulse shelf at the till is a tax on boredom, and it is shrinking.

I used to buy a chocolate bar at the till maybe three times a month. Now I stand in a queue looking at my phone. It lost the sale and gained nothing.

Self checkout took the shelf away. Phone queues took the attention away. The two things that made the rack work are both gone, and shops are still printing planograms for it.

What still works is the thing you cannot get anywhere else. A local shop near me sells a 90p bag of sweets made two streets away. Nobody buys those on impulse. They buy them on purpose, every week, and they queue for them.

The difference isn't the position. It is that one is available everywhere and one is not. If the till item can be bought in any petrol station, it doesn't belong at the till. Put something only you have. I stopped buying chocolate at the till two years ago.

Restocking overnight looks efficient and quietly breaks the shop.

We moved to night shifts to keep the floor clear during trading. Costs went up 18 percent in wages and down 6 in lost sales, which looked like a win until we looked at the shelves.

The night crew didn't know the shop. They put things where the plan said, not where they belong. Customers couldn't find the milk. The morning staff spent an hour fixing it and the fix cost more than the saving.

Then we tried a hybrid. Two people at 6am, one hour, before the doors. Same result as the night shift, a quarter of the cost. The trick was that the people doing it also served customers. They knew the aisle.

Knowledge is the expensive part of stocking. Not hours. I would pay a daytime wage for a 6am shift forever. Cheaper than a planogram nobody follows.

One supplier isn't a supply chain. It is a single point of failure with a payment schedule.

I learned this in a week. Our only supplier of a plastic clip went down for 11 days after a fire in a neighbouring unit. We had 300 units left and 900 orders. We shipped late to everyone and lost two customers who had been with us for years.

The clip cost 4p. The outage cost about 9,000 pounds.

We now dual source everything above a certain volume. Second supplier is more expensive, 6p instead of 4p, and we buy 30 percent from them every quarter just to keep the line warm. That costs us a few hundred a year. Cheap insurance.

The part nobody tells you is that dual sourcing is a relationship, not a purchase order. If you only call them in a crisis, you aren't a customer, you are a favour. Two suppliers. One phone call. Do the boring work before the fire.

Lead time is a range, not a number, and quoting the middle is how you end up apologising.

Our supplier said 21 days. What they meant was 14 to 48. We planned for 21, which is the worst possible choice, because it's the number you hit least often.

So we started tracking every delivery for six months. Not the average. The shape. We found that 80 percent arrived inside 30 days and the rest were chaos. We planned to 30 and told customers 35.

Late deliveries to customers went from 18 percent to 4 percent. Stock holding went up 9 percent. That is a trade I would make every time.

The number you want isn't the mean. It is the point where you can still keep a promise. Anyone who quotes one number for a lead time has not measured it. They have read it off a form. I check it every quarter.

Container rates are a betting market and most importers find out after they have paid. I shipped 40 foot containers for three years. The rate moved from 1,800 dollars to 11,000 and back to 2,400. Nobody on our side predicted any of it.

What we could control was the contract. Fixed rate for six months, with a volume commitment we could hit. We paid slightly over spot in the good months and slept through the bad ones.

Small importers get squeezed because they buy spot, and spot is where the panic lives.

The other lever is what you put in the box. We cut packaging volume by a fifth and fit 12 percent more units per container. That's a permanent discount on every shipment and it came from a design meeting, not a rate negotiation.

Freight is weather. The box is yours. I have the invoices in a folder.

Safety stock isn't a cushion. It is a bet you are making with money you have not got.

I used to hold a month of everything. It felt safe. It also meant 40,000 pounds sitting in a warehouse, plus rent, plus insurance, plus the slow death of anything that went out of fashion.

So we split the range. Twenty percent of products made up 80 percent of sales. Those got six weeks of cover. The rest got two. Total stock value fell 31 percent and availability barely moved.

My rule now is boring. Cover the things that hurt when they run out, and let the rest be slightly thin.

I find the hard part is admitting which is which. Everyone thinks their product is the important one. The sales data doesn't care what you think. Count first. Then buy. I still argue with the sales team about this every quarter.

My forecast was wrong every month and I kept using it, which is a strange thing to admit.

The spreadsheet said we would sell 1,200 units in March. We sold 680. In April it said 900 and we sold 1,340. It wasn't a forecast. It was a wish with formatting.

What worked was not a better model. It was asking three customers what they were planning. Two of them told me about a contract that would double their order, and one told me they were moving to a competitor.

That isn't scalable. It is also why I stopped trusting a number that had never met a customer.

Now I use the forecast for the shape of the year and the phone for the next 60 days. The spreadsheet handles the slow parts. People handle the sharp bits. Any model that has never been corrected by a conversation is decoration. I call three customers before I trust the sheet.

The minimum order quantity is where a good product goes to die in a warehouse. We wanted one new size. The factory said 5,000 units or nothing. We ordered 5,000 because the unit price looked great. We sold 1,100 in a year.

The rest sat there. Storage, insurance, and eventually a clearance sale at below cost. That unit price saved us 40p a piece and the dead stock cost us several thousand.

Now we ask a different question. What is the smallest order that lets me test the thing? Sometimes that means paying 30 percent more per unit and it is still the cheaper decision.

Factories aren't being difficult. Small runs genuinely cost them more to set up. But there is almost always a middle path, a shared mould, a colour they already run.

Cheap per unit isn't cheap per decision. Count the ones you cannot sell.

Air freight isn't expensive. It is expensive per kilo and priceless per week.

We had a launch date and a shipment stuck at sea with 30 days left. The air option cost 4,200 pounds for 300 kilos. The delay would have cost a launch, a press window and about 12,000 in preorders.

We flew it. The launch happened. The maths was easy once I wrote the two numbers down. But I have also seen people fly things that didn't matter, because the panic was about a date somebody invented in a meeting.

My test now. What actually happens if this arrives in six weeks? If the answer is nothing, it sails. If the answer is a broken promise to a customer, it flies.

Freight decisions are not about cost. They are about the cost of the date. Write the date down. Then decide. I still flinch when I see a spot rate. I plan the box, not the rate.

Two factories running the same mould don't make the same part, and this cost me a customer.

We moved 40 percent of a run to a second factory to reduce risk. The drawings were identical. The mould was the same. The parts looked the same in a photo.

They were 0.4 millimetres different. Enough that the assembly jammed on one line in three. The second factory had a different cooling time. Nobody lied. Nobody checked either. We had specified the drawing, not the process.

Now the spec sheet includes the process. Cycle time, temperature, the tool number. And the first 200 units from any new source go through the same gauge as the old ones, with a person holding both.

Dual sourcing without a shared measurement is just two ways to be wrong. Trust the gauge, not the signature. I keep both parts on the same gauge now. I check them at the door.

The component nobody can get is usually the one worth 20p and made by one company in one country. We built a product with 14 parts. Thirteen were easy. One was a connector made by a single supplier, and when they stopped making it, the whole thing stopped.

Redesign took four months. The part was 22p. The delay cost more than every other component combined.

Since then I ask suppliers a rude question. Who else makes this? If the answer is nobody, I treat it as a risk, not a bargain. Cheap and unique is a trap.

Another move is to design out the rare part before you need to. Two standard parts instead of one special one. Slightly worse, much more available.

Most supply chain plans spend their time on the expensive items. The expensive items have three suppliers competing. It's the 20p part with one factory that ends your year. Look at the small parts first. I look at the small parts first. I ask who else makes it.

A warehouse is a walking problem, and the pick path is the only thing that matters. We moved into a bigger unit and productivity fell 14 percent. Same staff, same orders, more space. The extra space meant longer walks and the walks were the job.

So we ranked products by how often they were picked and put the top 20 percent near the packing bench. No software, just a spreadsheet and a Saturday.

Pick time per order dropped from 3 minutes 40 to 2 minutes 10. That's a third of the labour for the same volume.

The mistake before that was organising by category. All the cables together, all the boxes together. Tidy and slow. Customers don't order categories. They order a cable and a box.

Rank by frequency, not by logic. The warehouse should look strange to a visitor and obvious to a picker. I would redraw that layout every year now.

Pallet height is a fixed number until somebody stacks it wrong, and then it's an insurance claim.

We had a delivery arrive at 2.4 metres. The trailer clears 2.6. It fitted, badly, and shifted in transit. Two hundred units arrived crushed on one corner.

The supplier had stacked an extra layer because it saved them a pallet. That saved them maybe 12 pounds and cost us 2,300 in damaged stock and a delay.

Now the purchase order states the maximum height in centimetres, in bold, and the delivery note is checked against it before the driver leaves. Two refusals in a year and the supplier stopped doing it.

The lesson isn't about pallets. It is that a spec nobody checks is a suggestion. Put the number where the person loading the truck can see it. Then check it at the door. I now refuse a pallet at the door.

A barcode scanner error is a data entry mistake that happens 400 times a day and nobody notices until stocktake.

We had two products with codes one digit apart. One was a 6 pound item, one was 60. Every so often a picker scanned the wrong one and the customer got a bargain or a complaint.

Our system was fine. The labels were the problem. They were printed at the same size, same font, with the difference in the middle of the number where the eye skips.

We reprinted with the last four digits in a bigger font and a colour block. Errors went to almost zero in a month. The technology gets blamed for this. The technology was reading exactly what was in front of it.

Design the label for the human who is holding it at 6am with 200 more to scan. A bigger digit costs nothing. Check the label before you blame the scanner. I put the block on the last four digits.

Annual stocktake is a ritual where a company closes for a day to find out it has been wrong for 12 months. We used to shut on a Sunday in January. Twelve people, 14 hours, a takeaway, and a number that was usually 4 percent off.

So we stopped. Now two people count 40 lines every Friday morning before the shift. It takes 50 minutes. Errors are found in days, not months.

The annual count still happens in accounting, because the auditor wants a date. But by then the number is already right.

The reason people resist this is that the weekly count makes you look at the mistakes. The annual count hides them in an average.

Small, frequent and boring beats big and dramatic. That's true of most operational things. Count a little. Often. Before it becomes a problem. I would not go back to the annual count. I like it that way.

Returns to a supplier are a negotiation, and most shops accept the first no.

We had 300 faulty units. The supplier offered a credit note on the next order. That isn't a refund, that is a discount on buying more from the company that sent you rubbish.

We asked for a replacement run instead. They said no. We asked for the tooling to be moved to a second factory. Suddenly a replacement became possible. Our advantage was not anger. It was knowing the tool belonged to us and saying so politely.

Two things to get right before this happens. Own your tooling, in writing. And photograph the defect against the spec on the day it arrives, not six weeks later.

Returns are a paper exercise until they are not. Keep the paper. The supplier isn't your enemy. They are also not going to volunteer money. I would ask for the tooling first.

Most transit damage is a packing decision made by someone who has never watched a parcel get thrown.

I stood in a sorting depot for two hours. Boxes fall about a metre, land on corners, and get stacked under heavier boxes. Nobody is gentle. Nobody has time.

Our damage rate was 3 percent and we blamed the courier. Then we dropped a test parcel from 1.2 metres, corner first, 20 times. It failed on the fourth drop.

So we changed the inner packing. A cardboard cradle instead of bubble wrap, corners braced, product floating 10 millimetres from the wall. Damage fell to 0.6 percent.

The new packing cost 18p more per unit. The old damage cost about 2.40 per order once you included the replacement and the support time. Test the parcel like a depot will treat it. Then pack for that. Nobody throws a box on purpose. It happens anyway. I stand in the depot every year to remind myself. I would drop it again tomorrow.

Customs paperwork is boring until it's the reason your stock sits in a shed for nine days.

We shipped a pallet to the EU with the commodity code copied from an old invoice. Our code was wrong. The pallet went into a holding area and stayed there while two brokers exchanged forms.

Nine days. Storage charges, a redelivery fee and a customer who had already sold the stock on.

The fix isn't complicated. One page per product, the code, the description, the country of origin, checked by a person once. Then reused forever. We keep it as a spreadsheet and it is the most valuable file in the company.

The second fix is having a broker you can phone. Cheaper than the one on the website. This is the least interesting paragraph in the business and the one that costs the most when it is wrong. Write it down once. Check it yearly. I keep that file on the shared drive.

Port dwell time is the number nobody quotes and it's usually longer than the crossing. Our container took 28 days at sea and 11 days to get from the quay to the warehouse. Everyone talked about the 28.

We started tracking both. The port leg was the variable one. Same route, same line, and the dwell swung from 4 days to 19 depending on the week.

Knowing that changed what we told customers. We stopped quoting the sailing and started quoting the door. Arrival estimates got accurate within three days instead of three weeks.

The second thing we did was book the haulage before the ship left, not after it docked. Trucks get scarce when a big vessel arrives, and the queue is real.

Look at the whole route, not the pretty part. The sea is the part that mostly behaves. Count the boring days too. I book the haulage before the ship sails.

A supplier audit is a tour of the parts of the factory they want you to see, and that is still worth doing. I have been on six. Every one started in a clean room with a display board and ended in a corridor where the real work happened, if I asked to see it.

The useful questions were never on the checklist. Ask what happens when a machine breaks, and who signs off a change. Ask to see the reject bin.

The reject bin tells you everything. If it's empty, they are hiding it or not checking. If it is full of something that should not have got that far, they are honest.

We found a supplier reworking parts by hand with a file. Not malicious, just fixing a tool that was wearing out. We paid for a new tool and the defects stopped.

Audits aren't about trust. They are about getting the tool maintained before it ruins a run. Ask to see the bin.

Batch traceability sounds like a compliance word until a customer gets ill or a part fails and you need to know which 40 boxes are affected.

We had a bad resin batch. Twelve units failed in the field. We knew the date they shipped and nothing else. So we recalled 800 to be safe, which cost about six times what a targeted recall would have.

Now every box carries a batch code and every batch has a record of the resin lot, the machine, the shift and the operator. It's a laminated sheet and a marker pen. That is all it ever needed to be.

The next failure affected 30 boxes. We knew the lot in 20 minutes and called 14 customers.

You don't need software for this. You need a code on the box and the discipline to write it down. Do it before the bad day. It is useless after.

Every demand spike looks like a trend for about three weeks, and that is long enough to order too much. We saw sales double in November. We ordered for a doubled year. It was a competitor's stockout lasting 19 days.

By February we had a warehouse full of the wrong amount of the right thing, and we spent spring discounting it.

The tell was in the shape. Real growth is broad. It moved a few products, in one region, for a short window. A trend would have been wider and slower.

The rule we use now is to wait one more week than feels comfortable. By then the competitor is usually back and the picture is honest.

I know how that sounds when the orders are coming in. It feels like turning away money. It is really just not buying stock you will have to pay to store. Spikes are events. Trends have legs. Watch which one you have.

I sold milk at 34p a litre and the shop sold it at 95p.

I know where the gap goes now. Processing, haulage, chilling and the shop's rent take the rest of it. Nobody in that chain is getting rich. The farmer gets 36 percent of the shelf price. It was 50 percent in 1995. We keep accepting it.

I asked a buyer why. He said it's what the market pays. The market is four companies. That is not a market.

So I stopped selling to them. Now I sell 60 litres a week at the gate for 1.20 a litre. It's more work and less money. I sleep better. A litre costs me 29p to make, and I did the maths on a napkin. I now print the price I was paid on the crate. Customers ask about it more than they ask about the weather. It has not changed the price they pay.

A third of the food we grow never leaves the farm, and most of it's fine to eat. I watched a field of courgettes get ploughed back in because the order fell through. Two weeks of work, gone. The reason was a supermarket changing its forecast.

The food was good. It was the wrong shape for the packing line and the wrong week for the buyer. So it went into the soil.

I started calling local kitchens the day before a harvest, not after. A restaurant will take 40 kilos of odd courgettes for soup and be glad of it. It costs me a phone call and a crate.

Food waste at the farm is mostly a scheduling problem. Not a moral one. Fix the schedule and the waste drops.

We lost 11 percent that year instead of 33. I keep a list of kitchens who will take a crate at short notice. It has nine names on it now.

Finding people to pick fruit is the hardest part of growing it, and nobody wants to say so. I need 14 pickers for six weeks. I can find nine. The rest of the work lands on the people who stayed, and they get tired, and then they leave too.

The pay is 12 pounds an hour. The work is bending in a field in the rain. It is not a mystery why the adverts do not fill.

We built cabins for 20 people. That helped more than the wage did. Then the season moved by three weeks and half the crew had other plans.

I don't have a clever answer. I have a smaller orchard and better planning than I had five years ago. Fewer trees, picked on time, beats more trees picked late.

That is a retreat dressed as a strategy. I know. I pay the return fare for anyone who stays the season. Two people did.

Soil tests cost 40 pounds and save you thousands, and most small growers never do one.

I spread lime for six years because my father did. Then I paid for a test. The field was already at the right pH and I had been wasting 900 pounds a year.

That is the whole story. Six years of habit, one afternoon of measurement. Now I test three fields every autumn. The results go in a notebook. I read the notebook in February before I order anything.

The test also showed one field was short on potash. We had been blaming the weather for a thin crop. It was not the weather.

I would rather be told I'm wrong by a lab than by a harvest. The lab is cheaper and it doesn't take a season to answer. Measure first. Buy second. My notebook now has six years of results in it. I read it before I order anything.

Watering at the wrong hour wastes half of what you pump, and the fix is a clock. We irrigated at midday for years because that is when the pump was switched on. Most of it evaporated before it reached a root.

Moving to 5am cut our water use by 40 percent. Same crop, same field, same pump. The only change was when we started.

I also put a moisture probe in two spots and stopped guessing. That is 300 pounds for the probes and it paid for itself in one dry month.

The hard part isn't the equipment. It's trusting a number over your hand. My hand said the soil was damp. The probe said 12 percent at 20 centimetres, and the crop agreed with the probe.

Now I check the probe before I check the sky. I also fixed a leak in the main line that had been running for a year. That alone was 8 percent of the bill.

Cold chain failures are quiet. The food looks fine and the customer finds out two days later. We had a chiller drift to 9 degrees overnight. Nobody saw it because the dial was behind a stack of boxes. Twelve trays went out. Nine came back.

Now there's a thermometer on the door with a minimum and maximum memory. I read it at 6am and write the number on a board.

The board sounds childish. It works because a person has to look at it. An alarm on a phone gets dismissed in a pocket.

We also stopped overfilling the chiller. Air has to move. A full chiller is a warm chiller. I lost one customer over that week. That's the cost of a dial nobody could see.

Put the number where a human walks past it. I write the temperature on a whiteboard by the door. Anyone can see it, including the driver.

Supermarket specifications reject food that's perfectly good, and the reason is a photograph. I sent a crate of apples that were the right size, the right colour, and slightly flat on one side. Rejected. The spec said uniform.

The spec exists because a shopper standing in an aisle wants the box to look like the picture. That is a real pressure and I understand it.

But the cost of that picture lands on me, not the shopper. I grew 40 tonnes and sold 26. So I started selling the flat ones as a box for 8 pounds. They went in a week. Same taste, worse photo.

There is a market for bent food. It's just not the same market that pays for the photograph.

I sell both now. One pays the rent, the other pays the mortgage. I sent photos with the next crate and asked for a reason in writing. It arrived three weeks later.

Fertiliser went from 280 pounds a tonne to 900 in a year and nobody had a plan for it. I had budgeted for a normal spring. The invoice arrived and I sat in the truck for a while.

What saved us was doing less. We cut the rate by 20 percent on three fields and watched. The yield fell 4 percent. The saving was 11,000 pounds.

I had been farming by habit, not by measurement. More input felt like more safety. It was just more cost.

The second thing we did was plant clover on the worst field and leave it for a year. No crop, no fertiliser, and the following wheat did better than the field beside it. That's a slow fix and a slow fix is still a fix.

I now price every input as a share of the crop it feeds. If the share is over 30 percent, I ask why. I now split the application into two passes. I only buy the second one after I look at the crop.

Rotating crops is free and most farms stopped doing it because the market rewards one thing. I grew wheat, wheat, wheat for four years. The yield dropped each year and the disease pressure climbed. Then I sprayed more and the margin went thinner.

Now it goes wheat, beans, barley, grass. The bean year fixes nitrogen and I buy less fertiliser. The grass year breaks the disease cycle.

My wheat yield is 8 percent lower than my best ever year. My profit is higher. That took me a while to accept.

The trap is comparing yields instead of comparing cheques. A neighbour with 11 tonnes a hectare and a 40,000 pound fertiliser bill isn't beating me.

I still get asked what my yield is. I answer with the margin and watch the conversation die. Rotation is boring and boring pays. I keep a map of what grew where for four years. It hangs in the barn and I look at it in January.

Grain stored at 15 percent moisture will rot in the silo and you will find out in February.

We filled a silo in August with grain at 16 percent because the dryer was busy. By January the top layer was crusted and the smell told the rest of the story.

Six tonnes lost. That's 1,400 pounds and a morning with a shovel. Now there's a moisture meter by the auger and a rule. Nothing goes in above 14.5. If the dryer is busy, the trailer waits.

The cost of waiting is a few hours. The cost of not waiting is a winter of hope. I also check the silo every fortnight with a probe. It takes 10 minutes and it has caught two warm spots since.

Storage is where good grain goes bad quietly. Look inside the bin, not at the invoice. I check the probe every fortnight now. It caught a warm spot in August.

Antibiotics in livestock are a tool, not a habit, and the habit is what gets a farm into trouble. We used to treat a whole shed when one animal coughed. It was fast and it felt safe. It also meant we were dosing 200 animals for a problem in four.

Now we separate and treat the sick ones. It takes longer and it costs more per case. The total spend went down 30 percent because the cases went down.

Ventilation was the real fix. Two fans and a better inlet, about 900 pounds, and the coughs mostly stopped. I am not against antibiotics. I am against using them because you haven't fixed the air.

Records matter too. Every treatment goes in a book with the date and the animal. That book has answered two inspections and one vet bill argument.

Fix the shed, then treat the animal. The book has answered two inspections. That's the whole return on it.

Selling direct is more work per box and worth it, but only if you count your own hours. I started a veg box scheme with 40 customers. It looked like a great margin until I added up the packing and the driving.

Three hours a week packing, two hours driving, and 12 pounds of fuel. My 8 pound margin per box turned into 3.

So we changed it. One pickup point in the village, one afternoon, customers collect. Packing time stayed, driving went. Margin back to 7 pounds.

The customers liked it less at first. Then they started talking to each other at the pickup, and two of them now share a box. Direct sales work when you stop pretending delivery is free. Someone pays for the drive. Either the price or the person.

I would rather charge for it than absorb it. I would do it again with a smaller radius. The driving was the part I underestimated.

A restaurant menu is a supply contract written in a nicer font, and chefs forget that.

I supply three kitchens. One sends me a list every Monday and sticks to it. Two ring on Friday because they sold out and need something by Saturday morning.

The Friday calls are where I lose money. I have to harvest early, pick what is ready rather than what is best, and drive it myself. So I put a rule in the contract. Orders by Monday 6pm. After that, it's whatever is in the crate.

A bakery throws away more than a farm does, and the reason is a display case that has to look full. I worked a till in a bakery for a summer. At 6pm the case had to be full. At 7pm it all went in a bin bag.

That rule came from head office. An empty case looks like a bad bakery. A full case sells more at 4pm. So we baked to fill the case, not to sell the bread. About 15 percent of the day's loaves went out the back door.

The fix we tried was a 50p box after 6pm. It sold out and the bin got lighter. Then head office stopped it because it was undercutting the morning price.

The local abattoir closed and the cost of that is 40 miles and a worse journey for the animals.

Ours shut in 2019. Now the nearest is 38 miles away. That is a two hour round trip on a good day, and animals don't have good days in trailers.

We book in a month ahead. If one animal is ready before the slot, it waits. If the lorry breaks, the whole week moves. Small abattoirs close because they cannot afford the inspection regime. That is a real cost and I am not pretending otherwise.

But the closure moved a cost onto every farm in the county and nobody added it up in the decision. I now pay 22 pounds more per animal and lose half a day. My customers pay a little more and mostly don't notice.

Infrastructure sounds like roads and broadband. It is also a building where a van can back up. I book in a month ahead and I hate it. It is the only way it works.

Seed costs have doubled and the varieties that justify it are not always the ones you get. I paid 78 pounds a bag for wheat seed this year. It was 39 five years ago. The yield gain over my own saved seed was 3 percent.

Three percent doesn't pay for the bag. So I saved seed from the best field and used it on 12 hectares as a trial. It came within 1 percent of the bought seed.

There are rules about farm saved seed and payments to the breeder. I follow them and I still come out ahead.

The honest version is that I was buying certainty and calling it yield. The bag is easier than the decision. Now I trial on a strip before I commit a field. It costs me a morning and a notebook page.

A variety that works is worth the money. A variety that is advertised isn't the same thing. I keep the trial strip in the same place each year. Two rows, no spray, a notebook. I mark the rows with sticks.

Weather insurance paid out once in nine years, and that once saved the farm. The premium is 2,400 pounds a year. Nine years is 21,600. The drought year cost me 40,000 in lost crop and bought hay.

I did the maths and it looks like a bad deal until you remember why insurance exists. It isn't an investment. It's a floor.

The claim was paid in 19 days. I had expected a fight. The assessor walked two fields, took photos, and asked for my receipts.

What I got wrong was the cover. I had insured the crop, not the cost of buying feed for the animals that ate it. That gap cost me 6,000.

Read the schedule, not the brochure. Then ask what happens in the second bad year, because that is the one that breaks you. I read the schedule with a pen now. I write questions in the margin and ring the broker.

Weeds that survive one spray come back with relatives, and the bill for that arrives in year three.

We used the same herbicide for eight years. It worked, until it didn't. Then a patch of blackgrass took a field and we spent two seasons getting it back. The cause was simple. We killed what died and bred what survived.

Now we mix modes. Different chemistry, later drilling, a spring crop in the rotation, and a bit of hand roguing on the worst strip. No single tool carries the job.

The hand work is 30 hours across the farm. It looks absurd next to a 40,000 pound sprayer. It is also the cheapest thing we do. Resistance is not a chemical problem. It is a repetition problem.

Change the plan before the field tells you to. I walk the worst field every Friday in June. It takes 20 minutes and it tells me the plan.

Compost is the only input I make myself, and it started as a way to avoid paying for disposal. We were paying 600 pounds a year to have manure and bedding taken away. Now we heap it, turn it, and spread it.

The heap needs air and time. Two turns in the first month, then leave it for six. If it smells, it needs turning. That is the whole method.

Three years in, the organic matter on the top field went from 2.1 to 3.4 percent. That holds water in a dry July.

It isn't free. It is about 40 hours of tractor time a year. But I stopped buying 6 tonnes of bagged compost and the soil works better in a dry spell.

The input I value most is the one I can make from what I already have. I turn it with the loader and a fork. I wouldn't go back to buying bags.

At a farmers market you are competing with a supermarket and losing on price, so stop competing on price.

I stood behind a table for three years. The first year I priced to match the shop and sold almost nothing. Why would anyone drive to a car park to pay the same?

The second year I put up a sign with the name of the field and the day it was picked. Sales doubled. Same produce, same price.

People weren't buying carrots. They were buying a Tuesday morning and a person who knew which field it came from. The third thing that worked was samples. A slice of apple costs 8p and sells a bag. Nobody walks past a free slice.

I still lose the price shoppers. That is fine. They were never my customer and I spent two years pretending otherwise. Sell the thing the shop can't copy. I still do the samples. They cost me 4 pounds a market and they work.

A freezer failure at 2am cost me 3,000 pounds and the alarm was working the whole time.

It rang a phone that was on silent. It rang for six hours. A compressor had failed and the temperature climbed to 14 degrees. We found out at 7am when someone opened the door and the smell hit.

Now the alarm goes to two phones and a siren outside the shed. If it rings and nobody answers in 10 minutes, the siren runs. The neighbours will hear it and one of them has my number.

The second fix cost 90 pounds. A temperature logger that emails a graph every morning. I see a slow drift before it becomes a loss.

Insurance paid for half. The rest was stock I couldn't replace in a week. An alarm you can't hear is a decoration. I check the logger graph with my first coffee. It has caught two drifts since.

Chasing yield is how a farm goes broke with a full barn. I grew 9.2 tonnes a hectare one year and made less money than the year I grew 7.8. The 9.2 year needed more fertiliser, more spray and a dryer running for three weeks.

The barn was full and the bank account was thin. That is a strange feeling and it taught me more than any course.

Two fields failed that test last year. One is now a wildflower strip and the other grows beans. Both make more than wheat did.

I still like a good yield. I just stopped confusing it with a good business. Full barn, empty account. Do the sums. I keep the field budgets in one folder. It's the only file I open every month.

Selling food means you are in the food safety business, and most small producers learn that from a form.

I got a visit from an inspector in my second year. She was polite and she found four things. No thermometer, no cleaning record, an unlabelled sack of feed, and a hand wash basin that drained into a drain.

Foraging is trendy and the rules are older than the trend, and people get this wrong. I pick wild garlic in two woods. I take leaves from the middle of a patch, never the flowers, and never more than a third.

The law where I am says you can take leaves, fruit and fungi from common ground, but not roots, and not from protected sites. That is a real line and it isn't obvious.

I have seen people fill a bag from one clump and post it. That patch was bare the next spring.

Selling foraged food adds another layer. You need a food business registration and you need to know what you are selling. Two people a year end up in hospital from the wrong mushroom.

I sell it as a small add on, always labelled, and I never sell anything I can't identify with certainty. Take a third. Leave the flowers. I take a third and no more. I have done that for six years.

Delivery radius is the number that decides whether a food business makes money, and most pick it by feeling. I delivered within 15 miles and thought that was local and sensible. Then I worked out the cost per drop.

A 12 mile round trip at 45p a mile is 5.40. My average order was 22 pounds with a 6 pound margin. The delivery ate almost all of it.

So I cut the radius to 6 miles and set a minimum order of 25 pounds. Orders fell 18 percent. Profit went up.

The customers outside the radius ordered a single item. They also complained about timing. I now do one run, twice a week, in a loop that never doubles back. That's 40 minutes for nine drops.

Pick the radius from the margin, not the map. I drew the loop on a map before I set the price. That's where the 25 pound minimum came from.

A menu priced by gut feel loses money on the dishes that sell best, and that's the opposite of what you want. I ran a small kitchen for two years. The burger sold 60 a week and the fish sold 12. I priced the burger low because everyone ordered it.

Then I costed every plate. The burger made 3.10 after food and the fish made 6.40. The dish I was proud of was the one paying for the rent.

We raised the burger by 1.50 and put a cheaper cut in the fish dish. Sales of the burger fell to 48 and profit went up.

I now cost a new dish before it goes on the board. Twenty minutes with a calculator. Gut feel is a starting point, not a price. I cost every dish before it goes on the board. It works. It takes 20 minutes and it has changed two prices.

I deleted four hundred lines of my own code this week. The app got faster. Build time went nine seconds down to four.

The lines were mine. I wrote them before I trusted the agent to touch that file. Duplicated helpers, a retry loop nothing called, two config paths that both ran. I wrote those at 2am and never looked again because they worked.

It found them in one pass. It didn't do anything clever. It read every file and listed the dead ones. Ten minutes later the diff was mostly deletions.

That's the part of AI coding that never shows up in a demo. The wins are boring. No applause for a smaller file. But the file is smaller, and the next change is easier because there's less to trip over. I'll take that trade every week.

Smaller is a feature. I used to measure a good day by how much I added. Now I measure it by how much I could remove and still ship.

The tool didn't get better. My prompts got smaller. I noticed that after two months on the same model, so I went back through the history and counted.

Average prompt in January was around ninety words. By March it was twenty. Output quality went up both times, which makes no sense if the model never changed.

Then I read the short ones. They all had the same shape. One file, one function, one expected result, and a way to check it. The long ones explained the whole project and hoped the model would infer the task.

Narrow beats clever. I've stopped writing context and started writing constraints. Give it the interface, the failing test, and the one thing that must not change. Then let it work.

That's a smaller job for me too. I spend less time explaining and more time checking. Which is the right split, since checking is the part I'm actually good at.

I shipped a bug that I asked the agent to prevent. It wrote the guard, I read the guard, and I still merged the version without it. That one is on me.

The guard checked whether a token had expired. It ran before every request. What it didn't do was handle the case where the refresh call returned a token with the same expiry. Two requests in the same second, both refreshed, both got the old value back. That's the bug.

I found it in the logs at 1am. Nine hundred failed requests in four minutes, all from one device. The fix was six lines. The review was eleven seconds long.

So I changed how I review generated code. I read the failure path first now, then the happy path. Error handling is where the model still guesses, because error handling is where the test data is thin.

That's the habit I'd give anyone using these tools. Read what happens when it breaks, not what happens when it works.

Three agents on one repo beat one agent on three repos. I didn't expect that. The first setup felt safer because nothing could collide. The second one shipped more in a day.

The reason is attention. One agent reading a whole project spends most of its context on files it will never touch. Three agents with one file each stay sharp. They also fail in different places, which makes the failures easier to see.

Coordination is the tax. Someone has to own the interfaces, and right now that someone is me. I write the shared types first, then hand out the slices. If I skip that step, two workers solve the same problem two ways and I spend an hour merging.

So the plan is the contract. Not the code. I've started treating the type definitions as the part I write myself, and the implementations as the part I delegate.

That split feels right. I keep the shape and hand over the filling. Six months ago I would have written all of it and complained about the time.

My editor autocompletes a line now and it used to write a paragraph. That's the shift that gets no press. The models got quieter.

Early on I let the assistant generate whole modules. It felt like magic for a week. Then I spent three days reading code I didn't understand, written in a style I wouldn't pick, solving a problem I hadn't described well.

Now the completion is one line. Sometimes four. A function signature, a branch, a loop I was about to type anyway. I keep the plan in my head and let the tool handle the keystrokes.

The diff got smaller and my confidence went up. I can read every line I merge because there are fewer of them. That's a better deal than the magic version, even if it looks less impressive in a demo.

That's where I think this settles. Not a replacement and not a junior developer. A very fast typist that knows the syntax and has no idea what the business needs.

I spent four months on a backend course and shipped nothing I could show anyone. Six hours a week, twenty three videos, one certificate. That's not nothing. It's also not a thing I could point at.

I quit a job with nothing lined up and told everyone it was a plan. It was a plan the way a spare room is a guest room. Both exist, neither is ready.

The first month I woke up early out of habit and had nothing to wake up for. Forty applications went out. Eleven replies. Three interviews, two of them for roles I did not want. That number is the whole story of a cold search.

What worked was one message a day to someone doing the job I wanted. Not a pitch, just a question about a thing they had built. Nine of those turned into a conversation. Two turned into work. It was slower than the applications and it cost less of my dignity.

I don't recommend quitting without a plan. I do recommend knowing the next step before the last one ends. Those are different sentences.

The hardest part of changing fields is not the skills. It's the story you tell about the years you already spent. I watched a friend move from accounting into product and that was the wall she hit.

She had twelve years of numbers. On paper that was a liability for a product role. In the interview it became the reason to hire her. She could read a spreadsheet a product manager would cry over, and she knew which number a finance buyer checks first.

The skills transfer. The framing is what people forget to prepare. Nobody asks what you can do. They ask why you are here.

Her first answer was about wanting a new challenge. That answer is about her. Her second answer was about a customer problem she had lived with for a decade. That answer was about the job. She got the second one by saying it out loud to four people and watching their faces. I asked her what changed and she said the story did. I took the note.

I keep a list of things I do not understand yet. It has forty one items and four of them have been there for two years. That list is the most useful document I own.

Every item started as a sentence I could not finish in a meeting. A column type. A cache invalidation rule. Why one query was faster than another. Every sentence gets written down with the date and revisited on Fridays.

Most items take an hour to close. A few take a month. The two year ones are usually not technical. They are organisational, and the answer is that nobody actually decided. Those stay open because the honest entry is that the system has a person shaped hole in it.

I don't keep this list to feel productive. I keep it because the gap between what I can use and what I understand is where the next bug lives. Forty one lines is a small price.

Saying no to a promotion took three weeks to decide and four minutes to say out loud. The offer was flattering and I knew it. The role was management. Six people, a budget, and no code. I wanted to be wanted more than I wanted the job.

The money was real. About eighteen percent. Running the number against the hours made it stop looking like eighteen percent. Half my week would be meetings about work I no longer did. That was the honest trade.

What made it hard was the story. A senior title is proof that someone saw you. Turning it down felt like arguing with that. The offer had to be separated from the verdict.

I asked for a technical track with a review in six months instead. They said yes in a week. Two years on, I still write code most days and I still like the work. That's the test I use now.

The number that matters is usually three clicks deep in a filing. I built a tool that pulls it out. The hard part was not the pulling.

Anyone can summarise a document with a model now. That part is cheap and fast. What people actually need is the receipt. Which page, which line, which quarter. If the answer can't be traced back, it's a guess with good grammar.

So every sentence our tool produces carries a link to the source row. Revenue for the quarter, click, there it is in the filing. If the figure was restated a year later, both versions show up and the difference is visible. That last part caused an argument on the team. I wanted to hide the second one. I lost that argument, which was the right outcome.

We still get it wrong sometimes. A filing with a weird table breaks the parser and the answer comes out thin. We show the failure instead of hiding it. That's the whole product, really. Show the work, admit the gap. The rest is formatting.

I spent five weeks building a screener and then deleted it. The feature let you filter 4,000 companies by margin, growth and debt. It looked impressive in a demo. Nobody opened it twice.

Investors don't screen first. They arrive with a company already in mind. Something got mentioned at dinner, or a position moved and they want to know why. The question is specific before the tool is opened. A screener answers a question nobody asked yet. So I removed it and put the same data behind a plain search box.

Usage changed within a week. The average session got shorter, not longer. People typed a company name, read four sentences, clicked one source, and left. That's a good session. I'd been measuring the wrong thing, counting features instead of answers.

The deleted code is still in a branch. I keep it as a reminder that a feature can be well built and still be in the way. Two other screens got the same treatment that month. It got smaller three times and each version was easier to explain. Smaller is the feature.

Every finance app ends up telling you what to buy. We wrote the refusal into the spec on day one. No price targets. No scores. No buy or sell label on any screen.

It cost us a growth channel. Recommendations are what people screenshot and send to friends. A tool that answers questions doesn't spread the same way. Investors kept asking for a rating, and saying no got easier after the tenth time.

The reason is boring. A recommendation is a claim about the future and we can't back it. We can show you that revenue grew 12 percent and that the margin came from one customer. What happens next depends on things we don't know. Putting a number on that would be guessing with extra steps.

People stay longer because of it. A tool that never tells you what to do is a tool you can use for years. The ones that rate stocks are entertainment. I'd rather build the boring one that's still open on your second tab.

The same question shows up in support every week. What did the company actually earn? Not the headline number. Not the number after one time charges, stock compensation, and a sale of a building.

I spent an evening on that question myself before we built anything. Three tabs, two PDFs, and a search result from 2021 that was wrong. It was in the filing the whole time. It just needed four adjustments and a willingness to read the notes.

Now the tool does the four adjustments and shows each line. The judgement is still yours. If you think the charge is really recurring, you can keep it in and the number changes in front of you. We don't decide which version is honest. We show both and let you argue with it.

Retail investors get told they can't read a filing. That's mostly a formatting problem. The information is public and the maths is not hard. What's hard is the hour it takes. Shaving that hour off is a decent product.

Fourteen of the last thirty support emails were about one button. Not a crash. Not a wrong answer. People could not find where to connect an account. The button was the same colour as the page.

I'd tested that screen twenty times. I knew where it was. I put it there. That's the gap between builder and user, and it doesn't close with more testing. It closes with watching someone else use the thing.

We moved the button, made it the only dark element on the page, and wrote a sentence under it. Support emails about connecting dropped to two in the following month. Fourteen to two. The fix took twenty minutes including the deploy.

Since then every new screen gets the same treatment. One action, one obvious colour, one line of plain text. No tours, no tooltip that explains the button you can't see. If a screen needs a tutorial, the screen is the problem.

Our newest game demo has 40 lines of NPC dialogue written by a model and 400 written by me. Players noticed the model lines first. Not because they were better. Because they were longer.

The claim on the store page was a living world. The actual build generated a greeting when you walked up to a guard. That is it. The guard still stood in the same spot for 60 hours. He still forgot the quest he gave me yesterday.

Memory is the part nobody demos. A model can produce a good line in 2 seconds. Keeping that line consistent with 3 hours of earlier conversation costs more than the line. We ended up storing facts in a small table and feeding maybe 12 of them back into each prompt. It worked. It was also a database with extra steps.

I like the tech. I don't like the phrase living world. A world is a set of rules that hold. A model is a very fast writer that forgets.

A studio I talked to last month ran 9,000 automated play sessions a week. The AI found 300 crashes and zero design problems. That ratio is the whole story.

The marketing says AI QA. What it does is cluster crash reports and replay a build. Useful. Boring. It catches the null pointer that happens when you open a menu during a cutscene. It does not notice that the second boss is unfun.

We use the same trick on a much smaller scale. Our last build had 14 crash reports from 6 testers. A model grouped them into 3 bugs in about a minute. I had spent an afternoon on that list before.

Where it fails is severity. It called a missing sound file critical and a save corruption minor. Both were wrong. A save bug ends a run. A missing footstep does not.

I still run it every build. I just read the output myself. The tool sorts. It does not judge.
