Concept art is where AI actually saves time on our team. We generated 200 thumbnails for a swamp level in one evening. We used 4. The other 196 were bad in ways that were useful.

What the marketing shots never show is the review. Someone still has to look at 200 images and say no. That took me 3 hours. The drawing used to take 2 days. The saving is real and it is smaller than the pitch.

Final assets are still made by a person. We tried a generated texture atlas once. It looked fine at 1080p and broke at 4K. The seams repeated every 512 pixels and the normal map was nonsense. We went back to a 3 hour hand paint.

I don't think the tools replace the artist. I think they replace the first sketch. That is the cheapest part of the job and the part that blocks everything else.

One thing nobody mentions. Style consistency is the hard problem. Ten good images in ten different styles are worthless.

Player support is the most boring place AI works and the one with the clearest numbers. Our ticket queue dropped from 90 a day to 30 after we put a model in front of it. Those 60 were password resets and refund policy questions.

False positives are the cost. It closed 4 tickets last month that needed a human. One was a chargeback. That one cost more than the bot saved in a week.

Moderation is worse. A model flagged 12 players for chat abuse in our test. Three were quoting the abuse to report it. Nine were real. A 75 percent hit rate sounds fine until you are the guy who got banned for a screenshot.

I use it for triage and never for the final call. It labels. I decide. We tested this for 6 weeks and the appeals queue stayed flat while the response time halved.

The pitch is AI moderation. The build is a sorting hat with a person behind it.

I asked a model to write a Unity interaction system last week. It produced 200 lines in 20 seconds and 6 of the API calls did not exist. That is the normal result, not the bad one.

The actual use is smaller. I use it to write the boring part of a system I already designed. Save load. A settings menu. A state machine with 4 states. It is fast at that and it never gets tired.

Where it breaks is engine version drift. The model knows Unity from a training set that is 18 months old. Our project is on a newer LTS. About 1 in 5 suggestions needs a doc lookup. That lookup is the job.

The pitch is AI builds your game. The build is AI writes the part you already understand and you check the rest. I still read every line. That is not caution. That is the only way I learn what the code does.

Two tools, one rule. The model drafts. I ship.

The melatonin gummies in my kitchen had more than three times the dose printed on the bottle.

I found that in a study that tested twenty five products from American shelves. Twenty two were off label. Some had almost none. One had three hundred and forty seven percent of what it claimed. Bottle said one milligram, the lab found something closer to three and a half.

That's not a scandal about one brand. It's what happens when a product is sold as a supplement instead of a drug. Nobody checks the dose before it reaches the shelf, and nobody has to.

So I stopped guessing with sleep. I cut the tablet into quarters and tracked what actually changed over three weeks. A quarter worked about as well as a whole one for me. The whole one left me foggy until ten in the morning.

That's a result with a sample of one. It's still more useful than the label.

Checking the dose is a thirty second habit now. I read the milligram column, then I read what the study actually tested. When those two disagree, I believe the study.

A smartwatch flagged my heart rhythm twice last year. Both times it was wrong.

The first alert arrived while I was carrying boxes up a staircase. The second came during a bad cold. My doctor looked at the strip and said the same thing both times. Movement and fever look like an arrhythmia to a sensor sitting on a wrist.

I still wear it. The useful part isn't the alert. It's the month of resting heart rate data I can hand to someone who knows what to do with it.

I keep coming back to the Apple Heart Study. Around four hundred thousand people joined. About half a percent got a notification. Of the ones who sent back a patch, roughly a third had atrial fibrillation confirmed. Two thirds were something else.

That's not a reason to bin the watch. It's a reason to treat a notification as a question, not a diagnosis. The study was built to find cases in a crowd. It was never built to tell you what your wrist means on a Tuesday.

Wearables are good at trends. They're bad at verdicts. I wish the alert said that.

Twelve hundred people started that supplement trial. Nine hundred finished it.

I read that line before the result, and the result stopped mattering. The people who stayed were the ones who could tolerate the pills and the schedule. Anyone who got a headache in week two quit. Nobody writes a headline about the ones who quit.

So the average at the end describes survivors. That's a finding about tolerability wearing a costume.

I took a multivitamin for six years. I stopped after one review found no measurable difference in the outcomes it tracked. Six years of a habit built on a shelf, not a study.

Nobody mentions the dropout rate in the ad. It's one number, usually in the first table, and it tells you who the result is actually about. If a third of the group left, the remaining two thirds are not a random sample of anything. They're the people who found it easy.

That's the whole check. One table, thirty seconds, and most of the confident claims fall apart on their own.

I stretched for ten minutes before every run for two years. It did nothing for the thing I was afraid of.

What I was afraid of was a torn hamstring. I got one anyway, at mile eight, on a cold morning after a perfect stretch.

The reviews I read since then keep saying the same thing. Static stretching before exercise doesn't clearly cut injury rates. Some of them found it slightly reduces power output, which is the opposite of what I thought I was buying.

The part that does seem to help is a warm up that moves. Easy jog, then drills, then the run. Five minutes. No holding a position. None of it is complicated. I switched and my first two miles stopped feeling like a negotiation.

I still stretch. I do it after, when I'm already warm, mostly because it feels good and I'm not going to pretend that's science.

That last sentence is the whole point. Some of what I do is evidence and some of it is preference. I try to know which is which, and I fail at that more often than I'd like.

A mouse lived four months longer on a drug and the headline said it reversed ageing in humans.

I've read that story maybe forty times. The mouse part is real. The jump to humans is not in the paper. Nobody in the press release wrote that sentence either, which is worse, because it means nobody checked.

The part I look for now is replication. Did another lab run it again and get the same result. If the answer is no, I file it as a maybe and move on. That takes one search and it kills most of what I used to save. The most common finding in science news is that nobody checked.

I'm not against animal work. I'm against reading a press release as if the sample was people. Mice are a first draft. That's useful. It's not a finding about you.

The same test works on any claim with a study behind it. Find the sample. Find the replication. Find the limitation paragraph, which sits at the end where nobody scrolls. Three things, one minute, and the headline either survives or it doesn't.

Most of them don't. I still read them. I just read them in a different order now.

A candidate asked what our on call week actually looks like. Best question I heard all year.

I have sat on sixty interview panels in four years. Almost every question was about the candidate. Nobody asked what the job does to the person doing it. That gap is why I changed my loop.

I started asking what they wanted to know about the first ninety days. The ones who asked about the last three releases worked out. So did the ones who asked about the salary band first, for different reasons. Both groups were reading the job, not the posting.

Our panel used to have no shared notes. Six people, six lists, and the same conflict question four times. That was an accurate sample of how the team ran. Now we write one scorecard before the loop. Then we read it together after. An interview is a sample of the place. The candidate is taking one too.

I wrote a job description that no working engineer could pass. Then I complained about the applicants.

That description had eleven tools in the requirements. Seven years of experience for a role that paid for four. One framework that shipped eight months ago. It also asked for a degree and a take home exercise that ate a weekend.

Three people applied in six weeks. Two were unqualified by that list. The third was excellent by the work, and my screen rejected him because he had not used the framework. That one still bothers me.

I rewrote it as three outcomes. Cut the deploy time in half. Own the billing bug queue. Mentor two juniors. No tool list. We hired in nineteen days.

A job description is a filter you design. Most teams design it by accident, one committee edit at a time. The person who could do the job reads fourteen reasons to skip it.

My first engineering hire spent four days waiting for a laptop. I called it onboarding.

Access came on day six. The repo came on day eight. He sat in eleven meetings where nobody knew why he was there. Two people had to approve his account and both were on leave.

He quit in month five. I was surprised, which is the embarrassing part. The work was ready. The environment was not. The team shipped the feature he was hired to own, badly, because nobody could answer his questions.

Now access ships before the start date. Laptop, repo, staging credentials, and a named buddy for the first two weeks. That takes one afternoon. Nobody remembers the offer letter. Everyone remembers the first week.

Onboarding starts before the contract is signed. If week one is chaos, the new hire learns what the place actually values. So do the people already there.

The strongest engineer I ever worked with failed our interview loop.

He blanked on the graph question. Ten minutes of silence, then a wrong answer with confidence. We thanked him and moved on.

A month later he applied for a different team. That manager asked about an outage instead of a puzzle. He walked through a bad deploy, a rollback, and the three days after. It was the clearest thinking in that hiring cycle. The panel scored him low and the score was all we looked at the first time.

He got the offer and shipped the fix that unblocked the quarter in week three. Same engineer. Different question.

I hired for confidence twice and both times it cost me a quarter.

One candidate had an answer for everything and code I could not read. The other was quiet in the panel and shipped clean work for two years. The first mistake taught me more. Two hires later, the quiet one is still here.

Every interview I run now starts with one question. What did you ship last quarter that you are not proud of. The rehearsed answer describes a feature. The real answer names a bug, a delay, or a decision they would take back.

It tells me whether the person can look at their own work without flinching. It also tells me whether they bring bad news early. That is the skill a team of six needs. Not leetcode. Not a framework. The willingness to say the release is not ready.

Hire for the bad news. Everything else can be taught.

Most managers I know have a decision queue and no idea how long it is. I kept one for two weeks and stopped counting at sixty. Sixty things waiting on one person.

The queue is invisible until it breaks something. Nobody files a ticket for a decision they are waiting on. They just slow down, ask again next week, and start routing around you.

So I cut the number. Three decisions a week that only I can make. Everything else gets a rule, a default, or a person who owns it. Writing the rule takes an hour and removes a hundred future decisions.

The strange part is the quality went up. I'm less tired when the hard one arrives, so I actually think about it. Fewer decisions, better ones. That trade is the whole job and it took me years to see it.

I handed off the part I was best at and watched it get worse for a month. That month was the price of the handoff and I almost cancelled it twice.

Delegation isn't a transfer of tasks. It's a transfer of judgment, and judgment only moves when the other person gets to be wrong in front of you. So the first attempts are slower than doing it yourself. That's the cost and it's real.

What made it work was writing down what good looked like. Not steps. Three examples of a finished thing and one of a bad one. Then I stopped reviewing the middle and only checked the end.

Six weeks later the work was better than mine on the parts I never liked anyway. I got back a day a week. That day went into the thing I'm actually hard to replace at. I should have done it sooner, and I'd say that about every handoff I've delayed.

A yes is a promise and I was making forty of them a week. I counted. Most were small, which is exactly the problem. Small promises don't feel like commitments until you're behind on all of them.

Saying no is a skill and it's not a personality trait. The version that worked for me is giving the reason once and not apologising three times. People handle the no fine. They just want to know the trade.

So I started keeping a short list of what I'm not doing this quarter. Not goals. The other side of the goals. It sits next to the roadmap and it gets the same review.

The relief was immediate and slightly embarrassing. Half the things I was protecting were things nobody asked me to protect. I made them up years ago and never revisited them. Saying no to those was free.

The meeting that fixed my team had no agenda and no status updates. Twenty five minutes, one question: what is slowing you down. That's it.

I used to run one on ones where I talked for most of it. I'd leave feeling useful and learn nothing. The status was already in writing, so the meeting was just me performing attention.

What changed was asking first and then shutting up. Silence is uncomfortable and it's where the useful sentence comes from. Someone will fill it, and the thing they fill it with is usually the real problem.

I keep notes in one file and read them before the next one. Patterns show up fast. Three people mentioning the same broken tool is not three complaints. It's one decision I've been avoiding. The meeting didn't fix the team. Noticing did.

I stopped measuring people by output and started measuring them by what they escalate. The change was uncomfortable and it fixed the team in a quarter.

Output is easy to see and easy to game. Escalation tells you whether someone knows the boundary of their own judgment. A person who escalates nothing is either brilliant or hiding. Usually hiding.

So I made the boundary explicit. Here's what you decide alone. Here's what you tell me after. Here's what we decide together. Written down, one page, no ambiguity.

The first month was noisy. I got questions about things that were clearly in the first bucket. I answered each with the page, not the answer. By month two the questions changed and they were the right ones. Ownership is a map, not a mood.

The listing said four bedrooms. The county tax record said three.

That took ninety seconds to find, and it's free. Every county posts assessments, sale history, and the room count the assessor used. It isn't always right. It is always worth reading before you fall for a floor plan.

I looked at a place in Flatbush listed at 1.15 million last spring. It showed a 2019 sale at 640,000 and a kitchen remodel in 2022 with an open permit. Two things came out of that. That number had a story, and the story had a hole. Nobody checks the permit.

An open permit is the part that bites. A finished basement without a sign off can become your problem at closing, or your problem at resale. A building department search takes ten minutes and costs nothing. I do it before I look at photos now, because photos are the seller's version.

I'm not saying walk away. I'm saying know what you're buying before the bank tells you what it's worth. The record is boring. Boring is the point.

#RealEstate #Brooklyn #NYC #Housing #PropertyInvestment #Markets #Investing #Finance #Mortgage #DueDiligence #Data #Research #Landlord #Rental #PropertyRecords

The cap rate on a decent Brooklyn building sits near 4 percent. The mortgage costs more than that.

That gap is the first thing to check, and it's arithmetic anyone can do. Take the rent roll. Subtract taxes, insurance, water, and a repair budget. Divide by the asking price. Then compare the result to the rate your lender quotes you.

If the answer is negative, you aren't buying income. You're buying a bet that the price goes up. That's allowed. It just needs to be named.

I ran those numbers on a six unit in Flatbush in June. Asking 2.1 million, rent roll 9,400 a month, taxes 18,000 a year. After a roof allowance I was at negative 1,200 a month. I checked the roof line three times because I wanted it to be wrong. The agent showed me the kitchen.

Rent rolls also lie by omission. Ask for the actual leases, then ask what the vacancy was last quarter. A building at 95 percent occupied is a different purchase from one at 78. Nobody shows you this sheet at an open house.

I signed a lease in 2019 without walking the block at night. I paid for that for twelve months.

The garbage trucks came at five. A bar emptied at three on weekends. Neither fact was hidden. Both were invisible in listing photos taken at 11am on a Tuesday.

Now I do two walks before any offer. Noon and nine at night. It takes forty minutes and it has killed three deals for me.

I listen for boring things. Delivery trucks. A train that passes twice an hour. A dog that lives outside. You can't hear any of that through a video tour, and a video tour is what most out of town buyers use now.

The same rule works for commercial space. Stand outside the door at the hour your customers arrive. A shop on a street with no parking after six is a different business from the one in the listing.

Photos are a sample. A walk is the data.

#RealEstate #Brooklyn #NYC #Housing #Renting #Apartment #Neighborhood #PropertyInvestment #Markets #Cities #DueDiligence #LocalBusiness #Walkability #Landlord #Leasing

There's a pattern in every listing site I check. The price shown is the current one, not the story.

A place that has sat for seven months and dropped twice looks identical to a fresh listing at the same number. The difference is in the history, and most sites hide it behind a click. Some don't show it at all.

I keep a small spreadsheet of every unit I've looked at in three buildings I know. Asking price, date, and any change. Six months in, four of the nine have cut. One has cut three times and is still 80,000 above where it started.

That history changes the conversation. A seller who has cut twice isn't holding a hard line. A seller who listed last week might be.

I also check days on market. It's often wrong on the big sites because relisting resets it. A new photo set and a new listing ID make a stale unit look new.

The county record doesn't reset. That's why I start there.

#RealEstate #Brooklyn #NYC #Markets #Housing #PropertyInvestment #Investing #Data #DueDiligence #Finance #Economy #Landlord #Rental #Negotiation #Research
---
I pulled the flood map for a building I liked in September. The listing didn't mention water. The map did.

FEMA publishes it free, and the address search takes a minute. Being in a zone doesn't mean the place floods. It means the lender will charge you more and the insurance quote changes the deal. People find that out at the closing table, which is the worst time to learn anything.

For a small building, the number I want first is the flood premium. Not the asking price. A 6,000 dollar a year policy on a 900,000 dollar building is a different asset from the same building outside the zone.

Then I ask about the mechanicals. Boilers and electrical panels in a basement are what water actually destroys, and a basement is where the cheap storage lives.

None of this needs a license. It needs fifteen minutes and a willingness to look at a map that might ruin a nice afternoon.

I've talked two people out of offers with it. One sent me a photo of the boiler room two years later, dry, and said thanks.

Four projects sat open on my desktop on Monday. I shipped one by Friday and archived the other three.

Closing them felt like quitting. It wasn't. Each one had a half built auth flow and a readme promising a demo. Each was costing me about twenty minutes a day in rereading, which is an hour a week spent on nothing.

So I made one rule. A side project gets a ship date or it gets archived. No third option and no someday list. Archived just means a folder and a note about why it stopped.

Two weeks in, the one that survived has eleven users. The other three are gone and I don't miss them. I also deploy twice as often now, which is the only number here I trust.

A solo week isn't about doing more things. It's about fewer open loops. I feel lighter, and lighter turns out to be faster.

A solo week has no meetings, which sounds like six free hours and isn't.

I logged mine for six days. Eleven context switches a day, and most of them were mine. Check the deploy, answer a support email, look at a bug in another repo. Each one cost about forty minutes to get properly back into the code. That's most of the six hours.

The fix wasn't discipline. It was batching. Email at eleven and four. Deploys at two. Everything else waits, and nothing has broken yet.

By Thursday I had a full day of unbroken work for the first time in a month. I shipped a settings page and a bug I'd been avoiding since August. Both were small. Both had been sitting for weeks because they needed an hour I never had in one piece.

Freedom without blocks turns into admin. That's the whole lesson, and it took a stopwatch to see it. Nobody manages my calendar, so I have to, and badly is still better than never.

#AI #BuildInPublic #VibeCoding #tech #SoloBuilder #Productivity #DeepWork #Focus #TimeManagement #Software #Engineering #IndieHacker #Startup #Learning #WorkHabits #Systems

One person can hold about three unfinished things before the week turns into admin.

I tested that this month with a whiteboard. Three columns, three slots, no overflow. Anything new had to replace something already on it. Sounds like a system. It's really a forcing function, because the board doesn't care how interesting the new idea is.

Eleven tabs became four. Two repos became one. My Friday review went from ninety minutes of sorting to eight minutes of reading the board.

I didn't get faster. I got honest about what was actually in flight. Half the stuff I called in progress had not been touched in nine days, and saying that out loud was the useful part.

Three is not a magic number for everyone. It's mine because four is where I start forgetting what I promised somebody. Pick a number, write it down, then count out loud once a week.

I built a dashboard nobody opened because I never told anyone it existed.

Fourteen days after shipping it, the analytics said two visits. Both were me. I had spent nine evenings on charts and zero minutes on one sentence explaining what it was for.

Solo builders don't fail at building. We fail at the part after, because it feels like marketing and marketing feels like a personality I don't have. The alternative is worse. A tool nobody knows about is a hobby with a database.

So now every build ends with three lines. What it does, who it's for, where to click. I paste those into the same two places and send one message to one person who might care. That takes ten minutes and it's the whole launch.

The dashboard got eleven visits the following week. Not viral. Just visible, which is the first thing it needed to be.

The best week I had this quarter shipped the least code.

I deleted nine hundred lines and cut deploy time from fourteen minutes to three. Nothing new went out. No feature, no announcement, no screenshot. On Friday the app looked identical to Monday.

That's the work nobody sees, and solo it's the easiest work to skip. There's no coworker waiting on the cleanup and no manager asking why the build is slow. You just live with it, and the tax shows up as an hour a day.

Deleting code is unglamorous. It also removed three bugs that never got filed, because they lived in a part nobody could read.

I used to measure my week by what shipped. Now I count what got smaller too. One number up, one number down, and the second one is the reason I can keep shipping alone.

I launched a tool to eleven people and called it a launch. Two weeks of work, one post, eleven signups. I refreshed the dashboard like it was a scoreboard. Four of them opened it. One came back on day two. That was the whole launch.

I'd built a checkout flow nobody reached because the first screen asked for an API key. The key was optional. The label didn't say that. So eleven people landed, read a form, and left. I spent the next weekend rewriting one sentence. I'd been blaming marketing. The first screen was the problem. A stranger decides in about nine seconds whether your thing is for them, and they decide using the part you built last.

That screenshot is still taped above my desk. Eleven signups, four opens, one return. It's the cheapest market research I've ever done.

Now I test the first screen with three people before I write any code. Three people is enough to find the wall. You don't need a survey to watch someone hesitate.

I changed the price from nine dollars to nineteen and lost exactly one customer. He emailed to say it was too much. Then he asked if I could keep him on the old plan. I said no. That was a bad call for a different reason than you'd guess. He was the only person who had ever sent feedback without being asked. I traded a source of honest information for ten extra dollars a month.

The rest of the list didn't move. Twelve people stayed, three upgraded, and my monthly revenue went from about a hundred to two hundred. Nothing else changed that week. I'd been scared of a number for eight months while I had maybe twenty users.

Most of the fear in this job is arithmetic you haven't done. I assumed ten percent would leave. It was eight percent.

I don't price on how I feel about the number anymore. I look at what it costs me to keep one account running and work from there. Support time, model calls, the hours I spend answering questions. Nineteen was still under that line.

I should have charged more at the start. Not because the tool was worth it then, but because pricing low attracts the people who need the most help.

Every signup that died, died on the same screen. It was step three, where I asked for a company size. Nobody needed that field. I added it because a form looked unfinished without it. I asked six people one question at the end of each call. Where did you stop? Five of them said step three, and the sixth had never opened the email.

So I deleted the field. Completion went from forty percent to sixty eight percent without a single line of new code. The fix took four minutes. Finding it took two weeks of guessing wrong.

The guessing was the expensive part. I had theories about pricing, about the landing page, about the model being slow. All of that felt plausible because I'd built the thing and knew where the weak parts were. Users don't walk your map. They walk the form.

Now I watch five sessions before I change anything. Not a recording, a screen share with the person talking. It's slower and it's the only thing that has ever told me the truth.

Build the smallest path to the first win, then guard it. Everything else is decoration.

The feature I spent three weekends on got used twice. Both times it was me, testing it. I found that in the logs and sat there for a while. It was a report builder. Drag a metric, pick a date, export a PDF. I thought finance teams would love it. I never asked a finance team. I asked myself what I would want, then built that for nine days straight.

What people actually used was the ugly text box at the top. They typed a question and read the answer. That was the whole product, and the report builder was scaffolding I'd mistaken for a building.

Deleting it was harder than building it. I kept the code behind a flag for a month, in case someone asked. One person did, in month three, and they wanted a CSV.

The lesson cost me nine days and it stuck. Now I ship the text box first and wait for three separate people to ask for the same thing. Three separate requests is a pattern. One request is a person with a specific job.

I still keep a list of those. It has eleven items, two are real.

Most of this job is reading error messages and deciding which one matters. Today I read the same stack trace eleven times before I understood it. Then the fix was two lines. Nobody films that part. The demo is the thirty seconds where the thing works. The other six hours are a cursor and a log file and me saying the same sentence out loud.

The work splits roughly into three pieces. Talking to people who use it, which is maybe an hour. Reading and testing, which is most of the day. Writing code, which is the small piece in the middle. I used to think the ratio would flip once I got better at code. It hasn't.

What changed is the cost of being wrong. I can try four approaches before lunch now. That means the judgment moves to picking which one to keep, and that part doesn't have a shortcut. A model will happily build the wrong thing at ten times the speed.

So I write down what the fix should do before I open the editor. One sentence. If the code doesn't match the sentence, the sentence wins.

That's the whole method. It's boring and it works.
